Title: Rethinking Central Banking
text: Rethinking Central Banking IMF/ECB/FRB High Level Conference 10 October 2010 USA Dr Atiur Rahman Governor, Bangladesh Bank 1. Post-crisis initiatives on rethink/ reforms of central banking have focused on financial stability, particularly on regulations found deficient in preventing and coping with the crisis; including, interalia, risk appraisal and containment; capital adequacy and liquidity; principal-agent relationship issues including executive compensation, cross border coordination in supervision of globally active large financial institutions. The ongoing revisions and refinements in macroprudential regulations and related policy tools will hopefully lead to stronger, more resilient financial institutions and markets and supervision regimes better able to anticipate and withstand shocks from occasional destabilizing events in the real or financial economy. Smaller less advanced economies like Bangladesh have little scope of playing role in the global consultation processes; but with limited size and external exposure of their financial sectors they can opt for slower, more gradual implementation of regulatory changes, in which support and help from more advanced central banks and global forums are of course welcome. 2. The regulatory reform initiatives will hopefully be effective in strengthening resilience of financial institutions and markets in coping with future instabilities; but it is unclear whether enough is being done towards preventing the underlying macro-economic imbalances that cause the instabilities. The recent global financial crisis was rooted in successive decades of cumulating global imbalances originating from spillovers of lax macroeconomic policies in some large economies; the international reserve role of their domestic currencies permitting them to run prolonged spells of external account deficits, causing global liquidity expansion well in excess of growth in real global output of goods and services. The global community of central banks needs to spearhead the necessary preventive initiatives with appropriate reforms in the global monetary order; with effective deterrents against buildup of global imbalances from adverse spillovers of lax, unbalanced domestic policies in the larger economies. The IMF in its current mandate has not been effective or particularly active in preventing buildups of global imbalances from actions of its dominant quota holder members. In the run up to the recent global financial crisis, no time series data on overall trends of global liquidity growth vis-a-vis growth trends in real global 1 output were available in IMF publications, in apparent unconcern about consequences of the global imbalances. 3. For a reformed monetary order to maintain global balance and stability effectively, it will need some mechanism tethering global liquidity expansion with growth rate of real global output. One option will be a reformed IMF mandated as the apex global monetary agency, issuing (or withdrawing) SDR allocations in line with actual or potential expansion (or contraction) in global output; with liquidity issues in national or regional currencies of members needing to be fully backed by SDR allocations. The mechanism will be in likeness of the erstwhile gold standard, with real global output growth substituting for gold. The current basic quota (voting power) allocations in IMF are legacies of past dominance of North America and Europe; these need revision to reflect current realities, with reallocations for smaller developing economies taking into account the size of global population percentage they represent, beside their current minuscule shares in global output. 4. Besides attention to monetary and financial system stability, central banking needs also to promote fuller financial inclusion of all economic activities and all economic sectors, towards supporting global real output growth. Dereliction of traditional central banking orthodoxy in this direction has perpetuated market gaps and market failures in financial services (even in the developed economies), with forgone opportunities and suboptimal global performance in growth of output, income and welfare; slowing down eradication of global poverty. It is opportune time now for the central banking community to redress the neglect of promotional role; effectiveness in this role will aid rather than hinder the stability preserving regulatory role. As the central bank of a low income developing country, Bangladesh Bank has of late been paying increased attention to fuller and deeper financial inclusion, with a view to redressing market failures and unleashing blocked advancement opportunities for the under served/ excluded economic sectors and population segments, promoting more inclusive economic and social growth. The attention to growth promoting potentials of financial inclusion is of course not at the expense of any neglect of usual concerns and market based policy frameworks for monetary and financial stability; the approach is a pragmatic, heterodox blend aiming at optimizing growth while maintaining and bolstering stability. 2

Title: Address in the inaugural session of the APG Typologies Workshop 2010 at Hotel Radisson at Dhaka, 26th October 2010
text: Address by Governor Bangladesh Bank in the inaugural session of the APG Typologies Workshop 2010 at Hotel Radisson at Dhaka, 26th October 2010. Excellencies, todays Chief Guest, the Honorable Prime Minister and the special guests honorable Finance and Law Ministers; Mr. David Shannon, Chief Executive Officer of APG; distinguished guests, delegates and observers; Assalamu Alaikum, and good morning to you all. As the public agency, entrusted by our money laundering prevention and anti terrorism statutes to put in place and maintain surveillance mechanisms to prevent and detect money laundering and terrorism financing activities, we at Bangladesh Bank, the central bank of Bangladesh are very happy that the APG regional AML/CFT Typologies workshop is being held at Dhaka. We have always been keen about exchanging experiences and upgrading skills in keeping our growing financial system and expanding external trade, workers remittance and capital flows free from influences of money launderers and financiers of terrorism. Always keen on responding to the relevant UN conventions and FATF guidelines, Bangladesh has been an APG member from inception, serving in its steering committee for three terms. Bangladesh was the first South Asian country to legislate a Money Laundering Prevention Act, in terms of which Bangladesh Bank put in place uniform KYC (know Your Client) procedures and suspicious transaction /cash transaction reporting procedures in banks and financial institutions. The updated 2009 Act in line with evolving international practices, when a new anti terrorism Act with clauses prohibiting financing of terrorism was also legislated. Following these, insurance companies, capital market entities, and NonProfit/Non-Government Organizations have also been brought under the purview of AML/CFT surveillance and reporting requirements. Training programs on a massive scale have been conducted throughout the country to familiarize the banking and financial institutions staff in the reporting entities about the AML/CFT reporting requirements and procedures. Recently, a cross country road show was organized by Bangladesh Bank in collaboration with banks, to heighten awareness in the general population about issues in preventing and combating money laundering and terrorism financing. Besides building up and maintaining the expanding AML/CFT database, Bangladesh Bank has also been forging contacts and cross border liaisons with counterparts in other jurisdictions, because money laundering and terrorism financing activities typically stretch across state boundaries. A number of Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) have already been concluded with Financial Intelligence Units (FIUs) in other jurisdictions; contacts and correspondences in terms of these MOUs are underway in a number of specific cases. I am confident that the sessions of this typologies workshop will be excellent occasions for participants for exchanging ideas and experiences across countries, deepening their perspectives on vulnerabilities to money laundering/terrorism financing risks and the ways of addressing them. I take this occasion to express our gratitude to the APG and our development partners for their continuing support and assistance in building up our capacities in combating and preventing money laundering and terrorism financing activities. I would like to thank APG for organizing the important regional workshop at Dhaka, and I must recall also that we owe a debt of gratitude to our honorable Prime Minister and two of her senior cabinet colleagues the honorable Finance and Law ministers for gracing the event with their personal presence. This certainly reflects a very high level practical commitment for addressing the issues related to AML/CFT by her government. I wish the workshop the best success and I, of course, wish the delegates from abroad a pleasant stay in Bangladesh, with happy memories to take home in their return journeys. I want to thank all the agencies, both national and international involved in successfully organizing this regional workshop. Thank you all for your patient attention.

Title: ADB Regional Forum: Session on 'Lessons for the Way Forward: Enhancing Economic Resilience, Sustainability and Inclusive Growth'
text: ADB Regional Forum Session on Lessons for the Way Forward: Enhancing Economic Resilience, Sustainability and Inclusive Growth ADB Headquarter Manila, Philippines 04 November 2010 Session II, 15:45-16:35 Dr. Atiur Rahman Governor, Bangladesh Bank Economic resilience: (i) At the individual enterprise level, resilience requires awareness of vulnerability to risks from sudden sharp changes in market trends and business environment, and preparedness of coping with such changes. In the recent global financial crisis many major globally active too big to fail financial institutions were caught unprepared to respond, deepening the fallouts of the crisis. It was only after onset of the crisis that stress testing drills for assessing vulnerabilities and contingency planning for crisis situations are getting greater attention. In general, resilience at the enterprise level is better where mixed bags of a number of business lines are pursued instead of excessive dependence on too few business lines even if these are currently booming ones. Those pursuing baskets of diverse business lines can compensate for crisis led downturn in some of these with upturns and new opportunities in some others. During the global financial crisis, banks in Bangladesh were in a liquidity glut, with swelling workers remittance inflows against slowdown in investment and export-manufacture related imports. Guided by BBs financial inclusion thrust, banks utilized much of this liquidity in expanding lending to under-served sectors including agriculture and SMEs, usefully supporting increase in output, income and internal demand. In the global financial crisis, problems in a small number of overly large globally active too big to fail financial institutions severely tested the resilience of the global financial system. Resilience of financial markets and systems is best safeguarded by preventing excessive concentration of business in a few dominant oligopolistic entities, instead maintaining an environment where multiple entities pursue diverse ranges of business activities without dominant systemic influence on particular business lines or segments. Sectoral regulators and competition authorities have proven negligent in creating and ensuring such environment. It is time now to pay corrective attention in this area. Basel based forums of global experts are bringing up modalities of cross border co-operation in effective collegiate supervision of large globally active financial institutions; it may be well worthwhile to explore options for preventing emergence of oversized too big to fail entities in the first place. (ii) In respect of growth strategies for national economies, resilience in coping with abrupt trend shifts or crises in the global scene hinges importantly on avoiding excessive dependence on any single strategic option (like export-led, commodity based, labor intensive manufacture based or high technology based strategy); a balanced mix of workable strategies is a better safeguard for sustained overall growth, compensating for cyclical or crisis driven downturns in some areas with upturns in others. For Bangladesh, apparels comprising four fifth of the export basket, and the bulk of it going to North American and European markets now beset by demand slowdown, are factors limiting resilience; now being addressed with thrusts into new export products, and new markets. Heavy import dependence for essentials of day to day survival like food weakens resilience, risking crisis in events of global output shortfalls and disruptions in global trade. Maintaining imported buffer stocks in sufficient volume is costly. To mitigate the risks from global shortages and trade disruptions, Bangladesh has focused attention on maintaining adequate domestic production of essential food grains, extending support to growers in their access to needed inputs and agricultural credit. It is now widely perceived that climate change associated with anthropogenic global warming is increasing the frequency of floods, cyclones and other natural disasters; posing survival and livelihood risks for population across vast regions of the globe. Bangladesh is well known for her resilience to natural disasters of floods, cyclones and coastal inundations; building up over the years capacity in the governments disaster management set ups for emergency rescue and subsequent rehabilitation of the affected population groups. The survival and livelihood threats from global warming driven sea level rise are however immense; far beyond means of low income countries like Bangladesh to cope with. Resilience to climate change threat will require coordinated global response, with adoption of environmentally sustainable practices in lifestyles and economic activities. Major part of the costs involved for developing countries in these efforts will need to be borne by developed economies with wealth accumulated from practices that have been degrading the environment since the industrial revolution, causing global warming. Sustainability (i) Appropriate public policies and major investment commitments from public resources are essential in responding to environmental sustainability challenges. Sustainability initiatives in developing countries like Bangladesh will require major resource support from developed economies. Contributions from the internationally active private philanthropies will be useful supplements, particularly in awareness raising and promoting sustainable livelihood practices in broad masses of general population. (ii) Financial sector regulators can adopt policies and market development measures to mitigate the risks and to lower the financing costs of sustainability projects. Public subsidy support including fiscal incentives like tax /duty waivers will enhance viability of the sustainability projects; but credit policies of central banks can also help in easing their access to and costs of borrowing. To this end, Bangladesh Bank is allowing lending institutions access to refinance lines against loans to sustainability projects. Also, in developing financial markets with limited menu of financial services on offer as in Bangladesh, emergence of new financial services like venture capital and private equity for startup sustainability (and other) projects can be usefully supported with appropriate policy steps. Financial sector regulatory authorities in developing economies should adopt sustainable, harmful emission minimizing internal processes and practices in their own establishments and installations; and should require all banks and financial institutions to do so as well. BB has initiated steps in this direction installing some solar power panels for illumination at the head office, and asking banks to install solar power panels in bank branches as a condition of grant of new branch licenses. The logical next step would be to require banks and financial institutions in their turn to insist on environmentally sustainable practices in their client businesses/projects. Inclusive growth (i) Strategy and policy pronouncements of developing economies like Bangladesh can clearly articulate commitment to inclusive economic growth to open up blocked advancement opportunities for the disadvantaged population segments of the society. The longer term Perspective Plan and sixth Five Year Plan of GOB articulate this commitment. Inclusive growth aims at equality of opportunities rather than equality of income. With concern for both quantity and quality of growth, it has the important additional dimension of social empowerment of the disadvantaged population groups in terms of their human development and advancement opportunities. The inclusive growth orientation of development policies of GOB is evidenced in the large social expenditure content (over a third of total) of annual national budgets, with steadily increasing poverty focused expenditure allocations for health, education and social safety net. BBs thrust on fuller, deeper financial inclusion of all population segments and all productive economic sectors is supporting and complementing the GOBs thrust for inclusive growth. BBs financial inclusion initiatives are steering banks and financial institutions into increasing engagement in lending to the under-served/unserved economic sectors and population groups, including micro and SME entrepreneurs, agricultural and other rural and urban farm and non-farm productive activities. Banks and financial institutions are being motivated into deepening and broadening financial inclusion both as their CSR obligation and as new opportunities of viable business in new client bases. Refinance support line from BB is also being made available to lending institutions in transient liquidity needs against lending to the thrust areas in financial inclusion. *****************

Title: Bangladesh 2030: Strategy for Growth
text: Bangladesh 2030: Strategy for Growth Organized by: Dhaka Chamber of Commerce and Industry (DCCI) 07 December 2010; 10:00 am Pan Pacific Sonargaon Hotel Dr. Atiur Rahman Governor, Bangladesh Bank Special Guest Hon. Chief Guest Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, Special Guests Mr. Abul Maal Abdul Muhith, Hon. Minister, Ministry of Finance, Mr. Dilip Barua, Hon. Minister, Ministry of Industry, Mr. Muhammad Faruk Khan, Hon. Minister, Ministry of Commerce, Hon. President of DCCI Mr. Abul Kasem Khan, Mr. Asif Ibrahim, President elect of DCCI, Distinguished Guests, Ladies and Gentlemen- Assalamu Alaikum and a very good morning to you all. I really must begin by heartily congratulating the DCCI for kicking off the quest of a growth vision for Bangladesh over the span of the next twenty years. Such longer term perspectives are powerful antidotes against speculative get-rich-quick short sightedness in business and election cycle based short sightedness in politics, and can indeed greatly aid stability and sustainability of the growth and development processes. Bangladesh government has already drawn up a perspective plan for the next ten years; it is very heartening now to see the business community coming forward in envisioning our growth path over another ten years into the future, up to 2030. This is certainly well crafted strategic move towards developing a synergy towards desirable growth momentum. I, wholeheartedly welcome this public-private partnership in our national thought process on the growth perspective. The governments Perspective Plan 2020 aspires for making Bangladesh a middle income country by 2020, which will require crossing the per capita Gross National Income (GNI) of USD 976. Our recent GNI growth trajectory shows promise that Bangladesh may cross the USD 976 threshold by as early as around 2014, but per capita GNI will need to be sustained at this or higher level for at least four years before formal recognition of transition to a higher income category. Formal graduation of Bangladesh to middle income country status may, therefore, not materialize much earlier than the timeline projected in the Perspective Plan. The DCCI concept paper envisions Bangladesh within 30 largest economies in GDP size in terms of PPP by 2030, from the current position of 48th. This ranking by GDP size is not a very relevant as measure of well being of the population; small population countries like Kuwait, UAE, New Zealand, and Luxembourg behind Bangladesh in ranking by GDP size are affluent while populous Bangladesh is still poverty ridden. The per capita GNI based ranking and grouping into low, middle and high income countries is the widely used clearer measure of how well off individual economies are. Becoming a lower middle income country by 2020 will be no mean achievement, although our ultimate aspiration further into the future would be yet higher, the attainment of prosperity for all our people. For 2030 Bangladesh may consider setting sights at crossing the next threshold to higher middle income bracket, with per capita GNI equivalent to USD 3,946 or higher at current prices. With an estimated 2030 Bangladesh population of 178 million reported in the concept paper, crossing into the higher middle income bracket will require raising our GNI to equivalent of around USD 703 billion at current prices by 2030, from current level of about USD 107 billion. Is this realistically attainable? In my opinion the answer would be a definitive yes, on a number of considerations. Firstly, we can expect our comparative advantage of ample supply of cost competitive young manpower pool to continue over the coming decades, provided that we keep upgrading and updating education and skills of the manpower pool. Secondly, room for substantial productivity enhancement in agriculture, fishery, dairy output is by no means exhausted; anecdotal reports of rural farmers active in developing new breeds of rice capable of withstanding drought, salinity and flooding are heartening examples of adaptive ingenuity responding to climate change threats. Thirdly, as the DCCI concept paper points out, our current GNI estimates leave out an informal economy of substantial size. The informal economy will progressively integrate into the formal reported economy, pacing up growth in GNI over the coming years. Major deficiencies in physical infrastructure are much brooded over as serious growth constraints; we need to remember that these are at the same time major investment and growth opportunities, provided we pursue right policies to crowd in domestic and external financing. Climate change threat is likewise a window of opportunity of breaking into new, promising growth areas in renewable energy generation and in innovating environmentally sustainable processes and practices in broad ranges of other productive activities. The key to success in graduation into higher middle income status for Bangladesh by 2030 will be in unleashing and utilizing the creative energies of our entire population; opening up blocked advancement opportunities for the disadvantaged population segments with inclusive growth policies. Bangladesh Banks recent campaign for broader, deeper financial inclusion supported by intensive employment of IT aims at contributing to the inclusiveness of economic and social growth in the country. You will be happy to know that we have been able to open about ten million new bank accounts for the farmers and extreme poor for transparent disbursement of agricultural subsidy and wages for employment guarantee scheme as part of financial inclusion. This has been greatly enhancing our domestic demand which has helped us cope well with ongoing global financial crisis. As a result, we got very good sovereign ratings from Standard and Poors (S&Ps) and Moodys. Besides maintaining macroeconomic stability, the main role of the government on the path of attaining higher middle income country status by 2030 will be in continuing high fiscal outlays for human development targeted predominantly to the lower income groups for rapid poverty eradication; substantial R&D outlays particularly in environment friendly agriculture, energy generation and manufacturing; continuous skill upgradation of our abundant young manpower pool, and maintaining congenial, competitive policy environment for local and foreign private sector entrepreneurs. We should also continue to take advantage of the opportunities arising out of emerging regional cooperation in many fields, particularly in the areas of infrastructure and other connectives. Bangladesh Bank will be proactive in measures needed for financial sector stability and financial markets development responding to newly emerging needs in the growing economy. In addition, Bangladesh Bank intends to drive swift IT up-gradation in the financial sector, substantially contributing towards achieving digital Bangladesh. In fact BB has already traveled a long way in the path of automation of the banking sector; including setting up of automated clearing house, online CIB, ERP, e-recruitment, e-tendering, mobile phone banking, national payment switch and e-payment gateway. I am sure all these innovative banking initiatives will enhance the pace of e-banking and e-commerce leading to faster pace of inclusive economic growth, which is the ultimate goal of Digital Bangladesh as captured in Vision 2021 strategy. Let me conclude by again thanking DCCI for its initiative in kicking off the consultative process for a perspective plan for up to 2030 for Bangladesh. Let us expect that the government and other major stakeholders will engage extensively and intensively in the consultation processes to firm up a perspective plan, perhaps by the end of 2011. Nobel Laureate poet Tagore thought One can put as much water as is the size of the pot. This is also true for a nation. The larger the dream, the bigger will be the prosperity of the nation. Therefore, let us think big and achieve high. In this month of Victory, let me salute the martyrs of the War of Liberation for whose blood we are a free nation now. Thank you all for your kind attention. ***********

Title: Inauguration of Workshop on New INCOTERMS 2010 and CDCS Certificate Award Ceremony
text: Inauguration of Workshop on New INCOTERMS 2010 and CDCS Certificate Award Ceremony Organized by: International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) - Bangladesh 07 December 2010; 03:30 pm BGMEA Conference Hall Dr. Atiur Rahman Governor, Bangladesh Bank Chief Guest ICC President Mr. Mahbubur Rahman, ICC expert Mr. Vincent Obrien, special guest Mr. Abdus Salam Murshedy, President, BGMEA, Mr. Mamun Rashid, other distinguished guests, participants and members of print media, a very Good Afternoon to you all. I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate all the qualified bankers on their successful completion of the Certified Documentary Credit Specialists (CDCS) examination and would also like to extend my heartfelt thanks to ICC Bangladesh for organizing this important workshop which has attracted many BGMEA members as well. ICC Bangladesh has been working closely with the government of Bangladesh in reforming laws and regulations governing businesses and in liberalizing trade policies towards greater economic integration with global market places. ICC has been promoting foreign trade and investment through reviewing trade policies, conducting business dialogues, seminars and workshops, harmonizing trade laws & regulations, legal reforms and so on. The continuous effort of business leaders and experts from ICC in establishing business stances on trade and investment policy issues as well as on vital technical and sectoral issues including financial services, information technologies, telecommunications, environment, transportation, competition law is really praiseworthy. I believe that exporters and importers of RMGs, pharmaceuticals, leather, and jute goods, transport companies, freight forwarders and other third party service providers will really benefit from the outcome of this workshop. I am happy to learn that Incoterms which was introduced in 1936 specifying responsibilities of buyers and sellers in delivery of goods under sales contracts has come up with its latest version Incoterms 2010 (eighth revision) to be effective from 1 January 2011. The new version has brought about major changes taking into account the spread of customs-free zones, increase in use of electronic communications, concerns about security following 9/11, latest developments in commercial practices, and updates of the earlier rules. I believe Incoterms 2010 is more precise than its older versions in reflecting current trade practices and is more user friendly with expanded list of explanations for users. It is therefore crucial to understand the new Incoterms for accurately negotiating or quoting sales contracts. Finally, I would like to thank the organizers once again for organizing this valuable workshop and hope that the participants will be able to play significant role in promoting international trade and integrating Bangladesh with the global markets. Bangladesh has been picking up both exports and imports at an accelerated proportion in recent months. Bankers have a significant role in maintaining this momentum. This initiative of ICC will certainly enhance the capacity of our bankers; entrepreneurs who have participated in this training workshop, will greatly benefit from this capacity building of the banking and the trading communities. Thank you all. ***************

Title: Emerging Economic Outlook and Policy Challenges for South Asian Economies
text: Third South Asia Economic Summit on Regional Economic Integration, Climate Change and Food Security Agenda for the Decade 2011-2020 Session on: Emerging Economic Outlook and Policy Challenges for South Asian Economies 18 December 2010; 8:30-11:00 AM Hyatt Regency Kathmandu, Nepal Dr. Atiur Rahman Governor, Bangladesh Bank Asia's outstanding performance during the global financial crisis has not only pulled the region out of recession, but also helped steer the world economy toward recovery. South Asia is projected to grow at high rate of 7.8 percent in 2010 and 2011(according to Asian Development Outlook 2010 Update), significantly above 2009 performance of 6.7 percent real GDP growth, underpinned by strong domestic demand. Sustainability of this rapid growth will require policies to boost consumption and investment. South Asia needs to continue efforts to rebalance sources of growth more toward domestic and regional demand, focusing on inclusive growth towards rapid eradication of still pervasive poverty. Bangladesh economy weathered the global financial turmoil well owing to the absence of toxic assets in the domestic financial market and limited, regulated openness to short term external capital flows. Even during the crisis period, Bangladesh maintained firm footing on growth path, with real GDP growth rates of 5.74 percent and 5.83 percent respectively in FY 09 and FY 10. The growth target for FY 11 is 6.7 percent, quite attainable given strong turnaround in exports and healthy growth in agricultural and industrial output. During first quarter of current fiscal, export receipts and import payments increased by 30.0 percent and 37.0 percent respectively. Closer regional cooperation in South Asia will greatly facilitate coping with the challenges of faster economic growth for rapid poverty eradication. A few of the issues of likely benefit from regional cooperation are as follows: 1. Manpower utilization: The emerging outlook for the South Asian economies is bright, given their favorable demographics with large pools of cost competitive young manpower for output activities in labor markets within the region and elsewhere; these pools of young population also comprising robustly growing bases of domestic demand. Challenges facing these economies in eradicating poverty and equipping their manpower pools with knowledge base and skills appropriate for the twenty first century global economy are also enormous. Sustained high fiscal outlays of social sector expenditure will remain necessary for human development and food security, in interventions targeted towards opening up blocked advancement opportunities for the less advantaged. Possible benefits from South Asian regional co-operation in human development and optimal manpower utilization remain largely unexploited. The regions productivity can be higher with freer labor mobility and extensive intraregional outsourcing of intermediate stages in manufacturing and in business processes; optimally exploiting the diversity in comparative advantages across the region, expanding trade and employment in manufacturing and services. Governments in South Asia can be proactive in fostering enabling environment for the private sector in locating and utilizing opportunities of intraregional outsourcing in output activities. 2. South Asian intraregional trade: Intraregional trade remains a minuscule part of overall external trade of the South Asian economies (excepting the landlocked ones), due mainly to low income levels limiting demand within the region. As indicated in the preceding section, export of final outputs from South Asia to the rest of the world can benefit from outsourcing of intermediate processing stages across the region. Apart from this, rising income levels and purchasing power in the faster growing economies in South Asia are imparting them capacity of absorbing more of the final outputs. South Asia needs therefore be proactive in promoting intraregional trade, in both intermediate and finished outputs. Liberalization of intraregional trade in South Asia is proceeding at snails pace, mainly for fear of the adjustment cost burdens within individual economies that regional integration of output and trade activities will entail. Greater gestures of generosity on the part of the larger, faster growing South Asian economies will be important in building support for and confidence in the integration processes in the regions smaller economies. 3. Investment for expanding physical infrastructure and output capacity: It is a major collective policy failing that South Asias substantial savings in the form of foreign exchange reserves enrich financial centers in the West, while real sectors in economies in the region remain starved of investment in much needed physical infrastructure to support output growth. For a substantial thrust in growth and poverty eradication, it is high time now for governments in South Asia to redeploy substantial parts of their foreign exchange reserves into sovereign wealth funds actively investing in infrastructure and other real sector projects in the region. The SAARC initiative of creating a regional investment fund has thus far proven feeble and disappointing, sovereign wealth funds of individual member countries would be much simpler to organize and activate fruitfully. 4. Food security, climate change threat: Food security in South Asia will hinge importantly on promoting output and maintaining openness to intraregional trade in essential food grains. Intensifying co-operation in research and breeding of new higher yielding seed varieties capable of withstanding the climate change challenges should figure prominently in the agenda for food security. Towards maintaining growth trend in food grain output, the region needs to draw up adopt an integrated regional plan for water resources development and utilization, keeping in view the climate change threats and the needs in individual member countries. One simple approach to operationalizing the SAARC Food Bank idea would be to support member countries in maintaining their own buffer stocks of essential food grains, and to commit to openness in intraregional food grains trade at times of pressure in global markets. Eradication of extreme poverty is a sine qua non for food security in terms of affordability; poverty eradication must therefore be a high priority in South Asia. The human development and socioeconomic growth initiatives must be inclusive; focusing on social empowerment of the disadvantaged population segments, opening up advancement opportunities for them. Co-operation and exchange of ideas and experiences in deepening social and financial inclusion merit being on the discussion agenda in regular South Asian regional co-operation platforms. ***************

Title: Address in the launching ceremony of BRAC Bank e-payment gateway
text: Address by Governor BB in the launching ceremony of BRAC Bank e-payment gateway Venue : The Westine Hotel Date : 19 December, 2010 Time : 7.00 p.m. I am glad to be invited to this launching event of BRAC Banks e-commerce payment gate way, pursuant to BB November 2009 instructions opening up e-payment settlements for internet based online purchases and sales of goods and services. It is a major step forward in materializing the governments vision for digital Bangladesh, and in the ongoing drive for deeper, broader financial inclusion. As traffic congestions and gridlocks keep worsening in major urban centers like Dhaka, it is getting increasingly difficult and time consuming for people to physically visit vendor locations to see goods and services on offer and to ascertain fairness of prices asked for. E-commerce is an attractive alternative around this difficulty, with purchasers visiting vendor websites online to see what are on offer at what prices, and to order the chosen goods or services at the best available prices. There are positive externalities for others as well, with increasing online transactions contributing to easing of pressure of vehicular traffic and crowding in high streets. While some banks already have engagement in e-payments for e-commerce transactions in varying degrees, I am told that BRAC Banks new e-commerce payment gateway is also integrating with VISA and MasterCard, which will enable epayment settlements through the BRAC gateway not only by BRAC Bank accountholders but also by clients of other banks holding cards issued by VISA and MasterCard. In addition to payment settlements related to e-commerce, the e-payment gateways of banks are useful for payments and receipts of utility bills, salaries, pensions, and so forth. BRAC bank has substantial engagement in SME financing; I will look forward to its initiatives in getting the SME borrowers individually or collectively to utilize the e-payment gateway extensively for web portal based sales of their products and services to buyers within and outside Bangladesh. BB will be happy to support such initiatives, and will provide appropriate procedural instructions about receipts against sales to buyers abroad. To further facilitate e-commerce and other electronic payment transactions, BB has already taken initiative to put in place a National Payments Switch connecting all e-payment switches (ATM, POS, Mobiles, Internet etc.) in the country, expected to be operational by the end of 2011. I would urge close co-operation and collaboration of banks in Bangladesh in developing cost effective, efficient e-commerce business models and solutions for different market segments; opting for sharing of solutions to the extent possible for cost saving. Co-operation and collaboration will be particularly important in ensuring security and safety in e-commerce transactions. Identity theft and fraudulent transactions are major threats to safeguard against in e-commerce transactions, awareness raising and continual upgrading of security and safety features will be necessary to remain ahead of fraudsters ever busy devising newer ways of breaching into the e-payment gateways and systems. BB will continue to promote and support expansion and upgrading of infrastructure arrangements for e-commerce and other e-payments; and as regulator will continually monitor developments in the operating standards and security standards in line with international best practices. Let me conclude here with congratulations to BRAC bank for this launch of their e-commerce payment gateway, wishing the bank all success in attaining their intended business and promotional goals.

Title: Key note paper on Financial Crises Regulatory Deficiency in Executive Development Programme at BBTA
text: Financial Crises And Regulatory Deficiency By A. K. N. Ahmed During the last few decades many countries of the world have been rocked with financial crises and suffered their consequences. The purpose of this paper is to describe what financial crisis is, its frequency, the efforts of various regulatory agencies to prevent and manage such crisis when they occur, and finally to discuss whether at present enough regulatory mechanisms are on the ground to prevent and manage such crises effectively. Financial crises are admittedly difficult to define and have often no precise beginning or end. A World Bank Staff Report defines them as financial events that eliminate or impair a significant portion of banking systems' capital (Episodes of Systematic and Borderline Financial Crises, World Bank, 1999). Another author has, rather pictorially, described that financial crises are to the financial system what heart attacks are to the cardiovascular system. The organs central to its operation begin to function erratically; in extreme cases they stop functioning entirely. Their convulsion interrupt the circulation to the rest of the body (of the blood or the credit as the case may be) placing other organ system at risk. If the attack is minor and the patient is otherwise in good health, he may stage a full recovery. The attack may then serve mainly as a wake up call for changes in life style like a more sensible diet, more exercise, and more regular visits to the doctor, (in economic terms better balanced monetary and fiscal policies, more vigorous prudential supervision and regulation and more frequent consultation with financial institutions). But a more damaging attack that casts doubt on the subject's recuperative powers may require to be checked into the hospital for angio-plasti or bypass surgery (for currency devaluation and debt restructuring in financial case). The financial crises have two dimensions. One is financial and the other is the panic, which often is the trigger. The first one is the debilitating and the massive shocks to bank's liquidity, payment systems and solvency. Typically there can be a crisis of liquidity and cash flows in which depositors can not withdraw their money and companies can not get the credit they may need to run their operations simply because banks have exhausted their cash reserves. There can also be disruptions in the payment systems in which everyday settlement and clearance of consumer and business transaction ground to a halt, become difficult to unwind, and place those expecting cash at the end of the day in the unfortunate position of being unsecured creditors overnight. There also can be a crisis of solvency if banks are forced to write-off huge losses and equity capital is significantly impaired or lost. Any of these problems in an individual bank does not necessarily constitute crisis; but it takes only a few large failing institutions or a large group of smaller ones (e.g. Thai financial companies, Korean merchant banks) to create systemic crisis. Second is a panic strike - a sudden and dramatic loss of depositors' and investors' confidence is often the precipitating event triggering a financial crisis. It is very difficult to ascertain when and why such panic occurs and spreads all on a sudden. For example, in Equador in 1998 depositor confidence quickly reached crisis proportion when banks could not meet their customers' demands for currency and the Central Bank's reserves were depleted. The crisis was compounded when authorities tried to contain it by declaring a weeklong bank holiday. Argentina also faced a similar melt down in confidence in 2001 and 2002 AD with ugly street riots and public demonstrations by angry depositors swept up in that country's fiscal and currency problems that finally impaired its financial sectors. Similar ugly riots marked the financial crisis in Indonesia leading eventually to the resignation of President Suharto. As stated above: when both the financial and panic dimensions collide, they set off a chain reaction and a country begins to spiral downward. As the panic and loss of confidence in financial sector spreads and persists, it starts having an effect 011 on real economy creating more problems there. Furthermore, in these days of globalisation the; problems in financial sector in one country may also spill over to the other countries as well. Like the SARS disease, financial spin-doctors have not been able to find a sure way to contain it within one country or to reduce the gravity, duration: and impact of such crisis. We will discuss more of it in the later part of this paper. The number of financial crises around the world has risen over the period of last two decades or so, and more sharply in the last ten years. During the 1980s, according to the World Bank count, there were 45 major systemic banking crises in which most or all of the banking system capital has been wiped out. In the 1990s there were 63 major banking crises, most of which were accounted for by crises in emerging economies, the emerging transitional socialist economies. Russia and East European countries. In the 1990s, there were major crises in every corner of the world involving banking system meltdown, major currency devaluation. A Table below lists some of the recent crises in the world indicating estimated GDP loss in consequence. Similar statistics for Bangladesh are not readily available. Nevertheless, one can form some idea of the total loss involved by taking into account the huge volume of non-performing loans of the banking system and the consequent credit crunch, inflation, government deficit financing and the inequality of income. Table Costs of Financial Crisis Country Period Cost in Percent of GDP Argentine 1980 - 82 55 Chile 1981 - 83 41.2 Finland 1991 - 93 8 Norway 1987 - 89 4 Indonesia 1997 - 98 34.5 Japan 1990 - 99 10 Estimate Malaysia 1997 - 98 19.5 Mexico 1995 13.5 Philippines 1991 - 97 3 South Korea 1997 - 98 24.5 Thailand 1997 - 98 34.5 USA (Savings and Loan Crisis) 1981-84 3.2 Source: Crocket (1997) Hawkesby (2000) and World Bank (2000) According to conventional and popular wisdom the financial crises subside in a few years, the government steps in to bail-out the solvent banks and liquidate the failed ones, depositors are offered guarantees and the IMF and the World Bank may give new loans to creditors. But contrary to this belief, many financial crises of the last two decades have lasted four or more years. After 1998 financial crises and currency devaluation it took four years before Russian banks could again issue international bonds. This would have been further delayed if the international price of Russian oil had not have gone up. In countries like Japan and Indonesia the lack of political will results in recurring crises that materialize almost every year. In case of long lasting crisis there is another substantial cost of foregone economic growth that is mostly overlooked by many of us. If the monetised value of this cost is added to the cost that the tax payers are required to pay through budget appropriations coupled the higher rate of interest the debtor country is called upon to pay in its international borrowing, the cost of financial crisis for a country becomes staggering indeed. A question is sometimes asked - why there have been financial crises with more frequency and geographical spread in the recent past? To find an answer to this question we have to go back to the financial history of the world since the end of World War II. From after World War II up to the end of 1960s, the combination of regulations, lack of capital mobility, diverse standards and the limits of technology, created geographic barriers in the global economy and financial markets strictly regulated competition between banks and other financial institutions. Countries like Germany and Japan used their financial systems to directly promote export industries and protect domestic Procedure and distributors. Economies largely operated within national borders and the main form of exchange between nations was the trade of goods and the money needed to finance that trade. Because central banks controlled the money supply, exchange rate, full-blown financial crisis particularly with repercussion on other national markets did not erupt frequently. When problems arose, they were typically limited to a single bank failing as a result of imprudent banking and weak supervision at management level. All of this began to change after the breakdown of Brettonwoods System of fixed exchange rate in 1971 - 72 in consequence of US action to de-link Dollar with gold. Because of this change the developed countries of North America, Europe and Japan adopted a floating rate of exchange and began liberalizing the capital accounts and allowing cross border investments. At the same time they began deregulating their national financial institutions to allow more competition and new forms of financial activities. The 1970s and the 1980s also saw steady growth of private capital flows across borders including growth of international bank credit under the compulsion of the need to recycle the huge petro-dollars arising out of oil boom and the surplus generated by US economy. In the beginning such flow of funds was limited mainly to the industrial world. By the time the Berlin Wall fell in 1989 a new era of financial markets had begun with the loss of national control over interest and exchange rates as well as rapid advances in digital communication gave fresh momentum to the speed of globalisation. The barriers that used to define local, regional and national financial markets began to erode. Emerging markets and trans- national economies from the former Soviet bloc joined almost under duress in the financial liberation efforts and opened up their financial system. Almost without any preparedness they opened their financial markets to free flow of foreign capital typically with the explicit arrangement and nudging of the IMF and the World Bank. Capital flows moved swiftly all over the globe reaching the furthest corners. This change of scene has led to volatile capital flows or so called "hot money" allover the world through banks, financial institutions particularly to emerging markets. This was aided by asset managers in the developed countries from Mutual Funds, Pension Funds, Insurance Companies, traders from investment banks and hedge funds - all allured by expectations of quick profits and by out- maneuvering the unskilled players in poor countries in the game. Behind this game was the implicit understanding that in case of crisis, investors and creditors overseas would be bailed out by IMF. It was almost an atmosphere of "gold rush". There was almost a clarion call to the poor countries by the developed countries to join the spree without making the adequate preparation. There are not too many people; both in developed and poor countries, to advise that poorly functioning financial markets all too quickly can spawn crisis and that the developing countries that lack the safeguards like adequate supervision, transparent accounting and financial reporting standards, crisis resolution machinery, good bankruptcy law and shareholders protection vigilant investors and corporate governance structure should first set their house in order before plunging headlong in globalisation. Even today, poor countries are not told that they should first learn to walk before they can run. From what has been stated above, it will be clear, why frequency of financial crisis is not likely to be less in the near future. Having described and discussed the nature of financial crises and why such crises will likely to be more and not less in the future we will now see whether and how such crisis can be predicted and successfully handled. Predicting financial crisis, unlike weather forecast, is like predicting earthquakes. Scientists are pretty certain in identifying areas and zones where earthquakes will strike but are still unable to predict precisely the range of time when this is going to happen. Subject to this limitation financial crisis can also be anticipated and handled by certain actions at micro and macro level. According to experts who have monitored such crisis in the recent past feel that vulnerability of a financial system to crisis may be assessed by watching the following indicators at micro level:  Value destruction of the private sector. When companies can not make enough money to cover the cost of money they borrowed a crisis may be brewing. The red flag starts flashing when the return on invested capital for most companies in the country is less than their weighted average cost of capital.  Interest Coverage Ratio. If the ratio between the cash flow and the interest payments falls below two, that company may be heading for a liquidity crisis.  Profitability of banks. An annual systematic return on assets of less than one percent for retail banks and / or annual net interest margin less than two percent are often signs of a crisis.  Rapid growth of loan portfolio. When bank's loan portfolio grows faster than 20 percent per year for more than two years, many of these loans turn out to be bad.  Shrinking deposits or rapidly rising deposits. When depositors start pulling their money out of local banks, particularly over two consecutive years, it is frequently a sign of imminent crisis.  Non performing Loans. III advised lending eventually ends up bloating non-performing loans portfolio when the volume of non-performing loans exceed five percent of the total bank loans, a red warning light should be flashing.  Interbank money market borrowing rates. When a retail bank is chronically short of funds, borrowing in the interbank market goes up. This is a sign that the borrowing bank does not know money management and the market in essence is voting no confidence on the over borrowing bank.  Term structure of foreign bank loans. Many companies in the emerging markets borrow from foreign banks in Dollars, Euros or Yen to take advantage of lower rates. Banks for their part typically lend in short maturities. This creates both currency and maturity mismatch for the borrowers. When twenty five percent of the foreign lending in particular, has terms less than one year, a warning light should be flashing since these loans are highly vulnerable to withdrawal in the event of a crisis.  Asset Price Bubble. Bubbles in the price of real estate, stock prices, luxury goods, cars, clothing and even the price of meals in restaurants and upscale haircuts are again warning signals for so called "irrational exuberance". As a rule of thumb, asset prices growth for any asset class more than twenty percent annually for more than a couple of years are signs of bubble building.  Rapid growth or collapse of international money and capital flows. When foreign investors, through equities, bonds and bank loans pour money into a country that is neither productive nor well managed, a credit binge results that may lead to a crisis. Such inflows can set the condition for a crisis. The rule of thumb is that when such inflow grows three times faster than the growth of real economy, it is a signal that conditions may be ripe for a crisis. It needs to be pointed out that judgment and common sense must be used while coming to a decision, by using the above warning signals. It is also equally important that data are accurate, timely and complete. Furthermore, one must not lose sight of the fact that global economy operates by rules that require that companies exact returns on investments equal to or be greater than their opportunity cost. If through the warning signals it is apprehended that a crisis is looming large in the horizon, what steps at micro management level should be taken by individual financial institutions? Here are the Ten Commandments of crisis management framed by an internationally known consulting firm, which has been called upon for managing more than one financial crisis. These commandments are the product of their distilled experience in this field. They are: 1. Accept the seriousness of the situation. 2. Deliver results, not plans. 3. Be prepared for a tough multi-year effort. 4. Explore all possible options in parallel. 5. Commit one hundred percent. 6. Be decisive; do not delay tough decisions. 7. Exercise top down leadership. 8. Remove key people who do not get in, or who do not move. 9. Tolerate no scared crows. 10.Stay focused until the job is done. Even if the above warning signals are heeded, impending financial crisis is anticipated and full-blown efforts, with the help of the ten commandments are made, the story does not end there and the victory is not always assured. For we should not forget that the above warning signals are merely symptoms which emerge out of the developments in the fields of fiscal and monetary policies at macro level, not only of the home government, but of other governments and international agencies, as well as international market forces which operate independent of any government. It is to these forces we will address our attention and discuss the important role played by them in originating and managing - sometimes successfully, and sometimes unsuccessfully -series of financial crises witnessed by us in the last two decades or so. To manage, and perhaps to reduce the impact and frequency of financial crisis the measures at macro level called for are transparency, standards, supervision and regulation and appropriate exchange rate policy. Market discipline is the first line of defense against financial crisis and imbalances. If market participants bear the consequences of their action they will have an incentive not to lend to governments with unsustainable macro economic and financial policies, and to banks and other institutions attempting to finance speculative or other financially non-viable projects. But lenders will have an incentive to work this way only if they are adequately informed of the activities and intentions of others whom they lend. This is where the importance of transparency lies. The information about the workings of the government and other players in the financial sector should not only be adequate, up to date, but also transparent and accessible to all who meet them anytime. Even if this arrangement is made, a lacuna still remains. The information in the real world is unfortunately, asymmetric where borrowers know more than the lender, giving rise to adverse selection and moral hazard. This is more particularly so in developing countries. Removal of the asymmetry to enhance transparency requires more monitoring, more screening and more application of technologies, which are costly. Individual banks and financial institutions, particularly in developing countries, either singly or collectively are not capable or willing to bear the cost of collecting, collating and interpreting such vast mass of information, This gap can only be filled by regulatory and supervisory agencies both multi-national and national. The transparency related initiatives currently underway are almost too numerous to narrate. It will almost take a book to describe them in detail and to evaluate them. We will therefore try to describe here, very broadly and very briefly, some international initiatives in this field leaving aside the national agencies doing the work in the same field. The International Accounting Standards Board has a broad comprehensive array of accounting standards for use by the private sector. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) has further elaborated these standards of relevance to bank supervision. The Federation of Accountants Standard has similarly formulated standard for auditing practices and audit statements. The United Nations Commission on International Trade has developed some standards for cross border insolvency procedure. The organization for Economic Development and Co- operation (DECD) has issued principles of corporate governance and the Basel Committee has circulated a report for how such principles can be applied to financial firms. The lMF has its own Data Dissemination Standard for information disclosures for the governments of countries participating in international capital market and codes of good practice for fiscal, monetary and financial policies. The International Association of Insurance Supervision has issued a compendium of principles, standards, and guidance papers and established a task force charged with developing a methodology for monitoring implementation. The International Organization of Securities Commission has developed and endorsed a set of principles of securities-regulation and disclosure standard for cross-border offerings and international issues. Such plethora of organizations and their web of directives, rules and regulations appear almost mind boggling to practitioners of banking, who, at times, feel like evoking T. S. Elliot and say "Where is the wisdom we have lost in information? Where is the knowledge we have lost in information? Besides, these standards and directives at times work at cross-purposes and lack either effectiveness or representation. As a result they are not owned by many developing countries that had no place on the tables of policy planners and who decided on these rules. Strengthening the supervision and regulation of financial system are no doubt key initiatives in the area of crisis prevention. But doing so only on the basis of resource allocation and the basis of assets price may not be suitable for all countries. Such an approach may undermine even the successful government-led model of development of some countries by removing some elements, but not putting something else in their place. Then again, where the banking system is weak and relatively inefficient these standards can not be put to use for producing the intended result. Out of this experience, G7 counties, after Mexican crisis, have come to realize that there has to be an international banking standard, defining minimally acceptable practices for the banking system in the emerging countries and advanced industrial countries. In consequence of this feeling three initiatives have been taken in the recent past. First, the Basel Committee has issued its core principles for effective supervision of banks. Second, IMF published its framework for financial stability, specifying measures that countries should take to strengthen the supervision and regulation of their financial institutions. Third, The IMF and the World Bank established their joint financial sector assessment program to identify financial vulnerability. These initiatives lent important impetus to the efforts of developing countries to strengthen prudential supervision. But in the process they also revealed why international principle framework and oversight' can fail to deliver the desired effects. As such they shed light on the limitations of the entire standard-centered agenda. Banks were given two years reprieve for having t(to met Basel Il' s core-capital ratio when the new ratio came into effect. While many countries complied with the requirements on paper, some of them could not avert financial crisis. Turkey, for example, while meeting the core principles of capital adequacy, prudent standards, accounting rules could not avert a devastating banking crisis in 2000 and 2001 AD. The application of Basel standards also revealed that there is no guarantee that the supervisory authorities, still ultimately accountable to the governments of the day, could effectively discharge their duties and responsibilities. A stark example of this is Japan where regulatory agencies including Bank of Japan, even though highly efficient and incorruptible, had to take account of the nods of the government before taking a major decision. Then again, there is also the problem of reglatory arbitrage. Capital as the operating cost is something that the banks have an incentive to minimize. This leads them to shift many items that are subject to high capital weights off balance sheet via securitisation and the use of derivative instruments while keeping on published balance sheet, others that are subject to low capital ratios. There are also number of unintended consequences of Basel directives. For example, low weightage for capital for short-term loans, low weightage of loans to OECD countries discriminate against other countries. Finally, Basel rules, which have no teeth also, do not question the adequacy of the approach that relies not on the rules, but on the will of the countries to enforce them and the regulators who will enforce them at national level. Basel standards also do not highlight the necessity of properly monitoring of a system, which performs well. Recent experiences indicate that successful projects, high dividends and capital gains, all need to be carefully monitored, because true quality of accomplishments is what counts. Being cautious in good times helps in mitigating the intensity of financial melt down. In other words, there has to be regulatory awakening even during booms, so that the busts are not unnecessarily tampered with. This and some other similar niceties of regulations have, for quite understandable reasons, been overlooked by Basel Standards. Nevertheless, they demonstrate the advisability of giving more leverage to national regulators in devising their regulatory system consistent with their local needs, instead of putting them in a straight jacket. Finally, there is a dilemma for enforcing policy standards on developing countries. On the one hand regulatory incentives: to loans to countries with high credit ratings all strong economies adopted in the name of strengthening international financial system create additional pressure on developing countries to take hard steps to secure investment grade ratings. On the other hand, the same measures, in the intervening period keep them away from the access to the world capital market on account of their poor ratings resulting in their slow growth and hindering their process of development. Basel standards or other international agencies have not yet come up with credible proposal to overcome this predicament. In the recent past, the toothless Basel standards are being influenced through the surveillance mechanism of the IMF, which has the necessary leverage over the borrowing countries through the enforcement of conditionality to ensure compliance. Both the World Bank and IMF are becoming closely involved not only with the recent work of Basel Committee in designing standards but also with monitoring compliance. This is most evident in the role being played by them in the development of the revised assessment methodology for qualifying the compliance and making cross-country comparison. A recent report which has evaluated the Fund's expanding role in this respect was however skeptical about the Fund's capability to participate in the development standards in areas such as accounting, auditing and corporate governance which have an ultimate link with bank supervision. It was felt that it may be difficult for IMF and the World Bank combining their roles as policy advisors with that of impartial assessor and that such a role should continue to be left to professional rating agencies in the market who have no finger in the pie. Coming now to exchange stability, recent experience has clearly demonstrated that there is a close link between exchange rate management and financial crisis prevention. One of the most prominent difference between the recent period and the century of international financial history that preceded it, is the frequency of currency crisis. In fact, the hallmark of the recent crises has been that there is twin crisis where disruptions in banking system and foreign exchange market often occur together at the cost of major output loss and making the impact of such crisis more severe on the country concerned. It is again the area where the so-called "Washington Consensus" propelled by the major economic powers of the world play a significant, and most of the time, determined role through the instrumentality of the IMF and the World Bank. Under the pressure of G7 countries including USA and their agents IMF and World Bank, all emerging countries are expected to maintain a stable monetary and fiscal policy and stable exchange rate to facilitate free entry and exit of foreign capital without adequate consideration for economic growth and equitable distribution of output produced. If a country, by following this policy, is faced with currency and banking crisis, it is asked to go for pro-forma massive devaluation of currency and restrictive monetary policy leading to shrinkage of demand, loss of employment, loss of output and increase of sufferings of the people, while foreign investors, more often than not, are bailed out by International Monetary Fund without even a so-called "haircut". We can wrap up the above discussion by saying that crisis prevention measures will never be perfect. Even the most developed countries like Sweden, Denmark and USA could not avoid financial crisis. There are world class institutions in USA like Enron, World Com, Merrill Lynch, Morgan Stanley, Citibank caught red handed in being engaged in "creative accounting" falsification of records, skimming money by top executives and cheating shareholders despite presence of sound accounting rules, most prudent supervisory regulations over the workings of all agents of the financial market and above all having a very transparent and effective democratic representative government. We must not also forget the fact that crony capitalism and greed are embedded in the working of free market system. These vices, like terrorism, can not be wiped out altogether. We must also remember that information will not be perfect since in he final analysis borrowers' and lenders' minds are unfathomable. As a result, adverse selection, moral hazard and market mobility will always be with us. When these factors take the form of sudden changes in the market conditions, they, like hurricanes, may sometimes damage the innocent bystanders and threaten the stability of the system. The key to some success in this field seems to be to focus on standards that bear on institutions and capacity building and leave some leverage for national governments who should be able to move independently of IMF and World Bank guidance all the time. As long as they are developing institutions ,conducive to transparency, right of creditors to demand information and evolution of prudential regulation with pace and sequence they think right and workable they should be left alone to do their job. In other words, we should give up the concept of "one size fits all" solution. Reserve Bank of India was right when it observed that ''National supervisors may be given discretion to implement the new accord in a phased manner by banks which are not internationally active and are predominantly engaged in traditional banking". (Comments of Reserve Bank of India on the Basel Accord 2000) All in all, regulations are always restrictive in nature curbing absolute freedom of everyone. But they are aimed at making the field level so that all players are enabled to play the game with a game plan and within the confines of a set of transparent rules. But there are many countries that have no level playing field. In some cases they have no playing field at all. In their cases the field has to be created and made level, players trained so that a fair game can be played. In the context of financial sector this will often mean, setting up banks, creating a banking system, developing a capital market, increasing banking habits of people, mobilizing their savings, imparting liquidity, training the players, creating nexus between savings investment and safety in the financial markets. While embarking on this task, the countries concerned have to be helped by developed countries at least to keep themselves afloat by keeping their noses above water with timely help in case of need. All these highlight the importance of allowing the developing countries much greater freedom and leeway to accomplish the mission as long as they are moving in that direction with common goal and purpose. In short, reforms, to be durable, have to be brought by homegrown reformers and not by pressure. Before concluding here are some proposals, not by way of firm propositions, but in the form of suggestions for attention of emerging countries who have embarked on fmancial crisis management. They are:  Financial crisis can not be prevented; nor can it be managed with reasonable success by dictated solutions coming from developed countries and international lending agencies that very often have inadequate perception of the problems in this field experienced by emerging countries. Such management, for its success, needs willing accommodation of their diverse problems .  Neither Basel Accord nor the IMF is now equipped to manage international financial crisis because they do not represent interest of a large number of developing countries at various stages of economic development. The llv1F in particular does not have sufficient clout either with its mentors or the developing countries. It is now under attack from all quarters. The critics on the left charge IMF of not being sensitive to developing countries and being busy with bailing out foreign creditors and not bailing in countries in distress at the time of financial crisis. Critics on the right spearheaded by US Congress appointed Meltzer Commission report charge IMF with squandering its resources in salvaging hopeless cases. In such a climate, it is highly unlikely; for IMF to receive additional funds from its members where voting rights are on "one Dollar one vote". It is also doubtful whether IMF with its existing administrative skill and mindset would really be capable of handling multiple financial crises at a time. Even a mighty superpower like USA is finding it difficult to fight multiple wars in different countries at a time.  A new international organization with adequate representation of developing countries is necessary for managing financial crises. Developing countries should have a big part in the deliberations for setting up such an institution. Per Jacobson, Managing Director IMF, was very perceptive when in 1959 he said, "Programs can only succeed if there is the will in the countries themselves". Unfortunately for developing countries, IMF now has moved away from this perception.  The right time for such deliberations and arriving at a consensus is now, and not when crisis is raging all over the world again.  Such consensus is however, unlikely without a prior similar consensus at political level on how the new-world order will be governed with USA as the sole superpower. Given the present situation and observing the conduct of USA the prospect of such a consensus seems to be very dim.  The developing countries should therefore have to brace themselves to handle financial crises on their own either singly or collectively by making regional groupings with other countries that have similar financial problems and convergence of economic interests. Such co-operation may take the form of arranging swapping of their currencies, creating regional hedge funds for exchange stabilization or by maintaining capital control measures as, for example, done by Malaysia, China, Chile and India.  Each developing country should also seek and find home grown remedies for its own peculiar banking and financial problems without depending too much on the aid and attendant advice of the external lending agencies.  Central banks of developing countries should not seek to pursue an independent monetary policy, and price and exchange stability, only to facilitate free entry and exit of foreign funds; for the following reasons. First, they are mostly not capable of formulating and enforcing such policies. Second, such policy, divorced from growth-oriented economic policy, is neither feasible nor desirable. Third, foreign capital in any case does not flow to a country lacking in security and strong institutional framework. They should instead tune their policy to the needs of the country's overall development policy.  Monetary policy, as mentioned above, should be followed with cleareyed understanding that this may result in slowdown of foreign aid in the short run. This has to be accepted as a price for steady growth in an environment of financial stability. Furthermore, this price may not be too high if in the intervening time, clear tangible steps are taken to eventually integrate their economies with the rest of the world when they are ready by acquiring new skills and techniques and strengthening their institutional set up.  Developing countries should give up their dependency syndrome but not their ongoing dialogues with IMF and the World Bank. After all, for poor countries they are the principal source so far for financial aid on soft terms and technical advice in many areas.  It should be clearly understood that no country now could hide from globalization. It should also be remembered that globalization induces growth but growth has not been globalized. Also globalization does not mean imposing homogenous solution in a pluralistic world. It means nourishing local insights and re- employing communicable ideas in the new geographies around the world. The more human beings belong to their own time, the more they belong to all times and place. Today's best global managers know the truth and nourish, as some one said "each blade of grass" .  Finally, for Bangladesh and other countries similarly situated, they should pay heed to the following advice of Nobel laureate economist Joseph Stigliz "Small countries are like rowboats on a wild and open sea. Although we may not be able to predict when the boat will be capsized, the chances of eventually being broadsided by a larger wave are significant no matter how well the boat is steered. Though to be sure bad steering probably increases the chances of disaster and a leaky boat makes it inevitable on a relatively calm day." (Speech at Manila in 1997 on Globalisation) To this should be further added that one should not venture to the sea with a leaky boat and without knowing at all how to steer.

Title: Tenth Nurul Matin memorial lecture on ethics in banking
text: Tenth Nurul Matin memorial lecture on ethics in banking by Professor Dr. Mohammad Farashuddin, former President and VC, East West University and former Governor, BB: Comments of BB Governor Dr Atiur Rahman Venue : Dhaka Sheraton Hotel Date : 03 January 2011 Time : 06.30 p.m. . The Nurul Matin memorial lecture series on ethics in banking is the lone major national level event to raise issues and to spawn thoughts and deliberations on ethical standards and norms in the financial services industry in Bangladesh.
