Investment Climate in Bangladesh  Macroeconomic fundamentals The economy of Bangladesh experienced more than a decade of resilient economic growth within a range of 5.3 to 6.7 % per annum. Furthermore, GDP growth has witnessed a higher trend compared to its peers (Hungary, Angola, Bolivia, Nigeria, Vietnam, India and Sri Lanka) in the last 5 years. Per capita GDP has increased from USD 843 in 2010 to USD 1190 in 2014. Gross domestic investment reached to 26.8% of GDP in FY 2104 from 23.1% in FY 2001. Robust export performance led to current account surplus of 1.9% of GDP in FY 2013. Bangladesh secured 8th position among the remittance recipient countries in 2013. Consequently, foreign exchange reserve reached at remarkably high level, i.e., USD 21.4 billion even after ACU payment as on 9 September, 2014, which is equivalent to more than six months of import payments. This level of cushion indeed provides a buffer against the external shocks. National poverty rate declined substantially from 56.6% in 1991-92 to 31.5% in 2010, which may have gone down to less than 25% by now. Driven by better revenue collection fiscal balance remains steady coupled with less reliance on borrowing from the banking sector. Government debt as a percentage of GDP has declined from 49.7% in FY 2004 to 39.7% in FY 2013 (estimated) implying stronger absorbing capacity to cope with domestic shocks. Global Competitiveness Index (GCI) ranked Bangladesh in the position of 110 in FY 14 compared to the position of 118 in FY 13 showing a gain of 8 ranks in just a year alone. Inflows of FDI increased to 1730.63 million USD in FY13, a rise of 44.84 percent from the preceding fiscal year. In sum, it is arguable that macroeconomic fundamentals of Bangladesh economy are highly in favour of foreign investment. The domestice investment has also been showing upturn lately following acute political instability during most part of last year. The domestic private credit grew at 11.75 percent last month compared to 10.25 percent the month before. According to trade confidence Index of HSBC released yesterday Bangladesh gains 38 points (i.e. scoring 141) over the last 6 months which is the second highest among 23 countries surveyed globally. This is due to growing demand for our apparels from western buyers and their perception of 1 phenomenal improvement in safety and other compliances of our factories. We outpaced UAE, Indonesia, China, India, Turkey, Vietnam and many such strong competitors. More than 40 percent of the respondents said that Bangladesh's biggest trading partner Europe offers best opportunity for business growth over next 6 months. Overall 70 percent of respondents said outlook for trade value will improve over the next 6 months. Over 80 percent have confidence in our currency management said this will have favourable impact of business growth over this month.  Policy supports The government has introduced various financial and non-financial incentives like tax exemptions for power generation, import duty exemptions for export processing industries, tax holiday schemes for undertaking investment in priority sectors and less developed areas, zero duty rates for the import of capital machineries and spare parts for 100 percent export oriented industries, almost no restriction on the entry and exit mode, and reduction of bureaucratic and systematic hassles in getting faster approvals of foreign products. Financial sector of Bangladesh has also been liberalized to make it investment friendly. By 1990s restriction on interest rates has withdrawn, while the current account became convertible during 90s followed by opening of capital account for non-residents along with a free-floating exchange rate regime. With the existing risk focused Basel II capital adequacy regime, Bangladesh is on the way of adopting Basel III version with revised capital norms and new liquidity coverage and leverage criteria. Together with all these incentives followed by a low labor cost structure with a liberalized financial regime, Bangladesh has been emerged as an attractive destination for FDI in the South Asian region. Recently the World Bank has ranked Bangladesh ahead of India, China and Vietnam in protecting investors' interest. Bangladesh is maintaining a most welcoming regime for FDI and FPI inflows. Up to 100 percent foreign ownership is freely permissible for FDIs in the industrial sector; FPI inflows are freely permitted in the local equity and bond markets. Post-tax profit or dividends earned by non-residents on that FDIs and FPIs are freely repatriable abroad including royalty/technical fee; disinvestment proceeds (at market value for listed companies and sale proceeds of foreign equity in unlisted companies at fair value based assets, income and earnings trend instead solely at net asset value) along with capital gains are like-wise also freely repatriable. Capital gains are free of income tax. Import tariff waivers/concessions on capital goods and serviced industrial zones are available for foreign and local investors. Recent new facilitation include enhancement of family remittance ceiling for expatriates to 75% of their salaries. Taka term loan from the domestic market and working capital financing in foreign currency from parent company are also now permissible for foreign owned/controlled companies engaged in manufacturing or services output activities in Bangladesh. No prior permission is required for investment in industrial sector (except for four reserve sectors including defense equipment, reserve forestry, atomic energy, currency printing and minting). Investment proposals need only to be registered with the Board of Investment (BOI). Public Private Partnership (PPP) in infrastructure investments offers a new window of opportunity for foreign investors. Fully serviced existing Export Processing Zones (EPZs), and Special Economic Zones (SEZs) are being expanded and developed for export-manufacturing with duty free import of inputs. The capital market is open for foreign portfolio investment (FPI) by individual and institutional investors. The Foreign Private Investment (Promotion and Protection) Act, 1980 and a number of bilateral intergovernmental agreements protect foreign investments fully, with assurance of no expropriation or nationalization without fair compensation. External trade has been liberalized in line with WTO rules, and Taka is fully convertible for current external transactions. Furthermore, the country has large young workforce. Exports of Bangladesh enjoy tariff-free access to many advanced and emerging economies including EU, Canada, China, and India. Global players like Samsung, Honda, Telenor, Nestle, Danone, Lever Brothers, etc. have already set up operations in Bangladesh. Competitive wages and low entry barriers for exports provide competitive edge in areas such as manufacture of textiles, ceramics, white goods, pharmaceuticals; physical infrastructure and software and IT enabled services. Payment and settlement system of the country has been digitized to provide prompt and hassle-free financial transactions for the foreign investors. Among the new initiatives, Bangladesh Automated Clearing House (BACH) and Bangladesh Electronic Funds Transfer Network (BEFTN) have been set up to modernize the 2 payment system of the country. Moreover, National Payment Switch (NPS) has also been established in order to facilitate transactions of different banks from a single platform. Potential Areas for foreign investment Major opportunities for foreign investors in Bangladesh exist in the infrastructure sector, including gas and electricity generation, roads, highways and bridges, hotels and other tourism facilities, tertiary health care hospitals, developing land port, seaport, airport facilities LNG storage terminals and other physical infrastructure, manufacturing of solar PV panels, light engineering including fabrication of automobile parts, pharmaceuticals, ceramics, garment and textile, leather and leather goods, service exports, tourism, hotels, and tertiary care hospitals. Software and IT enabled services are yet another new promising area for foreign investors in Bangladesh. Manufacturing for Bangladeshs own large domestic market with a sizeable middle class population segment would also be attractive for the international entrepreneurs. As the Chairman of Foreign Loan Scrutiny Committee of BOI and also Governor of Bangladesh Bank, I would like to reassure the foreign investors with our highest level of commitment to facilitate prompt decisions in collaboration with other ministries and agencies including BOI and NBR. in approving foreign private loans and addressing and resolving any related issue promptly as and when it arises. Let me conclude here urging you to take advantage of the ample investment opportunities on offer in the dynamically growing Bangladesh economy, in sustained, stable spell of six plus percent annual average real GDP growth for over a decade now. 3

Title: Speech at an ICC International Conference on Global Economic Recovery: Asian Perspective
text: ICC International Conference on Global Economic Recovery: Asian Perspective Talking Points of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Plenary Session: Global Economic Recovery: Contemporary Reality Date : October 26, 2014 Time : 9.30 am Venue : Pan Pacific Sonargaon Hotel, Dhaka His Excellency Dr. Abdulmoshen Al-Medeij, honorable Deputy Prime Minister of Kuwait, honorable Minister of External Affairs of Sri Lanka H.E. Prof. G.L. Peiris, honorable Minister of Industries and Commerce of Sri Lanka H.E. Mr. Rishad Bathiudeen, honorable Minister for Commerce of Myanmar, H.E. Mr. U Win Myint, honorable Minister of Commerce and Supplies of Nepal H.E. Mr. Sunil Bahadur Thapa, honorable Minister of Economic Affairs of Bhutan H.E. Mr. Lyonpo Norbu Wangchuk, honorable Minister for Commerce of Bangladesh H.E. Mr. Tofail Ahmed, ICC Bangladesh President Mr. Mahbubur Rahman, distinguished ICC officials from different corners of the world, business delegates from Bhutan, Germany, Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Kuwait, Malaysia, Myanmar, Nepal, Netherlands, Qatar, The Philippines, Sri Lanka, UAE, and Vietnam, representatives of Bangladeshi business community, other invited guests, ladies and gentlemen a very good morning to you all. It's my immense pleasure to be one of your panelists in this important plenary session. The global economy is still to recover fully from the fallouts of the global financial crisis of 20082009 originating far away geographically from Asia; banks in the Asia Pacific region did not indulge in sub-prime lending or the other lax, dubious practices that triggered the crisis in financial institutions and markets in North America and Europe. Fallouts of the crisis reach our shores pretty fast however, through trade and financial channels in the integrated global economy. In the trade channel, demand weakness in North America and Europe caused by chains of insolvencies and wide-scale job losses sharply weakened exports from the manufacturing hubs in our region. Intraregional exports declined nearly as fast, these mainly being primary and intermediate inputs consigned to the regional manufacturing hubs for onward export of final output to the North American and European markets. Tourist destinations in our region faced declining tourist arrival; migrant workers from the region faced pay cuts and job losses in host markets in recession, affecting remittance inflows to their dependents at home. In the financial channel, our region faced substantial net withdrawal of financial investments from the North American and European economies in crisis, availability of fresh inflows also narrowed sharply. Investments of the huge foreign exchange reserves and sovereign wealth funds of our region in markets in North America and Europe incurred substantial losses in bond defaults, collapsed values of equity and complex derivative assets, and exchange rate risks. These financial channel impacts triggered stock price slump and liquidity crunch in markets in our region, particularly in economies facing heavy withdrawals of foreign financial investments. These adversities roughly mirror those in the North American and European economies where the global crisis originated, but the distresses by way of corporate and personal insolvencies in our region were less severe, partly because of timely and appropriate intervention by fiscal and monetary authorities, but perhaps mainly because of much lower levels of indebtedness and higher reliance on equity and savings ingrained in the general cultural attitude of our region. We would be well advised to preserve this positive cultural trait while charting the future paths for our real and financial economies. Different countries in Asia have been impacted by the global financial crisis in varying degrees, depending on the structures and extents of external openness of their economies. Bangladesh was impacted relatively lightly because of her limited, regulated openness, particularly to short term capital flows. The financial sector in 1 Bangladesh remained free of toxic assets and contagion from the external turmoil, and liquidity conditions remain normal. The government and Bangladesh Bank adopted fiscal and monetary measures underpinning domestic demand and maintaining easy credit conditions, like other countries in the region. Domestic output activities remained well supported by inclusive financing of agriculture and SMEs promoted by BB. Consequent to these efforts, annual average real GDP growth in Bangladesh has remained on sustained stable six plus percent growth trend for well over a decade now, total GDP more than doubled with stable single digit CPI inflation, stable exchange rate, current account surplus, growing foreign exchange reserve, rating agencies S & P and Moody's providing stable rating with positive outlook and budget deficits below four percent of GDP. Consequently, favorable social development indices in particularly consistently falling poverty rates have been the hall marks of our successfully coping strategy with global financial crisis. The conventional short term business cycle focused monetary and financial policy approaches are failing to address the longer term needs of inclusivity and environmental sustainability in growth pursuits. As the BB Governor and a member of the advisory council of the UNEP's "Inquiry into the Design of a Sustainable Financial System" I remain well focused on sustainable financing and impart a deliberate directional bias in financing flows away from speculative and sustainability harming uses towards inclusive financing of green output initiatives. Such initiatives as demonstrated in Bangladesh, can be crucial in making the economy sustainable and enabling faster poverty reduction in our region. There are several areas where Asian regional cooperation can usefully strengthen and supplement the individual country responses to the ongoing global growth slowdown, current and possible future recurrence of global or regional financial crises. Firstly, Asias intraregional exports can and need to grow faster, not just in primary or intermediate inputs but also in finished consumer and capital goods; to reduce dependence on North American and European markets where demand recovery to the earlier debt fuelled high levels will take time as corporate and household deleveraging continues. Secondly, the governments and central banks in the Asia region may foster accelerated development of regional bond markets to channel regional savings into real sector investments within the region rather than investing the savings in opaque, complex financial assets of dubious quality in the western financial markets. The BRICS led just launched Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) initiative is a very welcome development in this respect. The swap arrangements between regional central banks for mutual support at times of pressure have lots of room for expansion, these arrangements are likely to be useful for individual countries in coping with adverse impacts from unwinding of quantitative easing and other unconventional monetary easing adopted by Western advanced economies in overcoming recessionary trends. Thirdly, Asian regional dialogues may urge the more affluent emerging economies to broaden their windows of concessional lending to governments of lower income economies, to help protect their debt sustainability. Asian regional intergovernmental dialogues need to discuss positive and negative externalities of domestic policies of the larger economies, to minimize the negative spillovers and to strengthen the benign ones. Fourthly, in dialogues in UN, IMF, WB and other global forums, countries in Asia region can present a unified front favoring a new global financial architecture that ensures global financial and economic stability by tethering global financial growth in some suitable mechanism to the trend of growth in real global output; with effective grasp on global liquidity growth to inhibit speculative bubbles and roller coaster swings in markets. 2 Finally, countries in Asia region can and need to work together in carrying further forward their significant attainments in promoting inclusive financing for equitable socioeconomic progress, extending the cooperation efforts also in accelerating well coordinated shifts to environmentally sustainable green output practices, lifestyles and financing approaches, as collective regional response to looming global climate change and environmental degradation threats. To conclude, Asias current levels of endowments in natural resources, human resources. In particular our demographic dividends and speedy adoption of information technology by our youths and vast aggregate stock of financial assets in the form of foreign exchange reserves clearly bestows on Asia the responsibility of taking up role as the key driver of global growth over the coming decades. To maintain a congenial environment for enduring trends in equitable and environmentally sustainable growth, cooperation among the countries of Asia in this role will need importantly to be at multiple levels, including between the governments, public sector institutions, business communities, civil society organizations and so forth. From this perspective, I wholeheartedly welcome this meeting of minds made possible by this high level international conference of ICC. Good luck to the organizers and thank you very much for your patient hearing. 3

Title: Speech at the inaugural session of a 3-day Intensive Training Program on "Developing an Efficient IS Audit System for Effective Management of IT Risks including Cyber Crimes, Failures & Vulnerabilities"
text: 3-day Intensive Training Program on "Developing an Efficient IS Audit System for Effective Management of IT Risks including Cyber Crimes, Failures & Vulnerabilities" Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank at the inaugural session Date : October 29, 2014 Time : 9.30 am Venue : Gulshan-1, Dhaka Mr. MH Rahman, Chairman of the INTIMATE, distinguished resource persons, guests, organizers and my colleagues from Bangladesh Bank who will be participating this 3-day long intensive training program: a very good morning to you all. Bangladesh Bank, being the monetary authority of the country, is at the forefront of governments firm commitment to be digitized. Our vision of Digital Bangladesh Bank in line with the Governments vision of Digital Bangladesh, have enabled us to be the pioneer institution in the countrys information technological development drive during the last five years through digitization and optimization of financial processes. Indeed, Bangladesh Bank has taken the lead position in encouraging and implementing IT based technologies in overall banking sector. The implementation of Bangladesh Automated Cheque Processing System (BACPS), Bangladesh Electronic Fund Transfer Network (BEFTN), Enterprise Resources Planning (ERP), CIB online facilities, Mobile Banking Service, establishment of the Data Warehouse facilities, adoption of core banking software are worth mentioning. Establishment of National Payment Switch (NPS) has proved a Big Bang for the whole payment systems. Bangladesh Bank has achieved a historic milestone in trade and business arena, departing conventional banking with the introduction of e-commerce; a giant stride towards digital Bangladesh. These are only a few examples of how fast the Bangladesh Bank is progressing in the process of digitization of its activities. In addition, it is also taking other banks and government agencies on board to ensure speedy, credible, userfriendly financial services to all. Indeed, consumerization of IT services is taking place at a high speed. Technology is no longer a game changer rather it has become a driving force for businesses. Although data and transaction security is of paramount importance in this era of rapidly expanding commercial and government computer networks and the emerging electronic economy, especially in the banking sector, the inherent challenges of the security issues have become a top priority. We must not forget that the IT risk issues like viruses, hackers, natural disasters, operational errors, fraudulent activities and other cyber crimes etc. may accompany with the benefits of these technologies. So our responsibilities will not end in only adopting the IT based technology, we need to ensure the adoption of safety measures as well. Therefore, sufficient safeguarding systems must be in place to make proactive analysis of the consequences and countermeasures to security breaches in relation to risks; formulate policies and create a carefully planned implementation strategy for integrating security measures into all aspects of our banking network. All these are extremely important in this era of digitization, e-Commerce, e-Governance and online transactions. As the technological advancements make financial services available to mass people, so any kind of mishap may create devastating effect on the total system. In this context, I am sure this 3-day long intensive training on the Cyber Security and IT Risk Management must enable the central bankers to be analytically insightful in understanding IT system monitoring and risk based auditing encountering IT related risks and minimizing the residual risk at most; and hence to shield the financial stability from toxicities of IT risks including cyber crimes, failures and vulnerabilities. Ladies and gentlemen, let me now declare the opening of the 3-day long intensive training program. I do wish the great success of this program and expect my colleagues to be enriched with optimal exploitation of the knowledge delivered by the distinguished resource persons. Thank you all for your patient hearing.

Title: Talking Points in the session of UNESCAP regional meeting on financing graduation gaps of Asia-Pacific LDCs
text: Resource Utilization Capacity Building for Bridging Graduation Gaps of LDCs to Middle Income Status Talking Points of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank as a discussant in the session of UNESCAP regional meeting on financing graduation gaps of Asia-Pacific LDCs Date : October 29, 2014 Time : 4.00 pm Venue : Pan Pacific Sonargaon Hotel, Dhaka  Bangladesh economys growth dynamism yielding sustained six plus percent annual average real GDP growth for well over a decade now with only modest levels of ODA and FDI infusion evidence substantial resource utilization capability rather than lack of it. Besides upholding its competitiveness in global apparels and textiles trade and diversifying into construction and manufacturing including in such modern sectors as pharmaceuticals, glass and ceramics, consumer durables, electronics, light engineering and so forth; Bangladeshs private sector has also made deep inroads into such services as tertiary education, tertiary healthcare, hotels and tourism, transportation. Several public sector segments also have likewise demonstrated similar resource utilization capacity, evidenced by social sector progress in areas of poverty reduction, healthcare, nutrition, education, rural infrastructure, disaster recovery management and so forth, reflected inter alia in attainment of a number of MDGs well ahead of timeline.  This superficially comforting picture is not the whole story however; there are trends signaling worrisome weakness in resource utilization capacity, particularly in the public sector. Annual ADP allocations routinely remain under spent; for quite some years now, actual fiscal deficits have tended to remain well below four percent of GDP against announced budgetary announcements of around five percent. Project implementation typically remains plagued with time and cost overruns; implementation lags in donor supported projects have swelled cumulative unspent donor aid in pipeline to several times their annual commitments. Utilization of PPP allocations have progressed at less than snails pace. Arguably, enhancing resource utilization capacity alone could largely close Bangladeshs graduation gap out of the LDC labeling, without requiring much more in additional resources. The delays in resource utilization in development projects persist not due to lack of procedural guidance but rather despite plethora of implementation guidelines and elaborate monitoring arrangements involving line ministries and others including the Planning Ministrys IMED. The problem may perhaps be in adherence to these arrangements more in form than in substance, with project directors hamstrung by various interfering influences. Lengthy resolution process of procurement related disputes is another familiar major source of implementation delays in Bangladesh.  Emulating the implementation approaches in success stories in Bangladeshs social sector projects may be the best way forward in improving project implementation capacities in the lagging sectors. Empowerment of project implementation authorities with free hand in decision making in their clearly delineated areas of responsibilities and accountabilities needs to be ensured, besides availing of the technical and managerial skills upgrading opportunities on offer from UNHRLL's Technology Bank for LDCs. The UNESCAP may help in project implementation capacity strengthening in member LDCs also by way of disseminating and promoting adoption of demonstrated best practice examples of project implementation in various sectors in various member countries. In fact, World Bank Group has already initiated this approach and started utilizing the services of best practice managers within the Group. Multi-lateral organizations like UNESCAP may also have a look into this experimentation and derive appropriate lessons for themselves. The same can be recommended for gainfully utilizing the country level best practice examples.

Title: Speech at the 5th HSBC Export Excellence Awards
text: 5th HSBC Export Excellence Awards Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : October 31, 2014 Time : 6.15 am Venue : Radisson Blue Water Garden Hotel, Dhaka His Excellency tonight's chief guest Mr. Abul Maal Abdul Muhith, honorable Finance Minister of Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, HSBC Bangladesh CEO Mr. Francois De Maricourt, distinguished Awardees, Editors of The Daily Star, Prothom Alo, Representative from Bangladesh Brand Forum and invited guests, Assalamu Alaikum and a very good evening to you all. Its an immense pleasure for me to attend this august HSBC Export Excellence Awards ceremony for the 5th time. Ladies and gentlemen, our economy, underpinned by strong external sector gains, has sustained a more than decade long spell of sixplus percent annual average real GDP growth amid all external turbulences including the last global financial crisis. Over the past several years our exporters have successfully affirmed a milestone for Bangladesh in the global trade map. The latest FY 201314 has experienced an 11.69% annual percentage growth, despite lacking of local primary inputs. Our people overwhelming support our marketbased open trade and investment policy. Recently, in a survey by Pew Research Institute found out 91% of survey Bangladesh supports this strategy of ours. We are next to Vietnam 95%, 8% higher than India & 18% higher than Pakistan. This has been made possible become of our unique post rent policy subsidy we give. The competitive efficiency of our apparel exports have outlasted the MFA phasing out and continued flourishing in the postMFA quota free WTO regime. Its optimistic that along with apparels, the export basket has been diversifying substantially with rising export of other manufacturing goods like shoes and leather products, ceramics, pharmaceuticals, light Page 1 of 2 engineering products including refrigerators and household appliances, horticultural products, processed foods, fisheries, handicrafts, marine vessels, IT enabled services, and so forth. Our shipbuilding and light engineering goods manufacturers have already in the global export market. As you know Bangladesh Bank (BB) has been facilitating the export sectors in all aspects it can ranging from Export Development Fund (EDF) to "Bangladesh Bank Disaster Relief and Social Responsibility Fund". Moreover, an MOU has been signed between BB and JICA for one billion Yen for rehabilitation RMG industries. Side by side, Bangladesh Bank is playing its due role by remaining constantly vigilant about the day to day movement in Takadollar exchange rates. HSBC has been a tested partner in our heroic journey of becoming the second largest apparel exporter of the world. In the last decade 9% of Bangladesh's total export has been channel through HSBC. This is the only foreign bank which is present in all the 8 EPZ facilitating almost 35% of the export volumes glowing out of them. HSBC's RMG customers contribute 20% to the total apparel exports of the country of which 45% is routed through HSBC. In addition, HSBC has provided financial support for the future generation of 1000 megawatts which represents about 10% of country's total electric generation capacity. HSBC has helped exports from Bangladesh ship products to 120 countries across the globe in 2013 through its global network. HSBC has been instrumental in providing foreign survey financing (over 1 billion USD currently) in Bangladesh with funds sourced from overseas creating significant financial cost savings for the industrial community. Indeed, this global bank has become truly local. I, therefore, heartily congratulate HSBC for this award initiative. These awards will be a milestone to inspire our exporters to expand their business horizons internationally, and will help them adopt international best practice standards. Finally, I urge the manufacturers to impart with BB's allout effort of ingraining environmentally congenial business ethos embedding ecofriendly business standards. I am confident, HSBC too will remain committed to our green financing journey. Congratulations again to all the winners of HSBC Export Excellence Award. Thank you all for your patient hearing.
