Title: Speech at a National Seminar on Banking "Future Vision"
text: National Seminar on Banking "Future Vision" organized by Association of Bankers, Bangladesh Limited (ABB) Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : November 01, 2014 Time : 9.00 am Venue : Radisson Blue Water Garden Hotel, Dhaka Mr. President and VicePresident of the Association of Bankers, Bangladesh Limited (ABB), Chairman of BAB Mr. Nazrul Islam Majumder, Deputy Governor, Bangladesh Bank Mr. S.K. Sur Chowdhury, Mr. Jan Vasko, Managing Director, Risk Solution Pte. Ltd, Singapore, distinguished panel discussants, reverent moderators, CEOs & ExCEOs of different Banks, Chairmen & former Chairmen of different Banks, fellow bankers and all other participants: a very good morning to you all. Its my great privilege to be the Chief Guest in this first ever national seminar held by ABB focusing on the future vision of banking in Bangladesh. I have been encouraging ABB for taking such professional initiatives for quite some years. I am pleased to see this finally happening. Also I am overwhelmed by seeing, so many bankers and exbankers together here. I am looking forward to seeing a similar international banking conference in the coming days. I am glad to see both real and virtual banking issues will be discussed today. Ladies and gentlemen, in this era of rapidly changing global financial environment, people's demand and society's needs are changing at a faster pace. Technological breakthrough also changes everything from customer relationships to business models. As elsewhere, banking in Bangladesh faces a multitude of challenges on the way forward, inter alia including adjusting to rapid technological changes in the ways banking services are delivered, risk management and stability challenges posed by increasing financial globalization, and challenges of harnessing creative energies of all population segments reaching out with environmentally responsible inclusive financing. There are ample sources of guidance on evolving regulatory discipline and best practice standards in shaping the future path for banking, but usefulness of all these depends crucially on the underpinnings of ethically driven high quality corporate governance involving the boards and senior managements. Lapses and slippages in ethical standards in bank boards and senior managements had much to do with causing the last global financial crisis, just as in recent local episodes of banking scams and loan fraudulences. As senior management the ABB members are fiduciaries safeguarding interests of depositors and other creditors; I would expect and urge the ABB seminar participants today to bear this especially in mind while envisioning their way forward in socially and environmentally responsible banking in Bangladesh over the years to come. Distinguished audience, let me now recount a brief anecdote of banking, with accompanied challenges, and my views on reshaping future path of banking in Bangladesh. 1. Paradigm shift in banking ethos: The banking sector in Bangladesh has grown severalfold since independence in 1971, in tandem with the uninterrupted spell of steady, stable growth of the countrys economy over the last two decades. Beginning as almost wholly stateowned sector making directed loans at prescribed interest rates, our banking sector has undergone successive rounds of major structural and regulatory reforms; transforming it to a vibrant private sector led market based banking system, largely shaking off the legacy of heavy default culture from the years of directed lending regime. A major part of the cost of default had to be borne by both the state and entrepreneurs not to speak of customers at large. But thanks to swiping reforms in the financial sector, Bangladesh economy has been continuing sustained spell of sixplus percent real annual average GDP growth for more than a decade now with the latest score of 6.12 percent in FY14. Steady and incessant drive of inclusive growth is causing poverty to recede fast; GNI per capita has risen to USD 1190 in FY14, with a continual uptrend. Bangladesh has impressive bank account access with low gender and income gaps relative to other South Asian countries. The share in the population above 15 years with a deposit account expanded from 26.7% to 41.3% over the last five years (end 2009end 2013). In comparison the average share of the population above 15 years holding an account in 2011 was 33% in South Asian countries, 23.7% in low income countries and 28.4% in lower middle income countries. The participation of bottom 40% population (income) in access to finance is also higher in Bangladesh (35%) than that of India (27%), Pakistan (4%) and South Asian nations (26%). Banking sector's assets in Bangladesh has also grown faster than any other South Asian nations. Londonbased research firm Business Monitor International (2014) found that total banking assets in Bangladesh witnessed a 19.1 percent compound average growth in the past five years followed by 18 percent in Sri Lanka, 17.2 percent in Pakistan and 16.7 percent in India. Banking assets as a share of GDP is second highest in Bangladesh (80%) after India (85%) but much higher than Pakistan (50%) and Sri Lanka (50%). If you add asset held by mobile financial services (20 million) and low end 14 million 10 taka accounts, Bangladesh may as well come out as number one. BB has steered this transformation by continually promoting market development in a broadly stable monetary and inflation environment. Recognizing early on that the conventional short term business cycle focused monetary and financial policy approaches are failing to address globally the longer term needs of inclusivity and environmental sustainability, mandated by its charter to support output and employment growth besides protecting monetary and financial stability, BB stepped in with initiatives of imparting a deliberate directional bias in financing flows away from speculative and sustainability harming uses towards IT enabled inclusive financing of green output initiatives. For that to happen, BB was successful in enthusing socially responsible motivational ethos amongst the captains of the industry. 1.1 Inclusive sustainable financing The motivational thrust of ingraining a socially responsible financing ethos continuing since 2008 has sensitized and activated our financial sector in reaching out to the underserved and excluded poorer population segments with the financial services they need. BBled events like the financial inclusion roadshows have drawn banks and financial institutions into closer contact with their existing and potential new client bases in the poorer communities. This transformation of the mindset of our bankers was led by not only corporate social responsibility by also motivation to capture business at the lower segment of the customer base. There is as yet no comprehensive impact evaluation of these initiatives in Bangladesh, but anecdotal evidences indicate that policy support for SME financing and development of mobile phone based financial services delivered through hundreds of thousands of local area agents are creating around four hundred thousand new employments every year. Green financing initiatives are likewise spawning new jobs in thousands, in manufacture/assembly, installation and maintenance of solar PV home systems and irrigation systems, energy saving lamps, bio gas units and so forth. Inclusive financing has upheld real sector output and employment growth momentum while also at the same time enhancing financial stability, reducing credit and liquidity risk exposures of lenders by diversifying and broadening their asset and deposit bases. BB guidance in this respect will soon extend further towards differential loan pricing and perhaps also differential equity margin according to environmental risk grading; entailing lower financing costs of borrowing proposals with low environmental risk grading and encouraging risk mitigating modifications in the higher risk rated proposals. The multifaceted financial inclusion initiatives of Bangladesh Bank are enhancing the intermediate target of reducing financial inequality with an ultimate objective of slimming income inequality down with job creation among the unserved and underserved population segments steadying the inclusive growth trajectory. Bangladeshs sustained spell of steady real GDP growth, and her pioneering promotion of socially responsible inclusive, green financing is attracting widespread attention and interest of other countries and supranationals like the UN agencies, IMF and WB. Its my immense pleasure to recall in front of you that recently, Bangladesh Bank was awarded 'the Alliance for Financial Inclusion (AFI) Policy Award' for its contribution in substantial expansion of Mobile Financial Services (MFS) in Bangladesh. Indeed, this credit goes to you all. The recently held Global Green Growth Forum (3GF) in Copenhagen also recognized Bangladesh's pioneering broadbased green banking initiatives. 1.2 Rapid digitization in banking sector A countrywide massive modernization of the financial sector IT infrastructure including fully automated online settlement of paper based and electronic fund transfers, online credit information and supervisory reporting etc. have spawned exponential growth of mobile phone banking, vastly benefitting the underserved poor. The rapidly digitized banking enabled ultrapacing mobile financial services will encourage the women more to participate in the financial services narrowing the gender disparity down since it may not even require their physical presence in the financial institutions to receive financial services. BB is active in spearheading initiatives of putting in place and upgrading countrywide connectivity backbone for the interbank settlements infrastructure; individual banks will need to be correspondingly proactive in installing and upgrading their own IT platforms in line with rapidly growing and evolving needs. With the progress already achieved in online interbank settlements and in mobile telephony, banks can and should now move fast in expanding mobile phone/smart card based banking services reaching out to new depositor and borrower customers in rural and floating urban populations. The imminent wideadvent of digital transaction by the virtue of quantum drive in paperless ebanking entails IT related various risks like viruses, hackers, natural disasters, operational errors, fraudulent activities and other threats from cyber crimes; so, the service providers should have the pragmatic understanding of IT system monitoring and risk based auditing to encounter IT related intrusion minimizing the residual risk at most to insulate the financial transaction from IT vulnerabilities since a single mishap may create devastating effect on the entire financial system. You will be glad to know that to strengthen the supervisory capacities of its officials BB has already embarked on intensive training courses on the Cyber Security and IT Risk Management to shield the financial stability from toxicities of IT risks including cyber crimes, failures and vulnerabilities. 2. Challenges and the path ahead for Bangladeshs financial sector: Apart from the aforementioned glimpses of the financial sector's strengths, the unfinished agenda on the yettodo list is also pretty long, with challenges demanding wholehearted commitment and engagement of sustained corrective efforts. 2.1 Corporate governance and regulatory discipline Lending resources of banks continue being channeled largely to well off borrowers, often with insufficient diversification and inappropriate assetliability maturity mismatches. Corporate governance weaknesses linger in many banks, allowing dominant equity holders to manipulate credit access, credit appraisal and internal control processes to their own advantage. Boards and senior managements fixated mainly on quick short term gains tend to get tempted towards speculative playing up of market volatility, heightening destabilization risks harmful for longer term institutional soundness and viability. Myopic vision and focus on immediate gains deprives bank itself of future earning opportunities from cultivating new customer bases in large population segments of small means (the so called bottom of the pyramid), besides failing to fulfill an important corporate social responsibility obligation of combating inequity and poverty in the society they profit from. The first step in overcoming these deficiencies and weaknesses and gearing up for attaining excellence in banking will be of properly orienting the institutional goals and objectives, shifting focus away from quick high gains from potentially destabilizing speculative activities towards prospects of stable longer term earning income streams from financing productive and socially responsible economic activities, including those of micro and small enterprises of the poor. BBs guidance circulars on Corporate Social Responsibility and financial inclusion drives are intended to steer our banking sector out of this weakness. Pursuit of excellence in corporate governance will follow next; requiring adherence to proper credit appraisal, risk management and internal control processes in letter and spirit, free of vested interest influences of dominant director groups or colluding senior management functionaries. BB expects the banks to adopt and adhere to higher risk management, corporate governance and risk management standards than the minimum regulatory requirement. Excellence in banking services will require quick attention to and remedy of customer grievances. As you all know, BB has accorded high priority to consumer interest protection concerns in banking services. Banks will need to accord the same high priority to this in their own strategic plans, putting in place processes and access channels like help desks; and above all, sensitizing bank personnel to respond properly and swiftly to customer grievance concerns. 2.2 Assetliability maturity mismatch and long term financing sources In our financial system, access of businesses and households to medium and longer term financing is inadequate. Let alone long gestation large infrastructure projects, even modest projects like hospitals and hotels needing financing of ten years or longer tenor usually have to make do with five to seven year tenors at most, leaving themselves exposed to cash flow difficulties going forward. Outstanding industrial term loans are mostly medium rather than long term. Long term housing finance needs of households are likewise insufficiently met, much of the outstanding housing loans being medium rather than long term. Eventual cash flow difficulties of businesses and households force to use financing of shorter than needed tenors create overdues and asset quality impairments in the books of lenders. The paucity of longer term financing arises from paucity of longer term savings. The entire aggregate of equity, reserves and subordinated debt stocks of banks is barely enough to cover the long term funding gap. Redressing the longer term funding gap will require policy and market reforms to bring in new long term savings and to create alternative liquidity augmenting mechanism at the long term end. Life insurers and pension/provident funds carrying long term liabilities are the main sources of long term funds, as they need long term assets to match the liabilities. Life insurance penetration remains very thin in Bangladesh; deepening life insurance penetration comes up therefore as an item in action agenda for augmenting long term savings. Pension/provident fund schemes in the public sector are mostly unfunded and run on pay as you go basis, in the small organized private sector such schemes are not in very widespread use, and none exists at all for the broader population including professionals and selfemployed others. Widening of provident/pension fund coverage comes up hence as another item in action agenda for augmenting long term savings. The only fiscal liabilities involved in defined contribution pension/provident fund schemes are firstly the income tax waiver on such savings, and secondly in running a pension/provident fund regulators office. It is high time for Bangladesh to go for earliest possible introduction of defined contribution pension/provident fund schemes for the general adult population. The broad demand base of pension/provident funds, life insurers, merchant banks and other institutional investors needed for debt issuance and loan securitization to thrive hasnt developed yet in Bangladesh, and capital market intermediaries lack familiarity with their various roles as issue managers, underwriters, trustees, market makers etc involved in primary securitization and secondary trading. Prospective debt securities issuers also find the steps in issue process costlier in fees and expenses than for bank borrowings. The action agenda for enhancing longer term funding availability need therefore promotion of loan securitization by concerted BBBSEC initiative of streamlining the issue processes and paring down the issue costs. Access to long term housing finance will be hugely facilitated by activation of market in mortgage backed securities; the government owned HBFC can conveniently be utilized for this purpose; mandating it to assume roles of underwriter and market maker in issuance and trading of securities backed by mortgage loans extended by other primary lenders, instead of its present role as a primary mortgage lender itself. 2.3 Debt restructuring and resolution Absence of a well functioning mechanism for debt restructuring and resolution comes next as a major shortcoming, leaving distressed businesses starved of financing needed for recovery and tying up lending resources in irrecoverable overdues. Banks and NBFIs in Bangladesh are barred by law from fresh lending to defaulting borrowers regardless of circumstances. BBs guidelines for loan rescheduling permit waivers from interest dues but none from the principal. Court supervised settlements in the alternative dispute resolution route under the Money Loan Courts Act can be of some use with downsized claims on principal, but this route remain very little used. Bankruptcy court processes of debt resolution through the insolvency route by court appointed administrators likewise also remain virtually unused. Availability of private equity and other hybrid bridge financing options that could help out debt distressed businesses is as yet insignificant and rudimentary in the local markets. The market failure in helping distressed businesses recover entails significant loss to the economy, not only in lost output and employment in the stricken businesses, but also in competitiveness erosion of other businesses that face higher cost of borrowing from lenders burdened with overdue from the debt distressed businesses in limbo. Redressing the shortcomings and their negative consequences outlined above will require careful rethinking and revision of current legal and regulatory provisions on handling of debt defaults, in light of practices in neighboring countries and elsewhere, to enable prompt resolution of debt distress of troubled businesses that have realistic possibility of turnaround and recovery; and prompt dissolution of the others through effective use of the insolvency route under the Bankruptcy Act. The judiciary may also think of allowing a separate bench at the High Court just for finance related disputes. Financing options available to businesses also need widening, with policy steps promoting private equity and other debtequity hybrid financing transactions by intermediaries at the capital marketfinancial market interface. A good start in this respect could be the restructuring of the government financed small Equity and Entrepreneurship Fund (EEF) for startups in a few specific sectors into a broader hybrid financing platform to support needed restructuring of ongoing businesses in all sectors, enlarging the fund with both increase in governments contribution and induction of private sector investment and management participation. Even foreign financing from multilateral organizations like IFC can be welcomed in this equity fund. 2.4 Financial globalization Besides the major shortcomings enumerated in the preceding few paragraphs, limited diversity of available risk management products is another significant concern, particularly following transition to market based flexible Taka interest and exchange rates. Apart from plain vanilla forward exchange rate covers and swap transactions, more complex derivative transactions like options, credit default swaps etc. are as yet largely absent in the local markets. Cautiousness in widening external openness of the economy is largely the reason why the needs and responding products have remained slower to arise in the local markets; and BB permits banks and their clients to access external markets on occasional needs of such products. However, this market deficiency is also indicative of slow pace of adoption of a proactive forward looking risk management culture in financial intermediaries, urgency of which will heighten as the economys openness widen further. BB has accorded high priority to addressing this deficiency by steps of phasing in Basel II and III risk based capital adequacy and forward looking liquidity management disciplines in banks and financial institutions; alongside prescribing guidelines laying down requisite minimum standards managing the various risks along lines of international best practices. At the same time, steps for firmly instilling a risk based financial sector supervision culture in BB have also been prioritized. BB is well aware that even though the Basel III is yet to be implemented in full pace, Basel IV is on the way to emerge requiring banks to maintain higher capital, liquidity and disclosure requirements for cushioning systemic risk buffer. BB is looking forward to steadily increasing openness and integration of our financial markets with the global financial system, for widening cost effective access to investment resources from the global savings pool. Hastening adoption of international best practice standards in corporate governance, risk management, internal controls and financial disclosures will facilitate strengthening of correspondent relationships with reputable banks abroad. Increasing external openness will bring in heightened exposure to volatility in global financial markets; risk management capacities in banks will therefore need to be upgraded and bolstered continually. Correspondent banks in advanced markets abroad are often useful sources of knowhow about new service and risk management approaches. Thank you all for your patient hearing.

Title: Speech on 'Commerce and Mobile Banking: Emerging Career Development Opportunities'
text: ECommerce and Mobile Banking: Emerging Career Development Opportunities November 01,2014 Presented by Shitangshu Kumar Sur Chowdhury Deputy Governor Bangladesh Bank Organized by United International University, UIU Dhanmondi Road 8A campus, Dhaka Introduction As a developing country, Bangladesh is striving to create an environment for rapid dissemination of ICT at all stratum of the society. In this respect, government of Bangladesh has shown keen interest in this sector. ICT is regarded as a thrust sector and the present government has pledged to build a digital Bangladesh within 2021. While the developed countries of the world have exploited the potential of science and technology in national development, developing countries have fallen behind. Resource constraint, inadequate ICT capacity, and lack of appreciation of the power of ICT may be cited as the reasons. The revolutionary development in the field of ICT has opened up new opportunities for developing countries to move forward in the path of progress by rationally exploiting its potential. In view of that, Bangladesh has been aspiring to achieve economic development through the application of Science as well as Information and Communication Technology (ICT). The government of Bangladesh has taken steps in this connection. The Government focuses on the reduction of poverty by applying ICT, increase in efficiency, productivity, transparency, access to information by the citizens. Citizens at large will be empowered with necessary information for efficiency performing their tasks. In recent years, the growing number of private universities has provided new and broader opportunities for aspiring IT professionals to pursue relevant education. The students pursuing IT education in the country have shown tremendous potential over the years  winning international programming contests, developing effective antivirus software and many other such achievements are very common for Bangladeshi IT students. Use of ICT in Bangladesh Bank When the overall ICT sector is moving forward Bangladesh Bank has also taken initiatives to present it as an IT based organization. You know that Bangladesh Bank has introduced fully automated clearing and settlement of interbank paper based instruments and electronic fund transfers which is hugely facilitating branch based, and mobile phone/smart card based banking. Bangladesh Bank has implemented Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) which is facilitating electronic accounting, budgeting, maintaining data warehouse, various sorts of data management. This electronic infrastructure of the central bank is encouraging commercial banks and other financial institutions to adopt electronic data management processes. Our online Credit Information Bureau (CIB) has been a great saver of time and cost of doing businesses for all banks. Entrepreneurs are already getting the benefits of this facility. During the last four years, Bangladesh Bank has been able to position itself as a progressive organization for technological advancement taking initiatives towards digitization of the Bank. These initiatives are working as milestones for materializing the government's dream of 'Digital Bangladesh'. It can be hoped that the pace of Bangladesh Bank's journey towards ICT will continue to speed up in the future. To build itself modern as well as IT based organization Bangladesh Bank also took initiatives to open modern payment systems in the country. E-commerce and Mobile Financial Services (MFS) can take as two examples. E-commerce E-commerce (Electronic Commerce) is the buying and selling of products and services by businesses and consumers over the Internet. e-commerce allows consumers to electronically exchange goods and services with no barriers of time or distance. Recently, e-commerce has become popular in the Bangladesh. It creates new market, reduces transaction costs and saves time. Bangladesh Bank issued the circular (Nov, 2009) declares some specific e-commerce related operations which can be offered by the scheduled commercial banks of Bangladesh which are stated below - 1. Online payment of utility bills from client's accounts to recipients accounts. 2. Transfer of money from one account of a client to his another account in the same bank. 3. Payment/collection of money from/to buyers bank account to sellers bank account for buy/sale of products under e-commerce system. 4. Transaction via internet using credit card in local currency. Besides these Customers of same bank can transfer money to each others account up to 5.00 lacs maintaining Money Laundering prevention Act and other related circulars. It may be noted that around 8.2million cards (debit and credit) are issued by the banks which is one of the vital instrument of e-commerce activities. Mobile Financial Services (MFS) The Mobile Financial Services (MFS) has been introduced to modernize the banking system of Bangladesh. This has been done for extending the banking services using the network of mobile operators in order to substitute conventional branch banking systems. In order to bring the vast unbanked/under-banked population under the umbrella of formal financial service, Bangladesh Bank has taken steps to introduce bank-led mobile financial services. Disbursement of inward foreign remittance and domestic fund; payment of utility bills, salary, allowances, pension; buying and selling of goods and services; balance inquiry; tax payment; government subsidy payment and payment of the benefits of social safety nets can easily and quickly be provided through mobile financial services. The opportunity to provide this service 24/7 is making it up-todate and admired. Bangladesh Bank has taken many policy initiatives to make the MFS more effective. The Guidelines for Mobile Financial Services was issued on 22 September 2011. Approval for starting MFS was given to 28 banks till date out of which 19 banks have started the same. These banks have engaged four hundred thousand persons and institutions as agents for providing mobile banking services country-wide. At the end of September 2014, the number of MFS customers crossed 20 million. The total amount of transaction in September 2014 is Tk.100 billion. The average daily volume is about Tk. 3.33 billion. Volume of transaction is gradually increasing. Carrier Opportunity in these sectors A well-functioning e-commerce system also creates market for online security system, software, IT technician etc. We know it very well that science based job field is very small in our country. If e-commerce becomes popular, a good number of jobs will be created. Anyone having technical savvy can work in this field. However, it also helps to have knowledge about and an interest in online communities and to be able to use things like the internet and email. In e-commerce market young generation can engage themselves as Web developer/designer Web editor Online sales/e-commerce IT support Graphic designer Search engine optimizer In MFS market Young generation can engage themselves as entrepreneur. The person wants to make business independently can work as agent of the banks in the MFS market. On the other hand the banks have taken NOC from BB to launch MFS in the country have also set up new wings for providing MFS to their customers. Thus they are going to employ young and enthusiastic IT as well as business oriented young group of population. Not only the banks the vendor companies selling solutions to the banks are engaging new workforce for their businesses. In conclusion it is assumed that in our country E-commerce and MFS are rapidly growing industry. This means that lots of opportunities are waiting here to engage yourself in the emerging industry. ..

Title: Closing Remarks as the "Chief Guest of Honor" at International Career Summit 2014
text: International Career Summit 2014 Closing Remarks of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank as the Chief Guest of Honor Date : November, 2014 Time : 6.15 am Venue : United international University, Dhaka Employmentcentric sustainable development has gained a heightened global attention following the severe disruptions caused by the Global Financial Crisis. The forces contributing to job losses and increasing poverty, endangering progress towards achieving the MDGs may result from large swings in economic activity, high inflation, unsustainable debt levels and volatility in exchange rates and financial markets. In order to generate decent employment at the required scale, countries, both developing and developed economics, will have to achieve sustained and inclusive growth. In Bangladesh, employment is considered as the binding knot between economic growth and poverty in the development strategies outlined in the Sixth Five year Plan as well as the mechanism of poverty reduction by inclusive sustainable development. With around 30 million unemployed people, our country doesnt see the right people at the right places. But I believe, we have that capability to overcome this and this career summit will be a bridge to wipe out the gap between these job seekers and job providers; a strategic response to unemployment problem by helping the job seekers to find a better opportunity and employers to recruit the best talents of the country; and a gateway to meet not only fresh graduates but also some future leaders from all over the country. Bangladesh needs to cash in on its demographic dividend. As service sector now contribute about 50% to GDP, higher productivity in service sector based job creation is to be of utmost priority. Female labor force participation in different industries should be encouraged for ensuring women empowerment and equal contribution to the national welfare. The components of an employmentfocused development strategy should thus include macroeconomic, environmental and industrial policies that foster structural change, investment and job creation, as well as sound social and labor market policies. We at central bank are also pioneering in creating jobs for the youths as reflected in our recent recruitments. For the last few years, Bangladesh Bank has recruited over more than 200 Assistant Directors through cent percent fair and transparent recruitment test opening a vibrant opportunity for the freshers. BBorchestrated countrywide campaign for financing of output initiatives of rural and urban farm and offfarm MSMEs is creating jobs for millions, besides selfemployment for the entrepreneurs; Massive BBled modernization of the countrys payments system and financial sector IT infrastructure has triggered rapid expansion of cost efficient mobile phone/smart card based agent banking in the remote rural regions; creating jobs in hundreds of thousands in the agent banking outlets. Green financing supported by BB refinance is creating green jobs in increasingly numbers, particularly in the areas of assembling, selling, installing and maintaining off grid solar PV systems in household, offices and other establishments. In an era of rapidly changing economic environment, job requirements are also changing. I would therefore advice the students to prepare them meeting the todays job market demands. I would also urge you to change your mindset of chasing only for jobs but also to explore your hidden potentialities for entrepreneurship. You will be glad to know that BB's initiative for SME financing alone has created 1.5 million jobs during the period of 2010 to June 2014. I am sure this summit is a great support and jumpstart for the students for their career building and thus contributes to spur the sustainable employment in Bangladesh along with a winwin situation for the employers to choose the right ones for the right places saving their time and cost. Thank you all for your patient hearing.

Title: Speech at the SANEM-ADB Conference on 'Linking Financial Sector to the Real Economy: Encouraged Financial Stability Indicators (EFSI) for Bangladesh'
text: SANEM-ADB Conference on Linking Financial Sector to the Real Economy: Encouraged Financial Stability Indicators (EFSI) for Bangladesh Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : November 03, 2014 Time : 9.00 am Venue : The Westin Hotel, Dhaka Dr. Selim Raihan, Executive director of South Asian Network on Economic Modeling (SANEM), Dr. Guntur Sugiyarto, Senior Economist of ADB, Special guest Mr. Golam Mostafa Kamal, Director General of BBS, my colleague Dr. Aktharuzzaman, Economic Advisor, Bangladesh Bank, key discussants Dr. A. K. Enamul Haque, East West University, Dr. Binayak Sen, Research Director of the BIDS, distinguished presenters, and other participants: a very good morning to you all. Its my privilege to be the chief guest in today's conference on "Linking Financial Sector to the Real Economy: Encouraged Financial Stability Indicators (EFSI) for Bangladesh " jointly organized by the SANEM and ADB. The global financial crisis of 20082009 and the lingering sluggishness in global growth in the wake of the crisis are still vivid memories of how imbalances and instabilities in the macroeconomic and financial environments lead to vicious circle of catastrophe in financial market and downturn in real sector growth feeding on each other. Financial market collapse and credit crunch emanated from the imprudent risk driven credit and asset price bubble bursts in major advanced economies harshly interrupted their own real sector development languishing financial stability and eventually precipitated the crisis by contagion across borders. The cautious stance of carefully managed external sector openness has kept Bangladeshs financial sector and the broader economy stable and well protected from adverse impacts of the global financial crisis and the earlier East Asian currency crisis. It is of utmost importance to remain watchful against risks or threats to stability and balance in the macroeconomic and financial environments, promptly addressing emerging new vulnerabilities and occasional localized small crises well before these can grow into wider concerns. Regional and global collective initiatives do have roles in addressing stability concerns, but the primary onus for maintaining macroeconomic and financial stability begins and remains at the country level to inhibit any recurrence of such crisis. Financial and nonfinancial sectors are interlinked and interdependent through their credit and financial market exposures. Financial sector risks often arise from misallocation and overindebtedness of credit by households as well as non financial sector of the economy. Irrational exuberance also occurs in financial market mainly due to lack of corporate entities' soft information. I believe, the invaluable information from SANEM's study will reveal hidden risks and fair price to the market participants and will have positive impact minimizing information gap between lenders and borrowers along with other market participants leading to a trust economy. Page 1 of 2 Bangladesh Bank (BB) is active in building up supervisory capabilities of early identification and addressing of any incipient systemic risks adopting regulatory and supervisory best practice norms and standards of the Groups of global experts based in BIS, Basel. BB regularly engages in FSAP self assessments and IMFWB/peer group assessments of degree of convergence of its regulatory and supervisory regimes with international best practice standards. Bangladesh Government's decision to go for ECF program of IMF was indeed prudent in encouraging financial stakeholders to opt for needed reforms to enhance fiscal strategy. Let me now recount some of our initiatives, BB started its financial sector's risk and stability analysis in 2006 through its publication "Financial Sector Review". In the analysis BB mainly considered macro as well as micro prudential financial indicators along with qualitative indicators to understand financial sector stability and structural weaknesses. However, considering new developments in global financial environment, BB promptly come forward to establish a "Financial Stability Department" ingraining the financial stability issue at its core policy platform and regularly assess the financial sector stability using modern tools and techniques including stress testing. BB also used to collect nonfinancial corporate data for its publication "Corporate Sector Balance Sheet Analysis" though it has been discontinued from 2003; I hope, the ADBSANEM's joint initiative will help fulfilling this gap as the recent global financial crisis has heightened its necessity to the stakeholders. Let me take the opportunity of mentioning how the stress on inclusive, environmentally sustainable financing in BBs monetary and financial policies is promoting macroeconomic and financial stability in our economy. In our economy, inclusive financing now enthusiastically embraced by the entire financial sector is supporting micro and small scale output initiatives of broad swathes of hitherto unserved or underserved population segments; banks and financial institutions are on the one hand diversifying and reducing credit risks of their investment portfolios by moving into broadened bases of numerous new inclusion clients, reducing large exposures to big corporates. Financial stability is gaining strength in the process. Because socially responsible inclusive and environmentally responsible financing has such clear positive link with macroeconomic and financial stability, I dont see why monetary and financial supervisory authorities should feel shy of promoting these in their monetary and financial policies. BB would certainly continue to promote such policy stances. I do certainly appreciate the great attempt of the ADB and SANEM to construct financial stability indicators for the nonfinancial corporates of six industries ranging from manufacturing, services, construction, retail and wholesale, transport and communications to real estate activities of some major cities. Indeed, it would be highly beneficial to the stakeholders if it could be done for the whole country. I hope the factors that are found in the GIS study by the SANEM would help understand the factors that affect the prices of apartments and buildings in some selected cities. Their study on interest rate, lending system and financial conditions of pawnshop, a source of credit for poor households in Bangladesh will hopefully provoke new thoughts on indicators of financial stability in informal sector of the economy to include them in broad based financial policy design. I do wish the best success of ADBSANEM effort and cherish the great attempt of their compilation of Encouraged Financial Stability Indicators (EFSI) which will indeed help the policy makers, academicians, researchers and all other stakeholders to foresee future direction shielding the financial stability from any imbalances. Good luck to all the researchers involved in this handson research. Thank you all for your patient attention. Page 2 of 2

Title: Inaugural Speech at a Workshop on SAS' Banking Event
text: Workshop on SAS' Banking Event Inaugural Speech of the Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : November 3, 2014 Time : 5.00 pm Venue : The Westin Dhaka, Gulshan, Dhaka Good afternoon dear participants and all present here. At first I would like to thank the organizer for arranging this event for the banking community of Bangladesh. All of you are aware about the topic of today's event and it is very much relevant to our recent banking activities. I am quite sure that you will be benefitted from today's event in managing 'Fraud and Money Laundering Risks' in your institutions. Criminals are using the banking sector for conducting different types of financial crimes and, Fraud and Money Laundering are most devastating financial crime for the sector. All of you are aware about the recent trend of fraud activities and money laundering offences in Bangladesh; these were probably taking place for years. But they are coming to the forefront as we have intensified our supervision both physically and digitally. Yet some of the criminals may remain out of our supervision net for lack of advance information. Had these been an act on whistle blowing we could have caught many more big fishes. No doubt criminals tend to conduct cheque fraud and different banking instruments fraud; sometimes they also try to collect money from a large number of people with a commitment to pay back with huge benefits. Some of naive people are easily convinced with the expectation to get the maximum benefits within a short period of time and they become victims of this temptation. In such a situation most of people lose their entire amount due to such fraudulent activities of the criminals and finally the criminals launder the criminal proceeds in different ways. Fraud and money laundering may indeed be interrelated and the proceeds of fraudulent activities in most cases are used for money laundering offences. In most of the fraud cases banks are not always fully compliant with the needed KYC requirements and we find that the officials are often reluctant to monitor the transactions and activities of clients properly. What is most unfortunate that some of the bank officials are engaging themselves in such criminal activities. Many a times they get caught by our investigation team and face the consequences. Yet the sector gets the hit due to reputational loss of some of the banks for employing such dishonest officials. You know, we have started the journey to combat money laundering and terrorist financing after the promulgation of Money Laundering Prevention Act, 2002 and Anti Terrorism Ordinance, 2008, and under the ICRG process of FATF we have taken several initiatives to come out from the ICRG process which includes enactment of Money Laundering Prevention Act, 2012, Mutual Legal Assistance in Criminal Matters Act, 2012 and amendments of Anti-Terrorism Act, 2009 in 2012 & 2013 and others to address all the gaps identified by the Regional Review Group. Since the enactment of these acts and 1 other initiatives, Bangladesh has made considerable progress with regard to the compliance with the international standards. That's why we could come out of grey list of FATF and also became a member of Egmont Group. These recent developments are helping us in overseeing the banking sector closely and efficiently to prevent fraudulent activities, money laundering, terrorist financing and other financial crimes. For shouldering the duties and responsibilities of Bangladesh Bank, the Bangladesh Financial Intelligence Unit (BFIU) is working hard and it has issued several guidelines, circulars and instructions for banking sector. But the success of our anti-money laundering drive depends to a large extent on your commitment for appropriate compliance. If you are reluctant to comply with the AML/CFT regulatory requirements then it will be very difficult for us to prevent all kinds of criminal activities in the banking sector. One cannot claim that banking sector is fully free from all these fraud and money laundering activities; therefore you will have to take effective initiatives for all kinds of risk management within your institutions. Bangladesh Bank is committed to standby you to go forward with a vision to prevent fraud, money laundering or any kind of criminal activities in the banking and financial sector. Wish you best of luck. Thanks to all for the patient hearing. I wish all the success of this event. 2

Title: Speech on Developing Zakat and Waqf System as part of Financial Deepening: Bangladesh Experience
text: 2014 Meeting of Central Banks and Monetary Authorities of the OIC Member Countries Suraybaya, Indonesia, 5-6 November 2014 Developing Zakat and Waqf System as part of Financial Deepening: Bangladesh Experience Delivered by Mr. Shitangshu Kumar Sur Chowdhury Deputy Governor, Bangladesh Bank Esteemed Governors of Central Banks and Monetary Authorities of OIC Member Countries, Distinguished participants, Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a great privilege and honour for me to share Bangladesh Experience on Developing Zakat and Waqf System as part of Financial Deepening. I would not make any detailed deliberation here;rather focus on some key developments in this area. The role and scope of Zakat and Waqf in addressing the problems of poverty is widely recognised. Zakat is one of the fundamentals of Islam and has direct economic implications. It requires Muslims to distribute a part of their wealth in order to alleviate poverty and achieve financial inclusion. On the other hand, Waqf is a voluntary charitable act that has wide economic implications. These instruments are able to solve the problems of poverty and extend social inclusion. Zakat as a tool of poverty alleviation is yet to receive much attention of economists, regulators and policy makers in Bangladesh. Indeed the Zakat management system in the country is crude with somewhat lack of institutional involvement in the process. Bangladesh has a dual system of Zakat management. There is no element of compulsion in Zakat. Payment of Zakat is voluntary and may be made to the Zakat Board of Islamic Foundation Bangladesh, a government agency under the Ministry of Religious Affairs or to several other private institutional collectors or even to private individuals. Matters pertaining to Zakat are governed by the Zakat Fund Ordinance, 1982. According to a research done by Islamic Economics Research Bureau, a private think-tank in Bangladesh, Zakat collection in 2010 was about BDT 110 billion or USD 1.4 billion, which was equivalent to 1.4 percent of GDP. Out of two key agencies that are working in the Zakat sector  Zakat Board of the Islamic Foundation Bangladesh collected BDT14.20 million during 2010 (1432H) and expects to collect BDT 25 million during the current year 2014 Page 1 of 3 (1435H). In Bangladesh, more than 90 percent of the population is Muslims; majority of them pay Zakat individually, mostly as token charity. Distribution of clothing (sarees and lungis) is a traditional method of Zakat distribution. Institutional distribution of Zakat is more diversified and takes the form of scholarship programs for poor students, rehabilitation and training for poor women, rehabilitation of widows, housing for the poor, and distribution of rickshaws for the unemployed young people in villages etc. Dhaka Ahsania Mission, a non-government organization having multidimensional development activitieshas established a Zakat Fund for the welfare of the hardcore poor people of Bangladesh. Zakats received from the individuals/organisations are solely utilised towards the development and welfare of the poor peoples, as per the choice of the Zakat payers. Generally the fund is being utilized for education support to the children of poor families; supports to the general treatment cost of the poor and helpless patients, treatment of cancer patients, marriage expenses of girls from poor families; helping the poor families in building or repairing their houses; helping the members of poor families to become selfsufficient through income generating activities; rehabilitation of orphan children; running a night shelter home for the destitute people who do not have any place to sleep etc. During the period 2012-13, a total amount of BDT 4.2 million was received in the Zakat Fund which has been distributed among the poor people for the above mentioned purposes. Many Bangladeshis living abroad do not find proper ways to disburse their Zakat to the really deserving people. Dhaka Ahsania Mission takes this responsibility on their behalf to ensure utilizing the Zakat for the welfare of the ultra poor people of the society who really deserve to get Zakat as per Shariah guidelines. Waqf is basically meant for creation of a common wealth for the benefit of the people. The poor, the needy and the orphans have always been figured as the most prominent beneficiaries of Waqf. Islamic Waqf went beyond the need offulfillment of the poor and the deprived to providing the means for long time empowerment and enrichment of the poor. This was done by equipping them with the tools of earning income and increasing the productive capacity by providing education and health care. Furthermore in many cases the elderly and handicapped were taken care of by the Waqf, economic burden on the low income group was lessened. In Bangladesh, an Islami Bank namely Social Islami Bank Limited issues Cash-Waqf Certificate to collect funds from the rich and to distribute gains of the managed funds Page 2 of 3 between the poor. Like those of Bangladesh, in other Islamic countries, a significant portion of the people are poor. Therefore, effectiveness of Cash-Waqf certificate program to help reduce poverty in Bangladesh gives hope that a similar program can be successfully implemented in other countries. Another form of Waqf, Public Waqf, is practiced in Bangladesh by most of the Islami Shari'ah banks, e.g., the Social Islami Bank Limited and the Islamic Bank Bangladesh Limited. The procedure of this plan is that: o The founder deposits money into Cash-Waqf based account in the bank. While depositing the money, the founder is given a list of the Beneficiaries whereby he/she can chose or specify his/her Beneficiaries. o The bank acts as a Mutawalli and invests the capital through Mudarabah Contract. The revenue generated channeled to charitable purposes or purposes specified by the founder. Alongside some other private institutions are operating welfare activities on Waqf basis, e.g., Hamdard Laboratories (Waqf) Bangladesh has introduced time honoured presentation of herbal medicine like capsule, tablet, syrup, ointment, elixir etc. The institution earns to spend in the pursuance of noble objectives, e.g., educational activities and human resource development programs. Though it is not directory involved with financial deepening, but indirectly contributing to social inclusion and thus financial widening activities. As per a survey conducted in 1986 by The Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics, there are about 1,50,593 Waqf Estates in the country. Out of which 97,046 are duly registered, 45,607 are verbal and the remaining 7,940 are traditional/customary/Waqfs by user. There are about 1,23,006 Mosques, 8,317 Madrashas, 1,400 Dargahs/shrines, 21,163 Eidgahs, 8,317 Graveyards and 3,859 Orphanages. All these Waqf Estates are located in the rural and urban areas of the 64 districts in Bangladesh. In fine it can be said that the role of Zakat and Waqf Estates managementin Bangladesh can be made more effective if the rich Muslim countries, Islamic Development Bank, Organisation of Islamic Conference (OIC) come forward and co-operate with technical and financial assistance to develop pragmatic Zakat and Waqf models to ensure poverty alleviation through functional re-distribution among different factors of production engaging Zakat and Waqf in true operation. Title: Speech on Policy making and institutions in Bangladesh
text: Policy making and institutions in Bangladesh Organized by Bangladesh Economists Forum (BEF) and Policy Research Institute (PRI) Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : November 08, 2014 Time : 10.30 am Venue : Policy Research Institute (PRI), Banani, Dhaka As elsewhere, government ministries, departments, and other public institutions in Bangladesh formulate and implement public policies in various macro and micro sectors. Needs for policy initiatives arise at two levels; in pursuing realization of the societys medium and longer term growth and development aspirations, and in coping with transient internal or external shocks and disruptions arising in day to day economic and social life. All macro sector issues, and most of the micro sector issues are interrelated with host of others; thorough understanding of trends of these interrelationships is essential for meaningful, useful policy making. This requires well thought out institutional arrangements, including inter alia: (i) Good quality research based on reliable data clearly bringing out the interrelations, policy options in the areas needing intervention, and the potential gainers and losers from the interventions; (ii) Multi-level stakeholder consultations by policy making public institutions to assess feasibility of the various policy options in the ground realities of extents of support for or resistance to the policy options. These stakeholder consultations can often be also useful as advocacy initiatives creating constituencies in support of intended policy reforms. (iii) Multi-level policy coordination between public institutions towards ensuring adoption of policy initiatives that are mutual consistent, mutually reinforcing rather than being at cross-purposes with one another. Bangladesh Bank (BB) has over the years been proactively strengthening its in-house research and policy analysis, alongside forging research liaisons and partnerships with academia and think tanks. In formulating and implementing monetary and financial sector policies BB engages extensively with the concerned government agencies, think tanks, civil society organizations, eminent scholars and former top level policy makers, trade and industry forums etc. Furthermore, Fiscal-Monetary Coordination Council, role of the BB in preparing Govt, Five Year Plan and in the Foreign Private Loan Committee (where BB Governor is the Chair) along with BOI and other ministries are fostering a better level playing field to serve as central bank of the country. Institutional arrangements in Bangladesh for public policy formulation and implementation broadly conform to the above outlined requirements, though perhaps not to uniform extent across all public institutions. Bangladesh economys track record of weathering the last global financial crisis largely unhurt and of sustaining stable healthy growth pace amid subsequent global growth slowdown evidences efficacy of Bangladeshs public institutions in policy making and implementation. As a key public institution, Bangladesh Bank (BB) has over the years been proactively strengthening its in-house research and policy analysis, alongside forging research liaisons and partnerships with academia and think tanks. In formulating and implementing monetary and financial sector policies consistently with overarching macroeconomic goals and objectives, BB engages extensively with the concerned government agencies, think tanks, civil society organizations, eminent scholars and former top level policy makers, trade and industry forums etc., on both ex ante and ex post basis. BBs experience with this approach of consultative, coordinated policy making grounded on analytical underpinnings is broadly positive; evidenced in substantial progress in mainstreaming inclusive, environmentally sustainable financing practices in the financial sector, alongside maintaining monetary and financial stability in terms of BBs core central banking mandate. BB has taken the financial inclusion as the key strategy to reaching the unbanked and underserved keeping it mandates intact. The linkage program formalized by BB regulation allowed private and foreign banks to provide at least 2.5% of total credit to farmers and small entrepreneurs. They have used regulated MFIs to enhance this access. Sharecroppers can now access to agricultural loan from a revolving BB fund of BDT 5 billion channeled through BRAC; more than 9 lakh sharecroppers have been financed till September, 2014 since its launching in 2009. In order to promote renewable energy and green financing in Bangladesh, BB has initiated a refinance scheme of BDT 2 billion in 2009. The end results of these inclusive interventions have been positive. For example there were 48 bank branches per 1000 sq km in 2009 which increased to 59 by the end of 2013. The number of branch per 1 lakh population increased from 5.1 to 5.7 during that period. Number of ATMs per 1000 sq km increased from 8 to 35 during this period. Deposit accounts per 1000 population increased from 267 to 413. Banking sector asset increased from 59% of GDP to 80% of GDP during this period. For the development of SME sector including women entrepreneurship, BB has established a refinance fund of BDT 21 billion from its own source along with IDA, ADB and JICA and disbursed refinance facility of BDT 3.45 billion to 41,952 entrepreneurs where 21.86 percent of credit was distributed among 9612 women entrepreneurs. In its latest move in August 2014, BB has launched new Entrepreneurs Fund and Jute Sector fund amounting to USD 13 and 25 million respectively. Till September 2014, out of the permitted 28 banks, 19 banks have provided mobile financial services to more than 2 crore and 7 lakh beneficiaries through 4 lakh and 77 thousand agents. These indicate significant financial inclusion and deepening. A key challenge in BBs policy making and implementation efforts is in dealing with external pressures resisting various policy reforms, like in scaling down of capital market exposures of banks, in enforcing international best practice standards of asset classification and provisioning, in enforcing accountable and transparent corporate governance, and so forth. Undesirable interferences in performance of statutory licensing and disciplining responsibilities of BB and other financial sector regulators have often limited their capacities of fostering corporate governance excellence in banking and other financial and capital market segments. Structural reforms for attaining longer term growth and stability objectives in various sectors require consistent, resolute and evenhanded implementation; overriding resistances from vested interests in status quo. While theoretical first best options are seldom implementable in practice anywhere, and recourse to second best or other less than ideal options is quite usual; an overall governance climate favorable for positive changes is important. Public institutions can be held accountable for performance lapses only when they are left with free hand in carrying out their clearly delineated responsibilities. This is something still largely amiss for policy making public institutions in Bangladesh, needing to be addressed. Of late there have been some progress in empowering central bank and it has been trying hard to bring discipline in the financial sector. We are already getting some results from this empowering process.

Title: Welcome address of Reflections on the First BEF Conference: Challenges Facing Economic Research in Bangladesh
text: Reflections on the First BEF Conference: Challenges Facing Economic Research in Bangladesh Welcome address of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : November 15, 2014 Time : 10.30 am Venue : BBTA, Mirpur-2 Dhaka Honorable Chairperson former Finance Minister Mr. M. Syeduzzaman, honorable Chief Guest Planning Minister Mr. A. H. M. Mustafa Kamal MP, Keynote paper presenter eminent economist and Deputy Chairman of the first Planning Commission of Bangladesh Dr. Nurul Islam, other distinguished invitees present here today, a very good morning and warmest welcome to you all on behalf of myself, Bangladesh Bank, and the BEF. We are deeply grateful to Dr. Nurul Islam for undertaking an arduously long journey at his advanced age from across half the world away to be with us today in this discussion event hosted jointly by Bangladesh Bank and the BEF. In April this year the BEF held its landmark event of the first BEF conference at Dhaka to comprehensively take stock of Bangladeshs socio economic progress in various areas, to identify the success factors and the weaknesses, and to chart Bangladeshs inclusive, environmentally sustainable progress path fully out of poverty and deprivation on to broad based prosperity by the fifth decade of this century. The BEF conference reaffirmed that this growth vision is no pipe dream, and is grounded on the base built up over the decades since liberation. Successes with our approach to inclusive, sustainable growth have attracted widespread external attention and recognition. Bangladesh economys six-plus percent stable annual average real GDP growth for well over a decade now is around twice the annual average rate of global GDP growth over the period. Attainment of many of the poverty related MDGs well ahead of the 2015 deadline evidenced inclusivity of Bangladeshs growth processes. Bangladesh has been maintaining sovereign credit ratings (Ba3, BB-, with stable outlook) typical of much higher income comparators for five successive years now. Bangladesh has been doing well in social development indicators also, ahead of her higher income large neighbor on most counts. Global forums including those in the ILO, UNEP, WB, and IMF are now discussing and studying Bangladesh Banks inclusive, green financing promotion initiatives. Bangladeshs financial sector has been capably supporting the countrys predominantly private sector led growth initiatives, without any systemic stress even at the height of global financial crisis. Institutional failure episodes in our financial sector have been very few and far between 1 compared to elsewhere in most of the developing economies. Investment activities and financing thereof are necessarily risky in nature, with slippages possible from errors of judgment or adventurism. Rapid growth and advent of new technologies also bring heightened risks of frauds and scams. These slippages, scams and fraudulence incidences often get overblown in media as scare stories. Due corrective and preventive attention of BB and other relevant authorities have prevented these sporadic incidents from blowing up into systemic stress or crisis. I discussed the strengths and weaknesses of the current structure of our financial sector at some length in my paper presented in the first BEF conference, and we are proceeding along the paths outlined in that paper towards building up governance excellence, strength, and resilience in our financial sector fully of the global best practice standards. Todays discussion event this morning is a sequel to the first BEF conference, focusing on the important area of requisites for formulation and successful implementation of high quality development policy initiatives by public institutions. I shouldnt of course be giving away in advance too much from Dr. Nurul Islams presentation in my welcome address, let me just mention that his presentation will highlight the need of adequate base of good quality research and analytical work bringing out policy options for public institutions in their respective fields, and the need of adequate and reliable data base to support such research and initiatives, besides dwelling on the challenges faced by public institutions in building up political will for policy reform initiatives in face of resistances of quarters benefitting from status quo. Needless to say, our research community is yet to rise up to the occasions to face these challenges. These are very topical issues for policy reform initiatives for all public institutions in Bangladesh including Bangladesh Bank. Over the recent years Bangladesh Bank has vigorously pursued strengthening of its in-house capabilities for surveys, research and analysis with new incentive structures including extensive higher training opportunities and higher weight age on publications for career advancement and so forth. Besides partnering and liaising with local think tanks and universities, BB has also been inducting NRB experts from global organizations and foreign universities, to strengthen the analytical underpinnings of the various policy initiatives. Ex-ante and ex-post stakeholder consultations are now routine procedures in BBs policymaking and implementation. Systematic evaluation of outcomes of policy initiatives is one area where more needs to be done, both by BB and by external think tanks etc. With his luminous career in academic erudition and his hands-on practical experience at the senior-most levels with development challenges both in the domestic and international arenas, there is none better suited than Dr. Nurul Islam to talk to us on the themes of todays discussion session. Our honored Chief Guest and Chairperson are also eminent personages with seasoned highest level experience in planning and execution of development policies and programs. We are extremely fortunate indeed to have them all with us today in this joint BB-BEF discussion event. Let me conclude here inviting Dr. Nurul Islam to kindly commence his presentation, and eagerly awaiting an exciting, stimulating session of lively discourse thereon. Thank you all for your patient attention. 2

Title: Speech at a Seminar on 'SME Development: Role of an Effective SME Association'
text: Seminar on SME Development: Role of an Effective SME Association Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : November 22, 2014 Time : 10.00 am Venue : Institute of Diploma Engineers, Kakrail Honorable Chair, Special Guests, Leaders of different SME Associations and Chambers, bank executives, representatives of the print and electronic media and guests-a very Good Morning to you all. I am pleased to be present in such a gathering of representatives from numerous national and international associations including IamSME of INDIA, business leaders, chambers representatives, inspiring women and SME entrepreneurs. I am confident that this congregation of leaders and entrepreneurs will result in a partnership that will benefit both the countries in the days to come. I appreciate SME & Special Programs Department of Bangladesh Bank (BB), BIBM, DCCI, RDA, CIRDAP, IDEB and BWCCI for their initiative to organize todays program. Id also like to thank Basic Bank Ltd and IDLC Finance Ltd for their cooperation in arranging this program. I especially thank RDA, Bogra for their cooperation in arranging this seminar and a field-visit to Bogra in cooperation with BBs GM of Bogra Office. MSMEs worldwide are treated as the engine of growth, drivers of innovations. MSMEs play a significant role in driving economic growth and generating employment. The rate of business creation in any jurisdiction indicates the rate of innovation and thereby indicates the rate of growth. Private sector is the main driver of growth in the todays world and majority of the private enterprises are MSMEs. In our country, in fact 99% of the private sector enterprises are MSMEs. MSMEs contribute up to 30% to GDP. MSMEs are providing employment to 25% of total labor force while 80% of industrial jobs come from MSMEs. MSMEs are widely distributed all over the country which means developing MSMEs play a major role in bridging the urban-rural income gap and contribute towards inclusive growth. In true sense, inclusive growth can only be achieved through a vibrant SME sector in a country like Bangladesh. It is heartening to note that the Government of Bangladesh has rightly identified MSME sector as the priority sector for transformation of Bangladesh into a middle income country. In line with Government's thrust, BB has been instrumental in designing and implementing MSME sector development initiatives as part of its development financing agenda. BB has shown the world that central bank can successfully manage its traditional role of monetary authority while playing the complementary role of development driver. BB has already become the role model in MSME financing in the international arena within a span of only 5 years. Our initiatives are being studied by other central banks in the world. We are regularly receiving delegates from other central banks who are looking at our success stories. Our targeted credit initiatives have become one of the world best practices. The Alliance for Financial Inclusion (AFI), a global institution has taken note of our innovative policy initiatives and included BB as a member of its Steering Committee besides giving this year's Policy Award. Through the targeted credit initiatives we have been able to finance 1.9 million MSME enterprises with 3.4 billion USD while we have financed 90 thousand women owned enterprises with more than 1.2 billion USD. The share of credit to micro and small enterprises in total MSME has increased from 43 to 56 percent in just five years. Credit flow to productive sector has also increased significantly making long lasting impact on sustainability. The banking sector financed 0.25 million new businesses with 6.4 billion USD during 2009-2014 (June) while more than 1.5 million jobs have been created by the MSME enterprises during the last five years due to this financing. Taking the ever increasing demand for jobs into consideration we here in BB has taken promotion of enterprise creation, entrepreneurship development and self-employment as the key policy strategy for job creation. We have successfully engaged various stakeholders involved in MSME development in our programs and initiatives. We have engaged and are continuously trying to further engage private sector in the MSME development initiatives. As MSMEs are small in size so cooperation among them are very much essential for competing and negotiating with the government and their large counterparts. I have come to know about IamSME of India and its initiatives. This Association is working in variety of areas which are essential for MSME development. This Association is run by entrepreneurs to facilitate and promote the growth and development of small business across India through services like credit facilitation, technology transfer, skill development, energy efficiency, lean manufacturing, export import facilitation, solar power and energy efficiency etc. The experience of IamSME of India can be a learning platform for our business associations in designing and implementing MSME sector development agenda. I have learnt that the Indian delegations will visit Bogra, one of the key MSME cluster in Bangladesh and RDA will be their local host. I wish the organizers will showcase our achievements and also learn from the visiting delegation how to further improve our MSME sector. Bangladesh and India, two close neighbors and strategic partners, see MSME development as a crucial driver for hastening inclusive economic growth, and clearly there is ample scope for deepening mutually beneficial cooperation and support between MSME policymakers and stakeholders of the two friendly countries. I heartily congratulate the organizers for arranging todays program and also I thank the Indian High Commission for its supportive role. As Governor of Bangladesh Bank I feel especially enthused seeing these local, regional and global initiatives for MSME promotion. You all know that BB has remained proactively engaged in this area with its ongoing financial inclusion strategy. In the financial inclusion campaign, BB not only supports the widening of access to finance for MSMEs, but also tries to motivate and facilitate their convergence in clusters suitable for networking among themselves and for developing backward and forward valuechain linkages with the input and output markets. Exchange of experiences and ideas in such networking clusters will help incubate innovation of more efficient processes and business practices. In the interactive discussions to be held in the second session I would urge the participating policy makers, associations and chambers from Bangladesh and India to actively engage in mutual sharing of knowledge about each others approaches and experiences, enabling them to identify possible areas of mutually beneficial cooperation. Participants from Bangladesh may find significant learning points in Indias approaches in promotion of entrepreneurship and innovation in collaboration with the visiting association. I wish the best success of this visit program of Indian team and todays seminar with engaging, interactive deliberations. I am looking forward to further deepening of bilateral Bangladesh-India engagements in MSME promotion. I am very glad to see that DCCI, IDEB and BWCCI have signed MOU with this Indian Association which will deepen relationship and initiatives with IamSME of India. I would like to extend my thanks to the organizers especially Mr. Sukamal Sinha Chowdhury, SME Department of BB for their concerted efforts to make this program a success. Thanks to Ekattor TV and its Managing Director for participating and focusing this program as a media partner. Also thanks to other representatives of media. Special thanks to the Chairman of IamSME of India and his team for taking the trouble for coming to Bangladesh for promoting broader relationship with associations, chambers and dedicated leaders of our Country. I wish a very successful program with IamSME of India and continued progress of future such initiatives. Thank you all.

Title: Address in the ceremony of souvenir coin set handover by Japan Mint
text: Chief Guest's address by BB Governor Dr. Atiur Rahman in the ceremony of souvenir coin set handover by Japan Mint. Date : Time : Venue : December 09, 2014 3.00 pm Head Office, Bangladesh Bank Chairman of todays august ceremony Mr. Abu Hena Mohd. Razee Hasan, Deputy Governor of Bangladesh Bank (BB), Special Guest His Excellency Mr. Shiro Sadoshima, Honorable Ambassador of Japan in Bangladesh, Mr. Takayuki Kawakami, First Secretary of Japan Embassy Mr. Kazuya Izumi, Director of Japan Min, representatives from Mitsui & Co., representatives of different print and electronic media, other distinguished guests, and my fellow colleagues a very good afternoon and warm welcome to you all on behalf of myself & Bangladesh Bank. At the beginning I would like to express my heartfelt congratulation to Japan Mint officials for gifting us 3000 Souvenir Coin Set consists of 6 Japanese coins and one piece 2 Taka Bangladesh coin. I would like to reminisce one of our closest bondages that took place in the beginning of the 20th century, when Rabindranath Tagore and Tenshin Okakura, a distinguished Japanese fine arts scholar, and Taikan Yokoyama, a Japanese master of painting were profoundly affected and influenced with each others work through their friendship. As a time tested friend Japan remains one of the largest development partners of Bangladesh since her liberation in 1972; in close association through economic and technical cooperation, cultural exchanges and mutual visits. Let me recount some facts that help understand how Bangladesh- Japan tie has been enhancing our mutual high fidelity in the trajectory of development and prosperity. Japan is the 3rd largest development partner of Bangladesh, 7th largest destination of our exports, 5th largest source of imports and in case of Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in Bangladesh Japan ranks 8th. As a part of BB implemented Financial Sector Project for the Development of Small and Medium-Sized Enterprise project, the Government of Bangladesh and Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) signed a loan agreement on 18 May 2011 with a fund of 5 billion Japanese Yen, including technical assistance. BB with cooperation from JICA also set up a BDT 1 billion revolving credit line to support RMG factories in Bangladesh. I am very glad to recollect the recent visit of Honorable Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina to Japan and Japan's premiere H.E. Shinzo Abe's visit to Bangladesh, that have renewed and reinforced the bilateral relationship between the two countries and will take this relationship further towards new heights. Looking at stronger and closer tie ahead between Bangladesh and Japan, I would like to earnestly welcome and urge Japanese friends present here to work together in taking full advantage of all the existing and new facilities and bring about a major new upturn in our bilateral trade, investment and business relations. Long live Japan-Bangladesh friendship! Let me conclude here. Thanks a lot for your patient hearing.

Title: Speech at UNGC Asia/Oceania Local Network Regional Meeting 2014
text: UNGC Asia/Oceania Local Network Regional Meeting 2014 Executive Speaker Session Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : December 10, 2014 Time : 10.20 Venue : La Vita Hall, Lakeshore Hotel Dr. Gowher Rizvi, International Affairs Advisor to Honorable Prime Minister; Her Excellency Mr. Hanne Fugl Eskjaer, Ambassador, Embassy of Denmark in Bangladesh; Mr. Farooq Sobhan, Representative, GC Network Bangladesh; Mr. Walid Nagi, Head, Local Network Team, UNGC and distinguished participants of this session, a very good morning to you all. Inclusivity, Sustainability and Responsibility are no more just buzzwords today. So, environmental conservation and caring human livelihood is no longer the sole responsibility of government agencies since more than a decade.
