Keeping this in mind, we have set up an independent Microcredit Regulatory Authority (MRA) for licensing and regulating MFIs, where the central bank Governor is the Chair. We remain committed to maintaining a stable macro and regulatory environment which safeguards peoples money while ensuring that the microfinance institutions have the flexibility to develop financial products to suit poor peoples needs. A significant number of households in Bangladesh still lack the full range of financial services, such as savings products and credit that are essential to insure against shocks and invest for the future. While Bangladesh has done well in the provision of credit, there still remains gap in the provision of credit for meso type activities which are between micro and small enterprises. IORA state members can work together to help poor households insure against health shocks and crop losses, which often reverses their hard-earned steady gains. To conclude, this workshop can be a great opportunity to share knowledge and expertise among the IORA members on the nexus between microfinance and economic development. IORA is one of the few international associations in the world which blends developed, developing and low-income countries, where some have achieved high level of development and economic growth, while some others are still struggling to achieve their development targets. The geographic and resource diversities of the IORA region therefore should be viewed as its strength. I hope that in the coming years IORA will emerge as one of the most effective organizations in the world in extending international cooperation and global integration towards improvement of welfare of the poor. For achieving this goal, civil society, private sector, and academia should also engage themselves in knowledge exchange 2 for the greater benefit of the people of this IORA member states. I am confident that microfinance for inclusive economic growth would be the point of IORA consolidation and cooperation. Thank you all. 3

Title: Speech on the Role of the Policy Makers and Central Banks in Promoting SMEs' Access to Finance - The Case of Bangladesh
text: The Role of the Policy Makers and Central Banks in Promoting SMEs Access to Finance  The Case of Bangladesh Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : 11 April 2015 Time : 10.00 am Venue : BIBM Auditorium Mr. Chair and DG, BIBM, special guests distinguished presence from Academia, the banking Industries, relevant public and private sector stakeholders representatives and members of the electronic and print media a very warm good morning to you all. I appreciate the initiative of INSPIRED component -3 which is working for the development of capacity of BIBM and BBTA in providing SME banking education and training to the Bangladeshi bankers. I am happy to be here in this policy seminar as the key note speaker which will discuss the role of policy makers and central banks in promoting SMEs access to finance. In fact, the role of policy makers and central banks is critical and I dont think we can have enough discussions in how to improve SMEs access to financial services. We should not talk much about it as we are talking for long time; its time to get things done. For the last 5 years central bank itself is not only talking about the role of policy makers but also has set examples for other stakeholders to follow. The seminar has taken a broad note by including policy makers along with central bank. Although central bank is the key policy makers for access to financial services but other policy making public institutions are also important in promoting and enhancing access to finance for SMEs. Let me speak on the role of central bank first then I will highlight the role of other policy making bodies in supporting SMEs agenda. On a theoretical note if we look to the policy makers and central banks, there are two distinctive schools, namely what is popularly known as traditionalist and the neo-liberal approach to central banking. Let me first to touch base on the so-called neo-liberal approach to central banking. The neoliberal is currently dominant so-called best practice approach to central banking in many developed countries. The neo-liberalism consists of the following: (1) central bank independence (2) a focus on inflation control and (3) the use of indirect methods of monetary policy administration (that is, shortterm interest rates as opposed to direct methods such as credit ceilings). I view this neo-liberal approach as highly peculiar as a package, it is radically different from the historically dominant theory and practice of central banking, not only in the developing world, but, notably, in the now developed countries themselves. However, throughout the early and recent history of central banking in the US, Europe, and elsewhere, financing governments, managing exchange rates, and supporting economic sectors by using direct methods of intervention have been among the most important tasks of central banking and, indeed, in many cases, were among the reasons for their existence. I am a strong believers of this school of thought and I am one step ahead of this; I see central banks not only as an agent of development rather it is central to achieving inclusive and sustainable economic growth of a country Virtually throughout their history, central banks have financed governments, used credit allocation methods and subsidies to engage in Sectoral development policy and have attempted to manage the foreign exchanges, often with capital and exchange controls of various kinds. The traditionalist view, therefore, argues that an active public sector involvement in mobilizing and allocating financial resources is needed to broaden access to credit, as private markets fail to expand access to broader general public. The question, then, is NOT whether policy makers and central banks have or should pursue developmental policy, but rather; what kind of developmental policy should they conduct? Here history also gives some guidance. Central banks have been most effective in helping to foster development, especially in late developers, where they have been part of the governmental apparatus of industrial policy implementation. Throughout the history, a continuing tension has been existed between the developmental roles of central banks and the stabilizing roles. Yet there is little evidence that the optimal solution to this tension is to abandon the developmental role entirely. We have been able to strike a balance in achieving the role of developmental central banking and financial stability On a broader scale government has the bigger role in developmental policy making and implementation and apart from central bank there are other operators who should also be engaged in creating a pro-development ecosystem and in making sure the open market operates on an open and fair basis. Now I would like to dwell on the case of Bangladesh in promoting access to finance for SMEs. The present government has rightly identified SMEs as the priority sector for transforming Bangladesh into a middle-income country by 2021. In line with government's thrust, Bangladesh Bank has been instrumental in designing and implementing SME sector development initiatives as part of its development financing agenda. Broadening financial access to cottage, micro and small enterprises and in particular women entrepreneurs has been in the fore front of Bangladesh Banks policy intervention and inclusive growth promotion agenda. Bangladesh Bank has shown the world that a central bank can successfully manage its traditional role of monetary authority while playing the complementary role of development driver. Bangladesh Bank has already become the role model in SME financing in the international arena within a span of only five years. Its initiatives are being studied by other central banks of the world. Bangladesh Bank is regularly receiving delegates from other central banks who are looking at the country's success stories, and I would like to highlight some of the important initiatives that Bangladesh Bank has taken in recent years:  The banking sector has been equipped with guidelines and prudential regulation to help them in doing business in the MSMEs segment.  Banks and NBFIs are being provided SME banking capacity development support so that banks and NBFIs are capable of serving the MSME sector more prudently.  Incentives and disincentives are in place for the banks and NBFIs to motivate them for broadening their MSME lending portfolio.  Multi stakeholder engagement in the way of joint promotion and capacity development initiatives  A credit guarantee scheme is currently being under development, and I trust that once implemented, additional MSEs and women entrepreneurs will be able get access to finance compared to the current situation where some of the SMEs are not deemed credit worthy;  A SME market segmentation database is being developed, and is planned to be completed within this year. Information from the database will  as examples -provide valuable contributions to financial institutions strategy including in which segments to focus on, both from a risk management perspective as well as from a marketing perspective. The database is unique, and Bangladesh is the only country in the world where it is being implemented;  A number of soft loan schemes  credit lines - are available through Bangladesh Bank for financial institutions for on lending to SMEs at a capped interest rate.  For women entrepreneurs promotion tailored policy intervention including earmarking of 15% low cost fund for Women entrepreneurs, clean lending limits up to 2.5 million BDT, priority in loan processing, engagement of women business chambers/associations in client sourcing, mentoring and capacity building support are being encouraged.  SME and women entrepreneurs Help desk at each bank level has been operational.  BB has established a Women Entrepreneurs Development Unit in SME and Special Programmes Department and each of its regional offices.  Bangladesh Bank has a fund earmarked for providing seed capital for start-ups; and finally.  Recently, requirements to financial institutions to lend minimum amounts out to women entrepreneurs. Other initiatives supportive to the specific MSME development initiatives among others are:  Mobile banking has developed very fast, and is of utmost importance, particularly for financial inclusion in rural areas;  Agent banking is progressing well, and is very suitable for financial institutions with a limited branch network in rural areas. Through agent banking, outreach can be considerably enhanced, and if planned and implemented intelligently, agent banking may be very profitable for the financial institutions as well;  Customer interest protection has been given utmost importance and a guideline on customer interest protection and grievance redressal procedures has been published. Multi window complaints submission facility is in place for the banking customers.  A credit information bureau is in place, and although there is always room for improvements, the bureau provide a very important tool for lenders in their risk assessment of the borrowers; the bureau has been digitized and further upgrading of credit information is planned by developing MFI CIB and integrating that with the current CIB. Although a number of initiatives have been implemented or are being implemented, there is still a long way to go before financial inclusion can be characterized as fully satisfactory in Bangladesh. A lot of initiatives have been taken in both developed and developing countries. Policy interventions, products and initiatives need to be tailored to the conditions prevailing in the jurisdiction so as such replication of best practices sometimes may not provide the best results. However knowledge sharing and mutual learning would facilitate more informed decision making. A vibrant MSME sector would demand private sector friendly and specially MSME friendly business environment, proper government support in the public goods for entrepreneurship development, innovation management and promotion and I suggest the following areas should be given high priority by the policy makers and central bank for promoting broader access to finance for the SMEs in the short and medium term: 1. Comprehensive review of MSME promotion framework of the country and identify the gaps and restructuring the MSME development framework with specific roles and responsibility assigned to each stakeholders. 2. Crafting a Separate MSME development policy which would provide strategic direction for the stakeholders. Based on the Strategic direction time bound specific output driven action plan should be taken. 3. Coordination mechanism among the various stakeholders should be formulated so that synergy is achieved. 4. Broadening financial access for cottage micro and small entrepreneurs should be the supplemented by government action in the way of capacity building for the entrepreneurs, reducing collateral requirement, amending relevant rules and regulation and by provisioning financial support for the innovative, export oriented, import substitute and key domestic demand supporting industries by way of credit guarantee scheme, business development services etc. 5. BB would create a policy and regulatory framework that is supportive for MSME banking and create a banking environment that is supportive and friendly to the cottage, micro, small and medium enterprise with particular focus in women entrepreneurship. 6. Currently at lending banks level in many cases SME lending is not profitable due to the lack of appropriate processes and low technological level. If the lending is not profitable, the banks will not proactively increase portfolio in the MSME segment. Therefore, banks should revisit their MSME Banking model to identify pitfalls and undertake Business Process Reengineering (BPR) in order to make MSME banking profitable, less risky, and more consumers friendly. 7. Consumer protection aiming at greater transparency should be ensured, so that SME customers are able to compare terms of different loans offered by financial institutions. This will in turn increase competition, and lower the margins for the creditors; and closely connected to that 8. Development of a standardized loan application package for use in all financial institutions in Bangladesh; 9. Establishing of a Problem Solving Centre for distressed SME loans. It is not an exaggeration to state, that financial institutions in general are not very good at handling non-performing loans. A Problem Solving Centre may assist the SMEs, in case of default, in operational improvements and in financial restructuring, and the Centre will cooperate with the financial institutions. The ultimate goal is to support SMEs so that they may regain their financial health; 10. Requirements to financial institutions to redesign their approach to servicing women entrepreneurs in relation to organization, processes and procedures, product offered including development of non-financial products, and finally development of a strategy for outreach to the segment. In conclusion, Policy makers and central banks should streamline their initiatives and come up with a comprehensive MSME development master plan. Banks and non-banking financial institutions need to have a tailored and explicit strategy for SME banking in order to build a solid banking policy to facilitate sound growth and profitability in SME banking, as well as having better credit evaluation mechanisms, product design, marketing skills, and knowledge of customer and product profitability. Moreover, in Bangladesh, we need to encourage the adoption of modern technology in MSMEs so that their products can compete with those of the competitors. Bangladesh needs to maximise the benefits derived from the MSME sector, as this sector plays a pivotal role in promoting and sustaining the industrial as well as overall economic growth. In making extraordinary progress in the field of improving SMEs access to banking, we all need to share knowledge with each other, cooperate, and realize what are the individual organizations strength and weaknesses. In other words, our mind-set could be, how should the additional initiatives be designed, and by whom, in order to optimize the end result, i.e. further sound development for the MSME sector, and thus for Bangladesh as a whole. Thank you all for giving me the support for carrying out the good job of working for an inclusive growth society.

Title: Inaugural Speech at a Workshop on Investment in Energy Efficient Brick Manufacturing Projects
text: Workshop on Investment in Energy Efficient Brick Manufacturing Projects Inaugural Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Venue: Conclave Hall in Long Beach Suites Gulshan -2, Dhaka Date: April 23, 2015 Time: 9.00 am. IDCOL CEO Mr. Mahmood Malik, UNDP Bangladesh Green Brick Initiative, presenters and resource persons, workshop participants from banks, financial institutions and brick manufacturers, other guests; my warm greetings and a very good morning to you all in this inaugural session of workshop on investment in green or energy efficient non polluting brick manufacturing projects in Bangladesh. I am glad to be invited to this session particularly because some years earlier we at BB took up energy efficient green brick manufacturing as a key initial thrust area for promoting green financing in Bangladesh. Brick-making contributes about one percent to the countrys gross domestic product (GDP), and provides employment for around one million people. The mostly coal based traditional brick making kilns are however highly polluting and wasteful in energy use, which is why we took this up as an area for early intervention. The ADB joined hands with BB in this initiative soon after its inception, and it is extremely heartening now to see the IDCOL also committing its investment resources for this cause; mobilizing external expertise from UNDP and other external sources besides drawing on its own significant in-house capabilities. Let me therefore take this opportunity of heartily thanking the IDCOL for its engagement in this important area. The ADB supported BB refinance support line for financing of energy efficient green brick manufacturing projects amount to around Taka 4.00 billion; the IDCOL joining this initiative with another Taka 4.00 billion is an auspicious occasion of doubling of the thrust for greening of output practices and processes in this sector. As you may already be aware of, BB is aiming at rechanneling of all our domestic financing away from polluting high carbon traditional output practices and lifestyles towards the environmentally sustainable energy efficient, low carbon green alternatives. Our thrust initiatives in areas like solar energy and green brick making have been successful in their initial pilot scales, and will need to be followed up with major scaling up and broader countrywide replication. BB remains active in rendering a clear pro-green stance to the countrys domestic credit and financing policies and practices, including facilitation of raising green finance from domestic and external sources. Creating mass awareness of importance of green financing, fostering technical expertise in drawing up green project initiatives, capacity building in financial appraisal of green projects and in lining up local and external financing for these warrant massive collective efforts of all 1 stakeholders. IDCOL already has successful track record of substantial engagement in financing solar energy initiatives, and I believe they will likewise excel also in their new area of financing green brick making. I hope and expect IDCOL to take lead in engaging with other local green project sponsors, financiers, and technology platforms towards setting up a networking platform for mutual support and knowledge sharing among themselves, and for liaising with financing and technical support sources abroad. On this note of optimism let me now take the privilege of declaring the workshop open, wishing it the best all round success. Thank you all for your patient attention. 2

Title: Speech at the Opening Ceremony of NRB World Conference Series 2015
text: Opening ceremony of NRB World Conference Series 2015 Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : 25 April 2015 Time : 10.30 am Venue : Pan Pacific Sonargaon Hotel, Dhaka Mr. Shekil Chowdhury, the organizers, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen a very good morning to you all. At the very outset, I would like to convey my heartfelt thanks to the Center for Non Resident Bangladeshis for continuing their effort for the wellbeing of the NRBs as well as the country. This year they are planning to arrange conferences across Dubai, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Malayasia, Australia, Europe, UK, USA, and Canada to promote Investment, Remittance and Financial Branding of Bangladesh. Its a great honor for me to be present at this years curtain raiser. Distinguished participants, as you know millions of our manpower are working abroad in almost 157 countries of the world. According to the World Bank, in 2013 Bangladesh ranked 7th position in the list of remittance recipient country in the World. In FY2014, remittance accounts for 66% of foreign reserve while it is almost 9 times of the current account balance in the same fiscal year. As per govt statistics, nearly 2.35 million workers have migrated in last 5 years. In 2014 the inflow of remittance was 14.94 billion. This demonstrates the inherent strength of our external sector and hence that of our country. Obviously, we must give credit to NRBs for attaining this strength and external stability. Stability of exchange rate is an incentive. There has been a gradual change in the share of remittance flows by regions shifting the focus from Middle East to the East Asia, Europe and the North America. For instance Malaysia has become fourth largest remittance source country for Bangladesh. Remittance inflow has always been gender biased representing the woman a little. However, there is a notable change in this tradition. Beside the traditional flows of male workers going abroad, the numbers of female expatriates are growing with significant pace. This trend added a new dimension in the Non-Resident Bangladeshi portfolio. I strongly believe that subsequent introduction of mobile banking and involvement of MFIs in inward remittances reduce the necessity of sending money through informal channel. Banks are now using the branch networks of the MFIs and Post Offices as the sub agent for remittance distribution. Remittances are also distributed through Agent Banking like Singer Bangladesh Limited outlets. All these payment facilities have virtually eliminated the informal remittance inflows reducing the risk of counterfeit. Furthermore, I want to remind you that Bangladesh Bank has established a separate department titled Financial Integrity and Customer Interest Protection Department to handle any complaints and suggestions by the customers or any stakeholders at home and abroad to ensure the smooth and hassle free services. There is a hotline 16236 to address customers hassle if any. I can assure that as an NRB your complaint will be dealt with highest priority. At the moment no bank can take more than two days in distributing the remittance to the designated beneficiaries. 1 Pa ge There is always a high demand for skilled workers abroad. In contrast, 55% of our migrant workers are unskilled and their wage rate remains low, which has a downward impact on the earnings of the migrant. I think, there is a considerable scope to improve their earnings if they can be further trained in different vocational training centres to develop and upgrade their skills. NRB remittance is very useful for Bangladesh development. It has kept Bangladeshs economy strong when others are facing financial crisis. Most remarkable of contributions of NRBs is the investing of their hard-earned money for the development of our countrys rural economy in the form of SMEs and investment portfolio as a whole. It is very praiseworthy that through this conference series, discussions will be held on positive achievements of Bangladesh and its ample potentials particularly with regards to investment remittance. Networking among the non-resident Bangladeshis and others will open a new era of understanding and opportunities. I am sure that the conference series will help aware and involve the NRBs in a more collective and united way so that their talents and resources can be better utilised for our nations development. I thank the Centre for NRB for their initiative which will benefit the NRBs and the prosperity of the Bangladesh and as well as the countries they now reside. I wish the World Conference Series 2015 a grand success. ........................................................................................................ 2 Pa ge

Title: Talking Points in the session of UNOSSC GOB UNDP High Level Meeting on 'Complementing ODA: new opportunities in South South and Triangular Financing for Development'
text: UNOSSC GOB UNDP High Level Meeting session on Complementing ODA: new opportunities in South South and Triangular Financing for Development Talking points of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : May 18, 2015 Time : 9.30 am Venue : Pan Pacific Sonargaon Hotel, Dhaka The concept note for this meeting rightly notes that developing economies in the South will need to foster channels of South South and Triangular FDI and development cooperation to substitute for traditional ODA and other development support from the advanced North now in prolonged growth slowdown. Bangladesh is already in substantial extent of South South and triangular engagements in trade and development cooperation; but with benefits asymmetrically skewed in favor of her Southern partners rather than of Bangladesh herself: (i) Bangladeshs manufactured exports to advanced economies in the North have sizeable imported input content from developing economies in the South; which is why Bangladesh runs trade deficits with partners in the South while running surpluses with advanced economies in the North. In the Asian Clearing Union comprising nine developing economies of the South (viz., Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Iran, Maldives, Myanmar, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka) we are active in fostering intraregional trade settlements minimizing involvement of external currencies, and swap support lines for members in temporary difficulties. However Bangladeshs imports from other ACU partner economies remain around twenty fold larger than her exports to them. The picture clearly indicates a case for urging further openness in South South goods trade; particularly of the larger, faster growing ones, to exports from Bangladesh and other Southern partners; in terms of tariff/non tariff barriers and value chain linkages. (ii) The same asymmetry prevails also in openness for South South services exports. Manufacturing establishments in Bangladesh employ substantial number of middle and higher tier experts and managers from fast growing developing economies of the South, but among the later only Malaysia has extended significant openness to (mainly low skilled) job seekers from Bangladesh. Further, while advanced economies in the North have significant IT enabled services outsourcing to Bangladesh, such outsourcing or value chain linking to Bangladesh from fast growing developing economies in the South remains insignificant. There is thus a case for urging greater openness also in South South services trade. (iii) South South knowledge sharing cooperation is afoot in fostering inclusive, environmentally sustainable growth; one such event is due next month in Dhaka bringing together central bank governors and senior officials from 11 SAARC Finance forum member countries. Large renowned NGOs from Bangladesh like BRAC, ASA and Grameen have also fostered significant and growing South South engagements in social and economic inclusion and empowerment initiatives for the poor in many developing economies in Asia, Africa and South America. There is no significant similar engagement in Bangladesh of NGOs from other developing economies in the South; while NGOs from the advanced North are phasing down their Bangladesh engagements as poverty incidence declines. (iv) Bangladesh is also yet to benefit significantly from recent increases in South South FDI flows, despite being a low wage manufacturing location. Physical infrastructure deficiencies in Bangladesh hampering FDI inflows are in themselves FDI opportunities that fast growing economies of the South can take advantage of; FDI policy regime in Bangladesh being among the most liberal and permissive. Bangladeshs joining the AIIB as a founder member will hopefully widen infrastructure investment inflows into Bangladesh the near future; but existing institutions like the ADB, the SAARC Development Fund and the sovereign wealth funds in the South also have more than adequate fund pools for expanded infrastructure investments in Bangladesh and other Southern economies. Fast growing Southern economies ahead in the curve of bond market development can usefully assist other developing economies in the South in this area. (v) Effective plugging of illicit outflows from developing economies in the South will also be important in augmenting investment resources, such outflows reported typically to exceed FDI and ODA inflows taken together. Build up and strengthening of South South cooperation networks between FIUs, AML CFT adjudicators, anti corruption/stolen asset recovery authorities, and tax/revenue authorities will be crucially important in stemming illicit outflows through trade misinvoicing, transfer pricing and various other means. Bangladesh authorities have remained proactive in these areas, domestically and as in regional and global forums.

Title: Speech at a seminar titled Development of Semi-Automated MSME Lending Platforms in Commercial Banks
text: Seminar on Development of Semi-Automated MSME Lending Platforms in Commercial Banks Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : 24 May 2015 Time : 9:45 am Venue : BIBM Auditorium Mirpur, Dhaka Mr. Chair, special guest, distinguished guests from the banking industry, representatives from the public and private sectors, microfinance representatives and members of the electronic and print media, a very warm good morning to you all. I must thank DFID for their continuous support, including this Business Finance for the Poor project in Bangladesh, for expanding the opportunities of access to finance for Micro and Small Enterprises in Bangladesh through various interventions like credit guarantee scheme, challenge fund and policy environment improvement. With their technical and financial supports Bangladesh Bank is implementing this project. I am happy to be a part of this much needed intervention on Development of Semi-Automated MSME Lending Platforms in Commercial Banks of Bangladesh. We know that the absence of track record in business and lack of real assets to offer as collateral hinders the eligibility of the potential clients of the financial sector players. Banks and financial institutions were primarily geared towards serving larger urban and semi urban based big businesses. Banking industry as a whole are in general neither well motivated nor well equipped to serve MSMEs in dispersed locations far off from business places. Besides because of higher risks in MSMEs lending, they also find MSMEs loan administration costlier as building and managing MSMEs lending portfolio requires higher unit cost. Commercial banks are not always interested to finance MSMEs because of the high supervision cost. In these circumstances MSMEs find it hard to get credit for inputs procurement and other expenses. These constrain MSMEs in accessing debt finance on affordable terms. I strongly believe project like this would create enabling environment to overcome these constraints. Bangladeshs inclusive growth strategy views MSMEs as crucially important drivers of sustained broad based output, employment and income generation as it accounts for more than 40% of overall employment and 80% of industrial jobs in Bangladesh. Bangladesh Bank, which is gradually emerging as a developmental Central Bank, has adopted a comprehensive approach in addressing MSMEs financing impediments and disincentives through aligning all the lending institutions for socially and environmentally responsible financing ethos in their corporate culture. We have separate and unique strategies in developing women entrepreneurs in Bangladesh as well. Because of our interventions every financial institution is currently having separate MSE/SME business segments with dedicated women desk. I am aware of the fact that not all the financial institutions have the right approach and strategic alignment in their MSME banking approach 1 including lending technologies and portfolio management tools. We have taken various initiatives for sensitizing and capacity building of the bankers in the area of MSME Banking through various in-house initiatives and development partner supported project. One such initiative is under implementation by EU through the INSPIRED project. SME Banking training capacity of BBTA and BIBM has been significantly improved by the INSPIRED intervention and we are hopeful that the banking industry will gradually train their officials on various aspects of SME Banking using their Trainers developed project interventions. We have made the bankers aware of the importance of MSME banking and now it is the time to acquaint them how this can be done profitably. The objectives of BFP-B project include expanding bank and NBFI outreach to rural areas and to women entrepreneurs and green businesses in particular. As all of us are aware, banks and NBFIs in Bangladesh are heavily reliant on manual loan application, credit analysis and approval procedures and protocols. Credit scoring is not widely known and practised in Bangladesh, and banks and NBFIs follow the same detailed, hightransaction-cost individual credit analyses for their MSME loans that they use for larger, more profitable, corporate portfolio. As corporate loans are much larger ticket items, they are more profitable for lenders and can better bear the cost of detailed credit analysis and in terms of unit transaction cost corporate lending is much cheaper. What is needed to enable banks to reach the target MSME population is a cost-effective, yet analytically robust credit analysis and approval regime, which combines as much automation as is feasible, yet preserves the analytical integrity that will prevent unacceptably high levels of non-performing loans. This will comprehensively reduce the non-performing loans and, on the other hand, increase the portfolio profitability of lending institutions. I am sure todays seminar leader would share international best practices in lending process automation and also provides insights on how the best practice can be tailored and internalized by the local intermediaries. I am also hopeful that todays seminar will be able to sensitize bankers, in streamlining and updating their lending platforms, incorporating such innovations as credit scoring, and templatizing their approaches to credit approvals. We are very pleased to welcome Mr. Chima Nnadozie, whose experience with a leading Nigerian commercial bank in SME seems extremely appropriate to our needs here in Bangladesh. We all look forward to learning more of the approach that the Nigerian bank and the IFC pioneered in Nigeria with the hope that it will aid us as we attempt to upgrade and improve the lending capacity of our banks and NBFIs, particularly in the area of MSME lending. Thank you all for attending todays seminar. 2

Title: Speech on CSR Support to earthquake victims of Nepal on behalf of Financial Sector of Bangladesh
text: CSR Support to Nepal on behalf of Financial Sector of Bangladesh Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : 01 June 2015 Time : 5.00 pm Venue : Aamari Hotel, Gulshan Dhaka Mr. Chairperson, special guest His Excellency Mr. H. K. Shrestha, Ambassador, Embassy of Nepal, Mr. S. K. Sur Chowdhury, Deputy Governor, Bangladesh Bank, Mr. Ali Reza Iftekhar, Chairman of ABB, Mr. M. A. Hashem, Chairman of UCBL and other distinguished guests from the banking industry, representatives from BLFCA, and members of the electronic and print media, a very good evening to you all. We, the people of Bangladesh are deeply shocked and greatly sorry for the sufferings of the Nepalese people who have been severely affected during the recent devastating earthquake. After the disaster I intervened immediately and called the financial sector of Bangladesh for assistance. Out of our intention to stand by our Nepalese brothers and sisters, we have already collected and delivered 56,328 pcs of blanket and 5,507 pcs of tarpaulin to Nepal. 27 Banks and BLFCA (Bangladesh Leasing and Finance Companies Association) had provided those relief materials in response of our call. The CEOs/MDs of those banks/FIs are present here today with a view to give some relief materials as a symbol of our solidarity with the victims. Also as per our commitment, we have collected some amount of cash assistance from different banks in Bangladesh which we are going to hand over to you today. I believe that we have the responsibility to make our services more humane, and respond to any disaster or human losses as part of our social responsibilities. Recognizing that Bangladesh Bank, besides its core responsibility of maintaining price and macro stability, has been motivating all banks and financial institutions into a broad range of direct and indirect CSR engagements. Under the CSR umbrella, Bangladesh Bank has taken a number of noteworthy initiatives such as supporting the victims and volunteers of Savar Tragedy with the contribution of one day salary of our employees. Also BB and all other FIs came forward with immediate cash support from their CSR fund to stand by the Rana Plaza victims. During both the Tazreen Fashions and Rana Plaza incidents, causing well over 1100 fatalities and manifold more debilitating injuries, our financial sector and the broader business community have come forward with prompt, generous fund support for the rescue and relief efforts. Together the banking community donated Taka 1.9 billion to the 'Prime Ministers Relief Fund' for creating employment for the victims. I would like to thank the contributing banks for being so generous and prompt to response to Nepal's distress call. I believe that the religion of the whole mankind is the same. It should be our first and foremost obligation to stand beside somebody who is in distress and in need of support. I would also like to thank those organizers who helped a lot at a short notice in arranging transportation facilities to carry the relief materials including the General Manager of Bangladesh Bank Rangpur Office and last but not the least the whole team of Green Banking & CSR Department of Bangladesh Bank Head Office. Executive Director M. Mahfuzur Rahman deserves special appreciation for overall coordination and implementation of this humanitarian campaign for our nearest neighbors. Let me conclude with heartfelt gratitude to His Excellency Mr. H. K Shrestha for his time and interest on joining todays event. We feel gratified to have worked with His Excellency in this noble cause. Thank you all for your patient hearing.

Title: Speech on Financial Closing Ceremony of Summit Bibiyana ll Power Company Limited
text: Financial Closing Ceremony of Summit Bibiyana ll Power Company Limited Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : 02 June 2015 Time : 6.00 pm Venue : Pan Pacific Sonargaon Hotel, Dhaka Summit Group Chairperson Mr. Aziz Khan, honorable Energy Adviser to Prime Minister Dr. Tawfique Elahi Chowdhury; honorable State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Mr. Nasrul Hamid; distinguished guests from ADB, IFC, MIGA, IsDB; other invitees and attendees present, my warm greetings and a very good evening to you all. I heartily congratulate the Summit Group for its successful lining up of USD 210 million long term financing from ADB, IFC and IsDB for its new 341 MW combined cycle base load power plant project in Bibiyana, Sylhet costing USD 300 million with GE participation in the projects equity. The Summit Group has already established a good track record in setting up and operating larger size power generation units; their USD 345 million Meghnaghat 337 MW dual fuel combined cycle power plant financed with loans totaling USD 190 million from DEG, FMO, CDC, IDCOL, and SCB is already in operation. It is a testimony of balance sheet strength and management soundness of the Group that both local and external lenders including bilateral and multilateral development financing agencies find it worthy of taking long term credit exposure in. I am happy to be invited to this loan agreement signing ceremony for the new Bibiyana II power plant project as I personally took initiative in introducing the Summit Group to IsDB, which is participating with USD 60 million in the lending package. Power sector projects rank high in priority of the BOI external term borrowing approval committee that I chair, power supply adequacy being a key prerequisite for manufacturing and other industrial investments. From 2009 till now, the BOI Committee has approved external term borrowing totaling USD 1100 million by private sector power projects. Besides this, the private sector power projects have also accessed low cost long term financing totaling USD 128.9 million from Bangladesh Banks (BBs) IDA funded IPFF window. In Bangladesh and elsewhere in our region, dependence on external financial markets for long term project financing will persist in the near and medium term, because long term mobilization remains underdeveloped in domestic financial markets. Bangladeshs financial market does not yet have long term pension and retirement savings schemes for general citizenry, and mobilizes only short term savings, from which long term investments create liquidity difficulties from large maturity mismatch. Efforts for both interim measures and lasting market structure reforms are on for widening availability of longer term local financing for real sector investment projects. The government and BB are working together with TA support from development partners towards introducing defined contribution pension/retirement saving plans for the general citizenry including NRBs. In the interim, opening up a WB supported medium term local lending window in foreign exchange for industrial projects is nearing finalization; this will be supplemented by another BB funded medium term lending window specifically for financing greening of manufacturing units in the export oriented textiles and leather sectors. Page 1 of 2 Loans in foreign exchange entail exchange rate risk for borrowers with revenue streams in domestic currency, loans at floating interest rates add further risks of large swings in interest rates. BB is maintaining an enabling regulatory regime for hedging against these risks in local and external financial markets. A new IFC initiative of raising long term investment funds for Bangladesh by issuing Taka denominated off shore bonds will also help significantly in widening access to long term financing in Taka, relieving businesses with Taka revenue streams from exchange rate risk in foreign currency borrowing. MIGA's guarantee enhances our rating facilitating better access to international fund for large industry, investment in infrastructure projects including power sector project. I look forward to the Summit Groups success example inspiring other private sector entrepreneurs in Bangladesh towards attaining world class standards of management soundness and transparency in public disclosures, not only to enhance confidence of local and external lenders on their credit worthiness, but also to build up their ability of affordably raising debt and equity on their own credentials from capital markets at home and abroad. I heartily thank WB, ADB, IsDB and other multilateral and bilateral development partners for their increasing engagements in financing our public and private sector investment initiatives, as also in supporting our financial market development initiatives. Title: Speech on India-Bangladesh Relation: Regional Prosperity and Amity
text: India-Bangladesh Relation: Regional Prosperity and Amity Organized by: Rastrabiggan Samity Senate Bhaban, Dhaka University 5 June 2015; 10.00 am Atiur Rahman, PhD Governor, Bangladesh Bank Principal Discussant Honorable Chief Guest Dr. Gowher Rizvi, International Affairs Adviser to the Honorable Prime Minister; Special Guests Mr. Iqbal Sobhan Chowdhury, Information Adviser to the Honorable Prime Minister, and Professor Dr. A. A. M. S. Arefin Siddique, Vice Chancellor, Dhaka University; Keynote Paper Presenter Barrister Harun Ur Rashid; President of Rashtrabiggan Samity Professor Dr. Gyasuddin Molla; distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, a very good morning. It is my pleasure to attend this seminar today on India-Bangladesh Relation: Regional Prosperity and Amity; a theme very topical on the eve of the honorable Indian Prime Ministers maiden visit to Bangladesh. Erudite keynote paper presenter ex. Ambassador Barrister Harun Ur Rashid has presented us a comprehensive review of South Asian regional cooperation efforts to date, highlighting recent strong momentum gain in India-Bangladesh cooperation initiatives. Let me add a few observations on some quick gain steps forward towards deeper economic cooperation from the current low trade integration (less than 5 percent), compared to other regional associations like ASEAN, NAFTA, and European Union. Under the dynamic leadership of our Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, Bangladesh is already a robustly growing developing economy steadily gaining in macroeconomic stability and external sector strength on transition path to a higher growth trajectory. With demographic dividend of large pool of low cost labor force, Bangladesh is now a fertile base for massive volumes of new investments in the areas of manufacturing, infrastructure, education and technology which are now growing in synchronize. India, our closest large neighbor is partnering with us in promoting trade and investment linkages, with much needed investments in railway and other communication infrastructure. Cooperation in this area has much further to expand and deepen, including in developing new Special Economic Zones (SEZs). Here lies the strategic importance of Indo-Bangladesh economic engagement which will lead to win-win outcome for people of both countries Here are some other possible quick gain areas of closer Bangladesh-India economic cooperation:  Indian authorities can encourage their businesses to utilize Bangladesh as low cost manufacturing base to produce goods for local, Indian, and external markets, taking into account favored market access for exports from Bangladesh.  Indian businesses can foster more extensive trade value chain linkages with Bangladeshi manufacturers, drawing from success example in the textiles trade sector. Bangladeshi business to reciprocate in the same manner in the investment hungry North-Eastern Indian Sub-region.  Deepening and widening of trade and economic cooperation in our region require major simplification and facilitation of customs clearance procedures in overland goods flows in the trade value chains, allowing cross-border movement of cargo laden vehicles. I look forward to the new regional transit agreement to be signed shortly as a key first step in this process.  Bangladesh's seaports, land ports and rail/road arteries need major expansion and modernization for handling increasing cargo volumes of regional transit trade traffic. Here, Indian investors, both public and private will be most welcome.  India's vibrant IT, healthcare, education, training and other service sectors are much welcome to take advantage of Bangladesh's large pool of relatively low-cost youthful tech savvy manpower to set up product research/design/development, world class tertiary education, training and healthcare facilities in Bangladesh, on joint venture or wholly foreign owned basis.  Deputing renowned Indian scholars in the faculty of Bangladesh's newly established Rabindra Biswabidyala, and in our technical universities will go a long way in reinforcing cultural bonds and in R&D cooperation between the two neighbors.  Indian tour operators including travel spots of Bangladesh in itineraries of inbound tourists will likewise be mutually beneficial. I am very heartened by the news of India deciding to facilitate visa procedure for visitors from Bangladesh. People to people exchanges will help develop confidence building, which is so vital in regional cooperation. Modi-Hasina will open Border Hat.  Indian investments in development of sea port/land port and transport arteries in Bangladesh will greatly facilitate export and intra-regional trade flows.  Bangladesh and India are already cooperating in strengthening AML CFT surveillance in our region; this will help promote a regional environment that both regional and external investors will feel more secure and safe. Page 1 of 2 Indo-Bangladesh relationship born in mutual sacrifices from both countries in 1971 certainly deserves to be taken to new heights, and discussion seminars like this will help carry this forward. I thank the Dhaka University Political Science Association for their welcome initiative. Page 2 of 2

Title: Speech on Public Lecture 'Going Bust for Growth: Policies after the Global Financial Crisis'
text: Introductory remarks on RBI Governor Dr. Raghuram Rajans Public Lecture Going Bust for Growth: Policies after the Global Financial Crisis Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : 11 June 2015 Time : 7.00 pm Venue : Le Meridian Hotel, Nikunja RBI Governor Dr. Rajan, distinguished foreign and local guests from central banks, government ministries and departments, banks and financial institutions, academia, think tanks; a very good evening to you all. It is an honor and a privilege to have Dr. Rajan with us today for a stimulating, illuminating public lecture session on the approaches to restoration of growth from the post global financial crisis slowdown back onto the buoyant pre-crisis track. This topical issue is being tackled at country, regional and global levels by both developing and advanced economies, with varying degrees of success. Dr. Rajans credentials as a Bates Award winner economist of global renown, with a spell as IMF Chief Economist, hardly need introduction. While most of us around here were groping with fallouts from the global financial crisis mainly in our developing economy context, Dr. Rajan was active at the very eye of the maelstrom, in the developed world. As RBI Governor he is for quite some months now at our end of growth efforts in the developing world environment; and it would surely be very refreshing to hear his views on the best way forward in cooperation of developed and developing economies towards putting the global economy back on robust growth path. Bangladesh and other developing economies in our South Asia region weathered the global financial crisis focusing mainly on upholding domestic demand driven growth to compensate for export demand weakness precipitated by the crisis in developed advanced economies. Monetary loosening in our region had a consciously chosen inclusive financing support bias for farm and nonfarm MSME output initiatives. On the whole, this enabled us in developing economies to weather the crisis fairly well, with no sharp dip in output growth during or following the crisis. In the advanced economies Quantitative Easing and other monetary easing initiatives for stimulation of growth lacked this directional bias. Much as before the crisis, liquidity pumped in flowed largely into commodity and asset markets, leaving SMEs and other startup businesses starved of financing. The ensuing prolonged growth slowdown was therefore no surprise. But liquidity glut accompanying slow growth in advanced economies is a concern not just for those in developed economies but for us in the developing region as well. This was what precipitated the global financial crisis in the first place, and with dialog on reform of global monetary order getting nowhere, eventually may well blow up again into a new crisis. Already, unwinding of QE in advanced economies is proving hard, and traumatic also for the heavily indebted developing economies. Our warm welcome to Dr. Rajan on his maiden visit to Bangladesh, which assumes added significance from being just after honorable Indian Prime Ministers maiden visit opening up a number of new doors of investment and economic cooperation. Let me express in advance our sincere thanks and gratitude to Dr. Rajan for agreeing to address us in this public lecture, and let us now hear from him about how his keen insight and sharp intellect envision the growth quandary currently facing the global economy; and about how best we can cooperate closer in putting global growth firmly on sustained rapid path of inclusive growth in a fairer, more equitable global economic order. 1

Title: Opening Ceremony of SAARCFINANCE Symposium on Financial Inclusion
text: Opening Ceremony SAARCFINANCE Governors Symposium on Financial Inclusion Atiur Rahman, PhD Governor, Bangladesh Bank Hosted by: Bangladesh Bank Pan Pacific Sonargaon Hotel, Dhaka 12 June 2015, 9:50 am Governors/Deputy Governors from SAARCFINANCE member central banks, other distinguished guests from government ministries and departments, banks and financial institutions, business chambers, think tanks, media, and my BB colleagues, a very good morning and my warm welcome to you all in this SAARCFINANCE seminar on financial inclusion. I believe all of us present here are as enthused as myself about financial inclusion being the topic of todays SAARFINANCE Governors Symposium hosted by BB. For quite some years now, governments and central banks/financial sector authorities in all SAARCFINANCE member countries are employing financial inclusion as a tool for promoting social inclusion and social empowerment of the underprivileged population segments; with evident gains in terms of faster human development and retreat of poverty. Besides, promotion of inclusive financing for MSME output initiatives of these underprivileged population segments have yielded important gains in domestic demand driven output and employment in the SAARCFINANCE member countries, largely compensating for weakness in export led growth due to prolonged demand slack in advanced economies since the global financial crisis. Indeed, financial inclusion initiatives in the SAARC region do deserve credit for the regions post global financial crisis output growth trend at nearly twice the rate of global output growth, with intraregional trade also growing much faster than global trade growth. In Bangladesh, promotion of inclusive financing and environmentally benign green financing are going together in a BB initiative of ingraining a socially responsible financing ethos in the countrys financial sector; with concerted package of sustained thrusts on motivation, enablement, appropriate policy support. All banks and financial institutions in Bangladesh are by now fully onboard with enthusiastic engagement in inclusive and green financing initiatives, and development partners like the IDA, ADB, JICA, IFC have extended helping hand in policy support (low cost refinance lines) and TA support. The government has also helped with interest subsidy in financing for farming of some high value exotic crops. Inclusivity and environmental sustainability are now issues routinely reviewed in formulation of BBs monetary and financial policies. BB is proactively engaging in regional and global cooperation and mutual learning forums like SAARCFINANCE, APRACA, AFI, UNEP etc.; BB is now a Steering Committee member of AFI, and co-chair of its SME financing working group. It is very heartening that all SAARCFINANCE member central banks are already actively engaging in financial inclusion and green financing initiatives with encouraging performance in upholding broad based growth and macro financial stability; while central banks in advanced economies still remain tied to directionless QE with mediocre growth outcomes accompanied by risk buildups in asset and commodity markets. We SAARCFINANCE member central banks can work closer together to steal a march on our advanced economy counterparts in better sustaining our growth and stability over the longer term. Besides knowledge sharing on each others approaches towards choice of optimal options, we can perhaps combine efforts in engaging think tanks of our region in systematic impact evaluation of the various financial inclusion approaches based on cross country data, as also in establishing firm theoretical underpinnings for our initiatives by clearly identifying the feedback paths linking the inclusion initiatives with output growth, employment growth, and macro-financial stability outcomes. Establishing of such linkages will put paid to skepticisms still prevailing in central banking orthodoxies in advanced economies about appropriateness of developmental role of central banking. I hope that the country presentations of SAARCFINANCE member central banks in our sessions today will provide us fresh insights and ideas on custom tailoring inclusion initiatives best fitted with specific local environments; and that discussions following the presentations will spawn useful ideas on collectively sponsoring impact evaluation and analytical studies for establishing financial inclusion-growth-stability linkages based on cross country data from our SAARC region.

Title: Welcome Address on 44th ACU Board of Directors' Meeting
text: 44th ACU Board of Directors' Meeting Welcome Address of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : 13 June 2015 Venue : Pan Pacific Sonargaon Hotel, Dhaka ACU Board Directors, Alternate Directors, Secretary General, invited observer from Da Afghanistan Bank and other attending delegates, my warmest welcome and a very good morning to you all in this 44th ACU Board meeting here at Dhaka. In my tenure as Governor, this is Bangladesh Banks first and only turn of hosting this annual ACU event drawing together central bank leaders of our region. As a newly elected Chairman, Im expressing my sincere thanks and congratulations to my predecessor, the honorable Governor of the Central Bank of Iran for his valuable contributions towards advancing the objectives of ACU. Besides its core function of ACU intraregional trade payment settlements in a way minimizing involvement of external currencies, the ACU is also a useful platform for networking and experience sharing on issues of topical interest, including macroeconomic, financial and trade policies. In todays meeting we have a special session on discussing how recalcitrant non performing loan levels are being handled in financial sectors of the ACU member countries, with a view to gleaning lessons from each other's experiences. Further, nine of our ACU members also being members including Bangladesh being also members of the South Asian SAARCFINANCE platform, we took advantage of presence of central bank leaders here at Dhaka by holding a SAARCFINANCE seminar on the financial inclusion initiatives in SAARCFINANCE member countries. I hope you enjoy your brief stay on this occasion at Dhaka; the summer here is hot but also pleasurably mellow with rich flavors and tastes of a large variety of ripening summer fruits including mangoes, pineapples, jackfruits, black berries, lichis, melons and so forth. To help relieve tiredness from stresses of the business sessions, this evening our dinner will be accompanied by a stage show giving you some the flavor of Bangladeshs cultural life; followed further next day by a sightseeing program. In recent years economic growth of our region is consistently outpacing overall global growth by a good margin, ACU intraregional trade is also growing much faster than global trade growth. These signify our regions heightening stature as a global growth hub. Inclusive approaches in Page 1 of 2 development policies are helping the regions growth vibrancy to accelerate social progress in terms of human development and poverty decline. The severe April, May 2015 earthquakes jolting much of South Asia including Bangladesh and causing major devastation in Nepal were bolts from the blue to this upbeat comforting broad picture, bringing in large scale death and destruction. Governments and civil society organizations in the region have been prompt in extending helping hands in solidarity with the affected. Before commencing todays business sessions, let us record our condolences for those losing their lives, and our heartfelt sympathies for the bereaved, injured, and rendered homeless by the devastating spells of earthquake. Title: Speech at a Seminar on "Enhancing SME Access to Bank Financing in Bangladesh"
text: Enhancing SME Access to Bank Financing in Bangladesh Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : 18 June 2015 Time : 10.00 am Venue : A.K.N Ahmed Auditorium, BBTA, Mirpur-2, Dhaka Honorable Chairman Mr. K. M. Jamshed Uz Zaman, Principal, Bangladesh Bank Training Academy, Honorable Special Guests H. E. Mr. Pierre Mayaudon, Ambassador and Head of Delegation European Union in Bangladesh; Dr. Toufic Ahmad Chowdhury, DG, BIBM; Seminar leader Mr. K. A. M Majedur Rahman; Prof. Ali Sabet, Team Leader of the INSPIRED Project; senior bankers, distinguished guests, participants, members from the electronic and print media - a warm good morning to you all. Let me thank INSPIRED Bangladesh component III for their timely, well thought out and need based seminar series - organized for streamlining SME Banking approach and SME banking education in Bangladesh. I am indeed happy to have been able to join this concluding seminar. You all know that European Union has been and is continuing to be an important development partner for Bangladeshs development initiatives. This flagship project of the EU in the SME sector has rightly targeted the SME Banking approach, SME Banking education and training, Business Advisory services through challenge fund and improvement in the regulatory and policy areas. His Excellency indicated about the socio-economic impact of MSME sector. Today's seminar leader has also noted that MSME's contribution to GDP is 30 percent. 90 percent of private sector enterprises are MSMEs, employing 25 percent of the total labor force covering 80 percent of industrial jobs and hence, reducing rural-urban gap with faster poverty reduction. As you all know that for the last 6 years Bangladesh Bank has relentlessly been working towards developing a MSME and women entrepreneur friendly banking system. As a result of BBs initiatives, positive changes have been taken place in the banking sector as well as in the mind-set of bankers. However, the changes are not to the scale we are expecting. The slow movement of the banks and financial institutions towards a robust MSME and women entrepreneur friendly banking system is attributable to a number of factors that require careful examination and several layers of interventions in the demand side as well as supply side. However, one of the critical factors that holds back banking industry from embarking on MSME and women entrepreneur friendly financial regime is that MSME and women entrepreneurs lending is wrongly seen as risky and as such comprehensive undertaking from the banking industry in taking up a strategic approach to MSME and women entrepreneurs focused separate business line is missing. 1 With our various initiatives along with the donor intervention, this perceived high risk notion has been changing. A number of banks and NBFIs have established that MSME and Women Entrepreneurs focused banking is profitable. Todays seminar topic is timely and relevant to the industry. Repeatedly, BB is trying to convey the message to the industry that MSME and Women entrepreneurs banking are not the usual banking practices - it requires specific strategic approach, customized and tailored business model, products and business processes. In my previous messages to the industry, I emphasized that for inclusive and robust economic growth of the country we have no alternative but to put more emphasis on enhancing access to financial services for the MSMEs and women entrepreneurs targeted banking products and services. In our banking industry, many banks and NBFIs have come up with focused MSME banking strategy and tailored products and services which have proven to be effective, where profitability and social responsibility come hand in hand as profitability is the bottom line of any commercial organization like banks and NBFIs. Making MSME and women entrepreneur banking profitable, banks and NBFIs need to look back to their business segments from strategic business models to have a full understanding of the dynamics of the segment. Based on the understanding, I would rather say that the banks and NBFIs must come up with appropriate profiling, need based identification and design of product and service offerings, delivery channel(s) and tools. Designing a profitable business models for MSMEs and women entrepreneurs calls for delivering a value proposition that offers complete business solution of the target market. I would call for the banks to look into their current business model and perhaps do benchmarking exercise with local and international counterparts to build a robust and profitable business model to serve the MSME segment. The banks and NBFIs may think of packaging the value proposition combining several services both financial and non-financial to offer long term relationship to the target customers. The services could be: Liability products (deposits); Tailored credit products; Remittances services; Business advisory services; Helpline; Training on business management and other related issues; Insurance, tax and other utility (business related) services consulting; Digital marketing services including social media marketing support; Networking club; Advantage card in collaboration with other business partners and so forth. I am sure todays seminar leader Mr. K.A.M Mazedur Rahman will be providing further insights into the issue that will help the bankers understand and visualize the proposition clearly. Lastly, I would thank the EU and the INSPIRED Bangladesh component III team for their efforts and contribution towards bringing awareness among the top management of the banking industry and creation of a large stock of MSME banking trainers for continuing the initiative in the future. I personally thank H.E. Mr. Pierre Mayaudon for the EU support in Bangladesh and request him to continue and enhance support to the MSME and women entrepreneurs program of Bangladesh. Finally, I must record my appreciation for Team Leader Prof. Ali Sabet and his able team for successfully completing component-3 of the INSPIRED Project. Results of this component have been fantastic, including desired capacity building of BBTA and BIBM, change in mindset of bankers and financial executives enhances. Visibility of MSME sector, particularly the increased enthusiasm amongst unbanked, unserved women entrepreneurs. Also my thanks to my colleagues at BIBM, BBTA and, of course, the Project Director from the Ministry of Industries and all the consultants local and foreign. Thank you all. 2

Title: Inaugural Speech at a Workshop on Energy Efficiency in Industries and CEA Certificate Award Ceremony
text: Workshop on Energy Efficiency in Industries and CEA Certificate Award Ceremony Inaugural Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : August 02, 2015, Time : 10:00 am Venue : Hotel Amari Dhaka, Gulshan 2, Dhaka. Mr. M. Motiul Islam, Chairman, IIDFC, Mr. Colin Holmes, Acting Director, EG Office, USAID/Bangladesh, Mr. Craig VanDevelde, Chief of Party, CCEB, presenters and resource persons, newly certified energy auditors, participants from banks and financial institutions, representatives from Textile, RMG, Frozen Food, Steel and Jute sector, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen; my warm greetings and a very good morning to you all in this inaugural session of workshop on Best Practices in Industrial Energy Efficiency & CEA Certificate Award Ceremony. I am glad to be invited to this session because some years earlier we at BB took up several green products particularly related to energy efficiency as a key initial thrust area for promoting green financing in Bangladesh. I congratulate USAID and associates for organizing such timely and mostly demand oriented energy efficiency program and workshop that will certainly play a significant role in promoting these products and its benefits thus gradually will ensure energy security for industries in the days to come. My meeting H.E. US Ambassador and her academic team also went very well. Energy efficiency has been referred as hidden fuel by some experts. However, in case of developing economy like Bangladesh, potentials and impact of energy efficiency is massive. We need to realize the fact that the more the energy efficiency, the less pollution and environmental degradation, less reliance on imported oil, improved power scenario and ultimately cost saving. Existing energy sources as of production of electricity from gas, fossil fuel or coal result in environmental pollution due to combustion of natural resources. Such pollutions are further enhanced due to incomplete and inefficient processes. Emissions of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases from fossil fuels are contributing to changes in the Earths climate that are causing widespread harm to lives, communities, infrastructure, institutions and budgets. Sustainable energy plays a vital role in order to solve these issues. 1 Furthermore, efficient utilization of energy in industry reduces cost of goods sold which ultimately yields in higher net profit. As you may already be aware of, BB is aiming at rechanneling of all our domestic financing away from polluting high carbon traditional output practices and lifestyles towards the environmentally sustainable energy efficient, low carbon green alternatives. You will be happy to know that the utilization by Participating Financial Institutions(PFIs) of BB 2 billion green refinance fund is 95.46%. BB remains active in rendering a clear pro-green stance to the countrys domestic credit and financing policies and practices, including facilitation of raising green finance from domestic and external sources. BB has undertaken a USD350 (IDA would provide USD300 million and the rest USD 50 million would be borne by BB) million project named Financial Sector Support Project with the financial assistance of the International Development Association (IDA). The objective of the project is to improve the financial market infrastructure of the country, strengthen BBs regulatory and supervisory capacity. Part of this fund will be utilized in establishing a long term financing window for greening the manufacturing firms and export oriented industries. These manufacturing and export oriented industries may be greatly benefitted from the green auditors in identifying green and green monitoring perspective. BB is coming up with 200 million dollar Medium to Long Term Green Fund for supporting textile, leather sector and other products for water use of efficiency in wet processing; water conservation and management; waste management (solid & liquid), resource efficiency and recycling, renewable energy, energy efficiency, heat and temperature management, air ventilation and circulation efficiency and work environment improvement initiatives. The technical and supervision guidelines of green auditors must be of immense help for these green industries and products. Creating mass awareness of importance of green financing, fostering technical expertise in drawing up green project initiatives, capacity building in financial appraisal of green projects and in lining up local and external financing for these warrant massive collective efforts of all stakeholders. I believe and expect our newly established Sustainable Finance Department will take greater initiatives in areas like solar energy and green products and will need to be followed up with major scaling up and broader countrywide replication. I sincerely believe that sponsors, manufacturers, technical experts, service providers, who are present here and those who are involved in different manufacturing industries such as textile, RMG, jute, frozen food, steel etc shall engage themselves in adopting energy efficient measures. Measurement of onsite energy and water use is important but accurate measurement is critical to recognize current use and to identify opportunities to reduce use of resources. SMART Meters are intelligent electronic 2 measurement devices which record consumption/ generation of resources such as water, energy, gas and steam and automatically feeds back that information to a central location. Newly certified energy auditors acknowledged by the Association of Energy Engineers (AEE) will be able to assist them in identifying scopes of suitable and feasible options. I congratulate all certified energy auditors and AEE-Bangladesh Chapter for their massive role in providing technical guidelines and supports for energy efficiency to industries, energy and power sectors. AEE certified energy auditors have been acknowledged by a recent BB circular to review energy efficient proposals. Banks and FIs can finance industrial energy efficient options along with LED bulb, auto sensors equipments, improved cook stove, Green industry etc. shall yield in efficient energy utilization and management. This is very encouraging that USAID-CCEB program has been supporting different industries by conducting free energy audit and providing grant fund for initial boosting. I am delighted to know that the program has already conducted energy audit for 100 industries in the past 3 years. It has a target of awarding USD 2 million to 40 industries who are interested in adopting energy efficiency program. It has already identified 27 such industries and disseminating a total grant of approximately USD 1.5 million for implementing Energy Efficiency Improvement Options that is in due process. Asian Development Bank (ADB), JICA, Danida, IFC have also extended their support for such a cause. Together we can surely achieve our goal of sustainable energy management. At the end, there may be a common question for us. Can we quantify the sustainability of our factories? The solution is with us. We can use the Higg Index to measure the current sustainability status of any factory. It is a suite of assessment tools that standardizes the measurement of the environmental and social impact of apparel and footwear products across the product lifecycle and throughout the supply chain. It was introduced by the Sustainable Apparel Coalition (SAC), which is a trade organization comprising of Brands, Retailers, Manufacturers, Government, and Non-Governmental Organizations and academic experts, representing more than one third of the global apparel and footwear market. I think many of us are aware of SAC which is working to reduce the environmental and social impacts of apparel and footwear products around the world. Now, the question is, are we ready? There is no other alternatives but to be ready to make our industries green and sustainable. That is how we can achieve sustainable development. We stand by with sustainable financing arrangement for such a development. Central bank itself has gone green. My office is energy efficient and green. Largest solar plant is on our roof top. LED bulbs, censor are making green buildings of central bank. On this note of optimism let me now take the privilege of declaring the workshop open, wishing it the best all round success. Thank you all for your patient attention. 3

Title: Speech at Agrow Award 2015 organized by SCB
text: Agrow Award 2015 organized by SCB E:\Attachment\2015\August\03082015\DSC_0139.JPG Speech of the Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : 02 August 2015 Time : 5.00 pm Venue : The Westin, Gulshan, Dhaka Honorable Minister for Agriculture, Government of the Peoples Republic of Bangladesh Begum Matia Chowdhury; Abrar A. Anwar, CEO of Standard Chartered Bank Bangladesh; Members of the Jury board for Agrow Award, good evening to you all. It is an immense pleasure to be part of the Standard Chartered Agrow Award 2015 as the Special Guest. Agriculture is the most important sector of Bangladesh. This labor-intensive sector has been providing employment to the poor, helping substantially eliminate poverty, ensuring food security, earning foreign currency through export, and meeting the nutritional needs for healthy mind and body development of 160 million people of Bangladesh. Diversification of agriculture is proceeding. Despite the challenges of climate changes and population increases, the Agricultural sector of Bangladesh has shown remarkable growth and resilience to support six-plus percent annual GDP growth for more than a decade. This sector is also significantly contributing in maintaining annual CPI inflation at moderate level by contributing from the supply side. Bangladesh Bank has been active in supporting the government for improving the agriculture sector of Bangladesh. We have benefitted greatly from the prudent advice of Honorable Minister of Agriculture in designing and implementing our agricultural credit policy. The focus on financial inclusion by Bangladesh Bank has led to stability in the financial sector. We have recently announced Taka 164 billion agricultural loan program which is 5 percent higher than last fiscal year. We have also achieved 102 percent of the target of agricultural loan of last year. We have taken many initiatives in this regard such as it is now mandatory for all banks to ensure a minimum of 2.5 per cent lending to the agriculture sector. Bank accounts for farmers have crossed 13 million, and easier farm credit has helped Bangladesh emerge as a net exporter of rice and become self sufficient in a number of crops. We have advised banks to treat all these no-frill accounts as normal bank accounts so that farmers can save, receive remittance, take agricultural loans without any hassle. The maintenance of these accounts should also be free of usual charges. Further, one million sharecropper families, covering 250 Upazillas of 48 districts, have benefitted from the sharecroppers loan program initiated in 2009 with a revolving fund of Taka 5 billion. All public banks are providing bulk amount of agricultural loans including the sharecroppers. Bangladesh Bank has been providing refinance line of Taka 2 billion to livestock sector and Taka 1 billion to tea sector to acquire virgin land. I congratulate Standard Chartered Bank for coming up with Agrow Award to recognize and honor the contribution of the heroes of our agriculture sector as a part of their innovative CSR program.
