I hope this initiative will inspire our grass-root farmers, dairy, crops and livestock distributors and marketers, and supporting research and logistics industries to enhance their commitment towards further development of this sector. As Tagore said farmers alone cannot improve agriculture. Scientists and others need to stand by them. We are standing by the farmers from that objective. My heartiest congratulation goes to the nominees and winners of the Standard Chartered Agrow Award 2015. I hope this award will inspire our grass-root farmers; dairy, crops & livestock distributors and marketers; and supporting research and logistics industries to enhance their commitment towards further development of this sector. Truly, Bangladesh agriculture is a wonderful story of progress that needs to be celebrated, that deserves to be shared. I am happy to be a part of this success story. I firmly believe together we can take Bangladesh agriculture sector to a new height. Thank you.

Title: Key note speech at a workshop on Enhancing Agricultural Insurance Access for Smallhold Farmers and Entrepreneurs toward Sustainable Rural and Agricultural Development
text: BANGLADESH CAPABILITY BUILDING WORKSHOP ON ENHANCING AGRICULTURAL INSURANCE ACCESS FOR SMALLHOLD FARMERS AND ENTREPRENEURS TOWARDS SUSTAINABLE RURAL AND AGRICULTURAL DEVELOPMENT Hotel Purbani, Dhaka, Bangladesh 4-5 August, 2015 Key note speech by S.K. Sur Chowdhury, Deputy Governor, Bangladesh Bank & Chairman, APRACA Mr. Amalendu Mukherjee, Executive Vice Chairman, MRA Md. Shafiqual Haque Choudhury, President, ASA Mr. Marlowe Aquino, Project Manager, APRACA FinServAccess Project Distinguished resource persons Dear participants Ladies and Gentlemen: Good morning, It is my great pleasure to join you in this Opening Ceremony of "Bangladesh capability building workshop on enhancing agricultural insurance access for smallhold farmers and entrepreneurs towards sustainable rural and agricultural development" jointly organized by Bangladesh Bank and FinServAccess Access Project of APRACA. On behalf of Bangladesh Bank and APRACA, I would like to convey my heartiest gratitude to all of you to participate in this workshop. You are well aware that, APRACA has been involved in the promotion of rural & agricultural development and facilitation of exchange of information and expertise in rural and agricultural finance in the region since it was established in October 1977. APRACA representing 70 member institutions from 21 countries in Asia and the Pacific since its inception and the growth and development of APRACA certainly is the result of active cooperation and unsparing support of the member institutions throughout these years. You know that, access to rural finance is crucial for farm and non-farm growth in rural areas of developing countries where demand for financial services outstrips supply. In the past several decades, many rural finance policies and innovative approaches have been developed, replicated and shared in many countries of Asia and the Pacific region to improve access to and sustainability of rural financial services in order to have greater impact on the rural poor. However, despite some success in increasing outreach and impact of rural finance delivery as well as achieving viability of rural financial institutions, many challenges still persist: high fixed and transaction costs, issues in combining financial and non-financial products, stringent lending requirements, seasonality and high exposure to risks inherent in agriculture. In recent years, the rural poor have faced additional challenges due to the rising prices of food and fuel, and the effects of global financial crisis. In addition, many countries are experiencing increased incidence and intensity of natural disasters resulting from climate change. The rural finance system, including rural microfinance, has not been able to fully deal with the problem of financial access, which is now more pronouncedly compounded by the problems brought by the emerging challenges with an adverse effect on the income and resilience of the rural poor in most countries of the region. To enhance the access of the rural poor particularly smallholder farm households and agri-related rural entrepreneurs, including women and rural youth- to sustainable financial services through policy dialogues, replication of best practices, capacity building of different stakeholders and knowledge sharing in rural finance FinServAccess Project is working for the past two years in this region. The objectives of the project are:  To provide avenues for critical assessment of rural finance sector and enhanced policy dialogue among different stakeholders in the four project countries in selected rural finance thematic areas including value chain financing, risk management strategies, renewable energy financing and microfinance for agriculture.  To promote replication of rural finance best practices and approaches in IFAD-supported investment projects and selected rural finance institutions in the four project countries.  To strengthen capacities of IFAD-supported investment projects and selected RFIs in the four project countries for the provision of sustainable rural financial services.  To strengthen knowledge sourcing and sharing among APRACA members, IFAD-supported investment projects and a wider audience through a range of communication tools and instruments. The main project countries are Bangladesh and Nepal in South Asia as well as Cambodia and Myanmar in Southeast Asia. India, Indonesia, the Philippines and Thailand will be the main sources of expertise and knowledge for testing and learning financial innovations. All APRACA-represented countries will benefit from participation in project activities and dissemination. The Bangladesh capability building workshop on enhancing agricultural insurance access for small hold farmers and entrepreneurs towards sustainable rural and agricultural development is a part of this ongoing activity of FinServAccess project. Distinguished speakers have been invited from the various concerned institutions from Bangladesh who will share with us their valuable experiences on major issues, challenges, strategies, best practices in agricultural insurance. I would like to convey my warmest thanks to them and Im confident that we will be benefited greatly from their thought provoking ideas, practices and experience. It is known to you that, agriculture of Bangladesh are facing enormous challenges due to impact of various natural calamities. Countries like Bangladesh are highly dependent on the production and exports of agricultural goods where natural calamities causes considerable losses of growth and export opportunities. So to cope with these challenges, it is now the high time to adopt agricultural insurance. I hope, outcome from this regional workshop will emerge as a best policy to adopt agricultural insurance as a remedial measure of Agricultural production loses in Bangladesh. Lastly, I would like to thank all the participants from the various institutions of Bangladesh for making time for participation in this workshop. I also would like to thanks Mr. Marlowe Aquino, Project Manager, APRACA FinServAccess project to organize the workshop in Bangladesh. Thank you very much for your kind attention. __________

Title: Speech at the Launching ceremony of 'Play, Learn, Act' project jointly collaborated by British Council and HSBC
text: Launching ceremony of 'Play, Learn, Act' project jointly collaborated by British Council and HSBC Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date :12 August, 2015 Time : 10.00 am Venue : Mohakhali, Dhaka My immense pleasure to be here, in the launching ceremony of 'Play, Learn, Act' project of the British Council. I would like to express my heartfelt thanks to the British Council for bringing in such an innovative philanthropic project in Bangladesh to help our underprivileged primary school going children taught with limited facilities available in school. I also express my heartiest gratitude to the Hong Kong Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited (HSBC) for its grant assistance to this altruistic project. The mandated objective of this extensive reading project 'Play, Learn, Act' by the British Council to groom up our primary school pupils in achieving better reading, writing and communication skills will surely flourish their better articulating capacity as well as will nourish the teachers' ingenuity to nurture them. It's undoubtedly, another big annexure to many other ongoing philanthropic activities by the British Council and the HSBC. Ladies and gentlemen, let me recount briefly some of BB's initiatives to bring the poor family children out of their inherited impediments. Bangladesh Bank (BB), the central bank of Bangladesh has been reorienting country's entire financial sector to the socially responsible financing ethos, which include uplifting our school children and street children, in sync with Government's various initiatives of assisting poor students to continue their studentships along with enhancing e-education even in the remote areas of the country to grow them up as tech savvy generation. BB's directive of providing nofrill accounts opening facilities to the school and street children at very affordable costs to the scheduled banks has been facilitating our kids to be familiar with banking services as well as growing savings habit among them from very childhood. It's inspiring that since its beginning in 2011, 886 thousand school banking accounts have been opened till March, 2015 with an outstanding balance of Taka 8.23 billion. Moreover, BB's financial literacy campaign has been helping school children to get acquainted with basic financial know-how beyond their regular school curricula. BB's corporate social responsibility (CSR) directives encourage the financial institutions to donate to the educational institutions for various purposes, including development of class room environment through modernization of class room infrastructure. It's heartening that under benevolent CSR activities, many financial institutions have been providing scholarships to the poor meritorious students, paving their path to higher education trajectory. Bangladesh Bank welcomes any initiative that aims to facilitate the education level of poor family children which in the long run helps them come out of vicious poverty circle. I highly appreciate this laudable initiative by British Council and the HSBC . I wish a grand success of this great initiative. Thank you all for your patient hearing.

Title: Speech at the National Convention on 'Financial Literacy and it's Impact on Inclusive Finance' organized by InM
text: National Conference on Financial Literacy and its Impact on Inclusive Finance organized by InM Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : 19 August 2015 Time : 2.15 pm Venue : Carnival Hall, BICC, Dhaka Good afternoon and greetings for honorable session chair, keynote paper presenter, panelists, and all others in the audience. Let me begin with my thanks to the InM for inviting me to this national dialogue session on financial literacy and Financial inclusion in Bangladesh. I congratulate Dr. Baqui Khalily and Mr. Pablo Mia for the research they have conducted on the status of financial literacy and of the financial literacy-financial inclusion nexus in Bangladesh. Mainstreaming of inclusive, environmentally sustainable financing figure high in BBs priority; and stocktaking of financial knowledge base of the target population segments is therefore a very welcome step. Findings of this research based on data gleaned from the InMs 2014 national survey on access to financial services being consistent with those from previous empirical studies broadly affirms the validity of the approach taken by Dr. Khalily and Mr. Pablo Mia in this study. The main findings of the study include: i) Enhanced knowledge about banking leads to greater formal access to finance; ii) Age and education also have positive relationship with access to finances; iii) MFI is important factor for FI; iv) Groups such as females, elderly people, people without higher education, people living in rural areas, laborers suffer from financial exclusion. We need such surveys both as baselines at the start, and also in periodical rounds of iterations assessing the cumulating gains in financial literacy and the impact thereof on our progress towards our financial inclusion goals. Erudite panelists have already discussed the study at length; I do not need to dwell further on this other than pointing out that it opens up many new avenues for useful further investigation. I remember that group-based microcredit began in Bangladesh with short periods of pre-lending group training sessions rendering rudiments of financial literacy to the group members. A survey in the microcredit client segment can assess the usefulness of this approach if still in use, and look into reasons if not, including what has substituted it. SME lending promotion is ongoing for some years now; a survey can look into information packages being offered by lenders to their startup SME client segments, assessing the usefulness of the financial literacy content of the information packages for this target client segment. Similar surveys can usefully be conducted also on Mobile phone based Financial Service (MFS) client segment, green financing client segment, capital market investor client segment, insurance sector client segment, and so forth. Such a series of client segment focused surveys and analyses will bring out financial literacy gaps and needs on financial services at all strata, primary, secondary and tertiary. The work burden of the segmented surveys and analyses can be shared among InM, SME Foundation, IDRA, BSEC, and BB. Reputed universities can also be co-opted to get some of this work done by their graduate students as part of thesis/project work course requirements. BBs 2015 Strategic Plan action agenda includes drawing up of a financial inclusion strategy paper for Bangladesh. The recently initiated UKAID supported Business Finance for the Poor Project has also a similar item in its action agenda. If taken up in right earnest, findings of the suggested client segment focused survey findings will provide crucially useful inputs for the financial literacy content of these strategy papers to be drawn up on financial inclusion. It may be possible for BB to extend modest fund support for the surveys on SME, MFS, green financing client segments; and I presume that modest financing support sources for the other segments may also be possible from InM, SME Foundation, IDRA, and BSEC.

Title: Speech at National Seminar on "Bank Finance in Light Engineering Small Enterprises in Bangladesh: Challenges and possible innovations
text: National Seminar on Bank Finance in Light Engineering Small Enterprises in Bangladesh: Challenges and possible innovations Chief Guest Mr. S.K Sur Chowdhury Deputy Governor, Bangladesh Bank Mr. President Director General, Bangladesh Institute of Bank Management, Dr. Toufic Ahmad Chowdhury, Distinguished Panel discussant, Research team members, members of the electronic and print media, distinguished audience a very warm good morning. I am very much privileged to be here in this national seminar on challenges and possible innovation in bank finance for the light engineering sector of Bangladesh. Light Engineering has been in focus as one of our potential industrial sector that can meet our domestic demand and be an alternative product in our export basket. Government and Bangladesh Bank as well as bankers are continuously trying to improve the condition of the sector by taking up and implementing various projects and programs. Small enterprises (SEs) play an important role in both developing and developed countries in the process of industrialization and economic growth. They are major drivers of industrial development and economical advancement. In terms of contribution toward balanced and sustainable growth, employment generation, development of entrepreneurial skills, small enterprises play a very significant role in a developing economy like Bangladesh as it is characterized by low per capita income, high level of unemployment, mass poverty and social deprivation. Small Enterprises generally use local resources to produce goods and services for local needs. They are more efficient in resource allocation as compared to large scale industry from a social point of view. In Bangladesh, SME sector contribute 25% to the GDP, about 40% of gross manufacturing output, account for 90% of the private sector enterprises and about 70% to 80% of the non-agricultural workforce working in the sector which is around 25% of the countrys total labor force. However, direct contribution of small Enterprise sector to GDP can be enhanced significantly to boost up the inclusive economic growth in the country. Todays national seminar has taken one of the key economic sectors i.e. light engineering where most of the enterprises are micro to small categories. At present, all the developing countries as a part of their development strategy have been intensifying their efforts to develop light engineering sector which acts as prime mover for growing a countrys industrial base. These industries have potentials to make enormous contribution towards technological and economic development along with wide opportunities for saving foreign currencies and employment generation. The sector has been playing a key role as support to all other industries by supplying various types of machineries and spare parts, and also industrial units and capital machinery. They provide strong & vital support to other sectors of the economy. Realizing its importance, the Government of Bangladesh has declared the sector as a most priority sector in its Export Policy 2009 and thrust sector in its Industry Policy  2010 along with 10% cash incentive for the export of light engineering products. Light engineering firms in our country spread over many sectors like spare parts, light manufacturing, machining, agro-machineries and like others. Light engineering has the power to feed the local need for imported spare parts while they can become one of the major export industries by partnering with international auto and other equipment manufacturers either as supply chain partners or in alliance with them in producing spare parts for the international markets. The light engineering industries enjoy a certain number of advantages including cheap labor, lower capital investment, lower job-creation cost, low risk factor, shorter start- up period, lower capital output ratio, less management problem, lower energy cost, moderate infrastructure requirement, promotion of entrepreneurial talents, more environment friendly production process, and promotion of agro  industrial linkages. These advantages indicate huge opportunity of the sector and thus the government should emphasis more for accelerating the rapid growth of this sector. These small industries are engaged in manufacturing and can reduce poverty, to some extent, by generating more employment through producing various import-substitute products. This sector depend less on imported inputs, can cater to both domestic and export markets and are better distributed regionally than larger firms. Therefore, it is necessary to build up the strong industrial base within the country by extending necessary support to the Light Engineering Sector for manufacturing the small machineries, spare parts which are locally desirable. In spite of having various advantages and opportunities, this sector is facing several multidimensional problems. Bangladesh Bank and commercial banks are providing funds to these light engineering enterprises all over the country. However apart from the financing problem the sector are also facing other challenges as well. Most of the businesses of this industry are still largely dependent on imported for machinery, equipment and use conventional technology in production process. Due to non-existence of Common Facility Centre (CFC), the light engineering firms do not have access to necessary services like metal testing, CNC technology training and heat treatment facility. These services are required to ensure quality product on larger scale. The high price of some raw materials like scrap, sorted scrap, plain carbon steel, alloy steel, furnace oil, copper alloys, stainless steel, etc. leads to increase the output price. As a result, they lag behind their foreign competitors. Light engineering firms use conventional technology due to lack of availability of skilled manpower and also lack of quality certification for which local machines and spare parts face branding problem compared to imported product. As a result most of the local buyers are reluctant to buy the domestic products. The present initiative of Bangladesh Institute of Bank Management is praiseworthy. I have gone through the report of the researcher and I found that they have analyzed the issue in question in great length and have come up with several recommendations to improve the challenges faced by both supply side and demand side actors in improving the bank financing to this sector. As the sector has potential to build up the base of heavy and high value adding industrial base we should take concerted efforts to further the development of the sector. I would like to place call for joint efforts by the sector associations and the bankers to remove the challenges and bringing in innovations in the area of product design, lending procedures, process improvement, recovery and delinquency management. Supply side innovation will help the bankers to better serve the sector while demand side innovation will help the entrepreneurs to do better business, expand and diversify product market which will be beneficial for them to repay the bankers timely and also look for product innovation, quality improvement and grab export opportunity. This way we can build a vibrant light engineering sector which will pave the way towards developing heavy industry like auto manufacturing and assembling and manufacturing of spare parts in the country. Solution to only financing problem will not bring the expected results unless we address other critical factors that are hindering the growth of the sector like technological improvement, skill development, fiscal and other economic support to the sector. The present government has given due importance to the small enterprise sector in achieving inclusive economic growth through utilizing the potentials of MSME sector in the country. Recently Government has taken a skill development program with the support from ADB to improve the supply of skilled labor for the MSME sector in Bangladesh and light engineering is one of the key sectors under this program. Bangladesh Bank is also implementing one component of the project. I would call for concerted efforts by the private sector as well as public sector to work closely to realize the potential of the sector and help the country to achieve middle income country status by 2021. Finally I would like to request the research team to take the suggestions, comments and feedback from todays seminar on the issue seriously and revise the seminar output and share it with all stakeholders so that informed policy decision and actions can be initiated based on the findings of the research team. I would like to personally thank the research team for their excellent effort and for the report they have produced based on field survey of the bankers and sector enterprises around the country. I am sure this output will definitely enrich the existing knowledge repository on the sector which will help future researcher as well. Thank you all for your valuable time and thanks to those who have contributed by providing, comments, suggestions and feedback.

Title: Speech at the First International Conference on Digital Education
text: Special Guest Address by Bangladesh Bank Governor Dr. Atiur Rahman at "The First International Conference on Digital Education" Organized by BacBon Foundation, BacBon Ltd and Center on Budget and Policy, University of Dhaka Date : September 2, 2015 Time : 12.30 pm Venue : Nabab Nawab Ali Chowdhury Senate Bhaban, University of Dhaka Mr. Chair, Dr. M. Abu Eusuf, Director, Center on Budget and Policy, University of Dhaka, Honorable Vice-Chancellor of the University of Dhaka Dr. A A M S Arefin Siddique, Guest of Honor of todays conference His Excellency the Ambassador of Japan Mr. Masato Watanabe, Chief Guest of the Conference Honorable Minister of Education Mr. Nurul Islam Nahid, Event Speaker Honorable Vice-Chancellor of Daffodil International University Dr. Yousuf Mahbubul Islam, distinguished Keynote Speakers Professor Yonekura Seiichiro, Hitotsubashi University, Japan and Mr. Youshida, CEO, NetLearning Inc., other presenters, speakers and participants, a very good afternoon to you all. I would like to convey my heartfelt thanks to the organizers specially the young fresh blood Mr. Maheen Matin, Founder of BacBon Foundation and BacBon Ltd. It's very heartening to see that beside numerous government and nongovernment initiatives and concurrent projects, our young generation is also taking many innovative initiatives to materialize the dream of nation to build 'Digital Bangladesh' in the near future. I must appreciate the continuous assistance of our time tested friends from Japan, who are helping us with their expertise as well as opening several doors of financing support to Bangladesh. Today's event The 1st International Conference on Digital Education is a very timely initiative in helping materialize country's long-standing aspiration of freeing Bangladesh from poverty, creating qualified human capital, wiping out disparity in the field of quality education amongst each segment of the population, irrespective of remote rural and urban areas. I would also like to express my appreciation for the Backbon Foundation's support for our disadvantaged students and their teachers in distant rural areas in terms of providing quality education lessons and techniques of expert teachers of renowned institutions through multimedia facilities under its 'e-Education Project'. You have heard Professor Seiichiro and Professor Youshida about the significant impact of E-education on various aspects of quality education. The outcomes are indeed effective and praiseworthy, leading to dynamic learning. This helps students become interactive and creative. Ladies and gentlemen, you may already know that in sync with government's multifarious efforts of achieving 'Digital Bangladesh' by 2021, Bangladesh Bank (BB), the central bank of Bangladesh has already reoriented its entire financial sector to ingrain the ethos of socially responsible financing with the enablement of financial digitization in full scale. Of course, BB is also very cautious about the emanated risks of digitization and their remedial measures. BB has not only digitized its operations by equipping its human resources through several trainings on Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP), Enterprise Data Warehouse (EDW), and various ICT and e-commerce related services but also it has been helping educational institutions, community organizations and non-governmental organizations in und as well as that of other financial institutions. BB has made it obligatory for the financial institutions to provide one-third of their CSR fund for education purpose including scholarships to the students of disadvantaged families living in remote areas like chars and haors. The educational CSR support was about Taka 234 crore in 2014 and first half of 2015. In addition, BB has provided regulatory space for developing e-commerce, outsourcing, and software development, which are enabling thousands of youths to get jobs and motivating some of them to emerge as successful entrepreneurs. The modernization of payment system has been a breakthrough in our financial transaction including introduction of Automatic Clearing House, Electronic Fund Transfer Network, National Payment Switch and RTGS (pretty soon); BB's mobile financial services, extensively lauded by international communities, transacting currently Taka 460 crore daily have been reaching off-branch remittance services to the mass people's doorstep in faster, hassle-free delivery mode. BB's financial literacy program has also been pursuing a wide range of population segments including the adult and school children. School banking directives of BB have attracted millions of our young kids to get bank accounts at a nominal cost of Tk.100 only; this initiative is not only helping our school children to get the knowledge of basic banking services but also motivating them to acquire savings habit from the very childhood. '10 Taka' accounts for the farmers, street children, cleaners, disadvantaged population segments and even for the third gender are part of BB's some of the developmental central banking innovations aimed at providing inclusive financial services to the masses. You will be happy to know that apart from existing apps in BB website, several other apps for getting latest information on priority areas such as women entrepreneurs and green financing will be available very soon. BB's latest move of engagement with social media such as Facebook and Twitter to disseminate information of its activities and to receive quick feedbacks or queries from the masses, especially from the students is yet another sign of BB's strict adherence to the motto of fast expanding digital financial inclusion. This is in addition to our on-going CIPC, hotline, dashboard etc. All of BB's initiatives, well coordinated with its mandated objective of monetary and financial stabilities, are aimed to help Government achieve its Vision 2021 and hence, materialize its dream of making Bangladesh an upper middle income country by 2030. For that to happen, improving human capital and reducing economic vulnerabilities are crucial. Over and above, we must enhance the speed of our inclusive growth process. And for all this, there is no way out except quality education for all. We welcome any private sector and non-governmental engagement, such as the one by the Backbon Foundation to come forward with such high spirit of reaching quality education to the disadvantaged students in each corner of the country, who suffer from lack of qualified teachers and teaching materials. I would like to take the privilege to urge the attending Japanese friends to continue their generous supports to our NGOs and other initiatives for expanding the scope of inclusive, digitized quality education campaign. Distinguished guests and audience, Bangladesh, the land of ample opportunities and hope, is on board to create countrywide tech savvy young generation to reap the highest benefit of our current demographic dividends and to eradicate vicious circle of poverty; I believe government's endeavors will get its best outcome only when people like you extend your able hands to lift our poor human capital to higher level of skills. I wish this important gathering will unfold many productive avenues to close prevailing gaps of quality education in rural areas and even many of the urban vicinities. I do wish great success of Backbon Foundation's creative endeavors. Last but not the least, I sincerely hope that many of our educated youths will be inspired by Mr. Maheen Matin to come forward with innovative models to unlock existing impediments in many other areas besides education which of course, remains our first priority. Let's make E-education a social movement, a change maker, game changer. Thank you all for your patient hearing.

Title: Speech at the Launching of the Millennium Development Goals: Bangladesh progress Report 2015
text: Launching of the Millennium Development Goals: Bangladesh progress Report 2015 Atiur Rahman, PhD Governor, Bangladesh Bank Special Guest Pan Pacific Sonargaon, Dhaka 16 September 2015, 11:00 AM My warmest congratulations to Dr. Shamsul Alam for a very heartening and elaborate presentation of the report on Bangladeshs performance in attaining the 2015 Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) and on Bangladeshs new post 2015 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) for 2030 that are identical or convergent with the UN sponsored global SDGs. This presentation aptly reflects the spirit of Rio20 where I too participated which aimed at making smooth transition to SDGs from MDGs. Besides, Intergovernmental Working Group, a High Level Political Forum was established to carry this process forward. Bangladesh has been a very active partner of this process of transition. That is how together we have been able to build up a 'Global Shared Vision' which 70th UNGA will endorse this month at the UN Headquarters. A close look at the succession of Bangladeshs development strategy, plan and policy documents over four plus decades now would reveal these to be underpinned by a broad social consensus aspiring for inclusive, equitable and environmentally sustainable socioeconomic growth leaving no one behind, as espoused in the new UN SDGs. I would attribute Bangladeshs successes in attaining or exceeding most of the 2015 MDGs in large measure to the inclusive development agenda of the government with active participation of citizens in the various development initiatives. In the process, Bangladesh has emerged as a role model to the rest of the world with sustained, stable 6% equitable and environmentally sustainable economic growth for more than a decade amid external shocks like the Global Financial Crisis. We hope to get into the new trajectory of 7 percent growth rate from current fiscal year. Major macroeconomic indicators such as inflation, exports, remittance earnings, fiscal position, and so forth remained benign over the last decade. Along with sound macroeconomic fundamentals, performance on the social indicators have been quite commendable, particularly in the area of poverty alleviation, education, income and gender equality, adaptation to climate changes, reduction of infant and maternal mortality, and Page 1 of 2 women empowerment. With steady economic and social performance, Bangladesh has proudly joined the (lower) middle income group recently. We are now proceeding steadfastly to attain the upper middle income status in the coming decade or so. That the attainments were possible even as external assistance fell far short of expectations is a further affirmation that a proactive inclusive policy agenda as reflected in the national budgets and plans of the government supported by social consensus driven citizens engagement has played major role, and I believe it will play similar role also in attainment of the new 2030 SDGs. I believe further deepening of citizens engagement alongside our public initiatives will heighten our development performance by enhancing transparency in roles, responsibilities and accountabilities of institutions and individuals implementing the development initiatives. Like other governmental organs and public institutions, Bangladesh Bank is proactively supporting and carrying forward the governments multifaceted development initiatives. The financial sector has been playing a crucial role of mobilizing financing resources and allocating these efficiently to real sector output initiatives; and Bangladesh Bank, the countrys monetary and financial sector regulator is in a position of influencing the financial flows away from support of wasteful, environmentally unsustainable output practices and lifestyles in the real sector towards inclusive financing support for environmentally sustainable output and lifestyle options for all population segments. This is what we at Bangladesh Bank are pursuing avidly in supporting attainment of the governments MDGs and SDGs; with our CSR, financial inclusion and green financing mainstreaming initiatives in the financial sector. These initiatives are in turn cascading down and influencing output, consumption and lifestyle practices in businesses and households in the real sector towards the desired socially and environmentally responsible directions, boosting and underpinning sustainable growth and development. BB is also pursuing steady opening up and integration of our financial sector with the global financial markets, to help mobilize domestic and external financing in the massive volumes that the 2030 SDGs will require, besides such concessional assistance as may be forthcoming from global partnerships. No less important will be the broadening of tax base and crackdown on corruption and illicit financial outflows, as rightly highlighted by the Intergovernmental Committee of Experts. To conclude, I am much gratified and enthused by Dr. Shamsul Alams presentation of Bangladeshs latest progress towards MDGs, and the new SDGs for 2015-2030, striking all the right notes and wholly in sync with the UN sponsored global SDGs. Bangladesh Bank will continue to engage proactively in our governments and citizenrys efforts of attaining or exceeding these goals; as before in ways that bolster rather than compromise macroeconomic and financial stability. Thank you all for your patient attention. Page 2 of 2

Title: Guest of Honor's address in the MPB program inaugural event at the University of Dhaka
text: Guest of Honors address by Bangladesh Bank Governor Dr. Atiur Rahman in the MPB program inaugural event at the University of Dhaka Date : October 18, 2015 Time : 4.30 pm Venue : Senate Bhaban, University of Dhaka Distinguished Chairperson the Dean of Business Studies Faculty Professor Shibli Rubayat-Ul-Islam, Honorable Chief Guest Vice Chancellor Professor Dr. A A M S Arefin Siddique, Special Guests Mr. Richard Staunton and Professor Dr. Md. Kamal Uddin, other distinguished guests and attendees; my warmest greetings and a very good evening to you all. I am indeed deeply gratified and honored to be invited to this inaugural ceremony of the Master of Professional Banking (MPB) degree program first time launched in the country in the Department of Banking and Insurance in my Alma Mater the University of Dhaka, one of the few cradles of tertiary education and research in South Asia, as always in the forefront with new initiatives responding to new needs emerging from our regions sustained growth and development dynamism. My heartiest congratulations to the Business Studies Faculty Dean and the honorable Vice Chancellor for carrying forward this tradition of readiness in identifying and responding to upcoming new needs. Our avowed national aspiration of joining the community of advanced economies by early years of the decade of forties will entail a faster than ever before pace in opening up and integration of our trade and investment linkages with the global economy. This in turn will entail matching rapidity in further opening up and integration of our domestic banking and financial markets with the global financial markets, anchored securely in institutional soundness and capability of attracting from the global savings pools new investment resources in the massive volumes needed in meeting our growth and development aspirations. Increasing openness and integration with the global economy will necessarily bring in tow increasing vulnerability of our domestic financial institutions and markets to risks from destabilizing swings in the global markets. Equipping our financial sectors current and future human resource pools with state of the art knowledge and capabilities in managing the diverse range of risks; and instilling in them a socially responsible inquisitive, innovative mindset in addressing the inclusivity and environmental sustainability 1 imperatives of the new 2030 global SDGs unanimously adopted in the UNGA in September 2015, are in my view two overriding priority areas for our academic community to play key role in. These priorities in course programs on banking and finance would be best served not by treating individual subjects in separate silos but instead in cross-cutting holistic approaches highlighting interconnectedness of the various subjects, with reference to the overarching global best practices in corporate governance, accounting and auditing, capital adequacy, liquidity, leverage and disclosure comprehensiveness in financial and sustainability reporting. Emerging trends in new priority areas of financing infrastructure projects, green and social impact investments, inclusive financing of productive MSME initiatives and so forth need adequate coverage in the course contents. I trust the course curriculum for the new MPB program has been designed with due attention to these priorities, but would nevertheless suggest frequent revisiting of the curriculum, flexibly accommodating to any perceived adjustment need. Equipping our financial sectors current and future manpower pool with state of the art knowledge base in traditional areas of safeguarding institutional soundness and stability, and at the same time instilling in them an innovative mindset anchored in an ethos of socially responsible inclusive, environmentally sustainable financing will be just as exciting and stimulating a journey of discovery for our academic community as it has been for Bangladesh Bank (BB) in its steadfast countrywide promotion of socially responsible inclusive green financing. BBs track record demonstrating successful use of socially responsible financing as a stability enhancement tool has attracted widespread attention and recognition in the global community, so would pioneering initiatives of mainstreaming these new financing approaches in core course curriculums in centers of tertiary education and research in Bangladesh and elsewhere. I am much glad to note that the Department of Banking and Insurance is planning for academic collaboration with external organizations in conducting the new MPB program, and I congratulate the department for the collaboration agreement it has already concluded with ACCA, an external partner. BB will remain ready and willing in extending a facilitating hand in the new Programs forging of potentially useful new collaboration agreements with new external and local partner entities. Hosting for short spells guest 2 faculty members with extensive experience in the financial services industry besides the required academic background may also be useful in enhancing practical relevance of the course contents offered in the program. It's very heartening to know through this event that from now on the meritorious students from the Banking and Insurance Department will receive RI Khan scholarship in memory of the renowned banker Rafiqul Islam Khan, father of current Business Faculty Dean Professor Shibli Rubayat-Ul-Islam. I do appreciate the benevolent activities of ACI group and their gold medal awarding to the top result holder in Banking and Insurance Department. I also duly appreciate the personal endeavor of Mr. Dilip Das Gupta to provide financial assistance to this department students. Let me conclude with thanks and congratulations to the University of Dhaka and its Faculty of Business studies for launching the new MPB program, earnestly wishing it to be a stimulating and rewarding new journey on the path towards excellence. Thank you all for your patient attention. 3

Title: Speech at 2nd Bangladesh Economists' Forum (BEF) Book Launch Event: 'Bangladesh Vision 2030'
text: 2nd Bangladesh Economists Forum (BEF) Book Launch Event: Bangladesh Vision 2030 Speech of the Hon'ble Governor Bangladesh Bank Date : 24 October, 2015 Time : 9:30 AM Place : BBTA Honorable Chief Guest Bangladesh National Parliament Speaker Dr. Shirin Sharmin Chowdhury, erudite BEF members including those authoring and editing the new flagship BEF publication Bangladesh Vision 2030, Honorable State Minister of Finance and Planning Mr M A Mannan, MP, Mr Syeduzzam, former finance minister, my respected predecessors Dr. Mohammed Farashuddin and Dr. Salehuddin Ahmed, Professor Wahiduddin Mahmud, Dr Hossain Zillur Rahman, Mr. Manzur Elahi, Dr. Shamsul Alam, member, GED, Planning Commission, Mr. Enam Ahmed Chowdhury, Former Secretary, ERD and advisor to Chairperson, BNP and other attending distinguished development professionals and academics, a very good morning to you all. Dr. Sadiqs welcome address and Dr. Mohiuddin Alamgirs statement outlining the development achievements and aspirations embodied in Bangladesh Vision 2030 have already given us rich flavors of what to expect in the new flagship BEF publication outlining multitrack, multi-dimension pathways for needed concerted progress, on multiple fronts in pacing up our inclusive, sustainable, socioeconomic growth and development momentum, towards attaining higher middle income country status by 2030 and advanced economy status by the early years of decade of forties. Illuminating, insightful remarks from our chief guest the honorable Speaker of Bangladesh National Parliament following her formal launching of the new book, have enlightened us further on important aspects of our development challenges and opportunities. In my view, comprehensiveness of coverage, objective appraisal of traits of strengths and weaknesses, and a confident optimism, solidly grounded on Bangladeshs broad social consensus for inclusive, equitable socioeconomic development are the defining features of this new BEF publication, bringing together papers presented in the first BEF conference held in 2014 by BEF founder members, erudite academics and seasoned development professionals. I believe that even a cursory browsing through, of this voluminous publication, would evoke in Bangladeshi readers, a sense of enthusiasm and engagement for the countrys growth aspirations and efforts; not least because we succeeded in crossing over the lower middle income country group income threshold expected for 2021 as early as in 2014. I, Page 1 earnestly look forward to seeing the broadest possible dissemination of this new publication, among our policy makers, academia, development professionals and civil society organizations; both for deepening discourse and debate on development issues and for stimulating new activism on the multiple fronts and dimensions comprehensively covered in the publication. Let me take this opportunity to share with you my perspectives on some of the major pathways for growth and development, highlighted in the publication, in light of the current state of play in the global and local scenes. We cannot possibly rely as much on export led growth as we expected earlier, given that the potential gains from the thrust of WTO led trade liberalization and globalization have largely run their course. Global trade growth is no longer outpacing even the current tepid global output growth, and is actually trailing it. Developed economies and some of the developing economies are seeking to uphold trade driven growth by shaping up new plurilateral trade blocs, outside the WTO framework for preferential trade between bloc members. Countries outside the trade value chains of these blocks are going to face heightening barriers for their exports to markets in these blocks. Joining one of such blocks will not be an easy option for lower income economies like Bangladesh either; the heavy social costs of immediate withdrawal of the remaining few protections for domestic producers required in joining such blocks, may not be always politically feasible. Yet we must remain focused on removing anti export bias, if any. Domestic demand driven growth is therefore the alternative that we will have to rely more on. This though is no cause for despair and entirely doable in our economy, with rising income in the large domestic market with population of 160 million. In Particular, our rising middle and affluent class is going to be a source of new demand for tech savvy outputs and services. In addition, Governments seventh five year plan and Bangladesh Banks five year strategic plan have together articulated these desired priorities. Efficient land use planning has emerged now as another new high priority area of attention for Bangladesh; with scarcity and high cost of land suitable for sitting industrial projects seriously impeding new foreign and local investment, and with sprawls of low rise rural habitats shrinking the area under agricultural production. We need new in depth work on appraisal and policy options for addressing this issue snagging progress on our growth path. Fortunately the new authority on Economic zones led by Honorable Prime Minister herself is very serious about identifying khas and even private lands for developing at least 100 economic zones with all regulatory comfort and required services for the investors. A number of private economic zones have already been allowed to be developed and they have started their ground work. Adaptation to looming global warming driven sea level rise threats facing our vulnerable population segments, and the needed broader countrywide transition to energy efficient low emission environmentally sustainable output practices and lifestyles are in my view the other major new priority areas for attention. Bangladesh Governments and BBs pioneering initiatives in these areas have already earned global recognition, but our initial Page 2 steps need to be followed up by much more broad based engagement of experts, academics, entrepreneurs and civil society activists. Simultaneously, our tariff structure needs to be redesigned, refined and made transparent to attract global actors in renewable energy projects. I would like next to doubly underline the high priority already accorded in the BEF publication to good governance and strengthening of institutions in addition to improving our human skills, which of course, government has already started focusing on. Our education system must now respond to this urgent call if we really want to remain productive and competitive in the global trade. Public institutions like the monetary, financial and capital market regulators in Bangladesh have suffered much from undue external influence denying them free hand in decisions on licensing, regulation and supervision of financial markets and institutions; management efficiency in some SOEs has remained abysmal for much the same reason, eroding accountability and entailing enormous drain on public resources. Only full empowerment of institutions in pursuing clearly defined objectives can bring efficiency by making these fully accountable for results. The need for good governance and accountability is paramount not only in the executive, but also in the other organs of governance including the legislative and judiciary, for upholding equitable, socially just and environmentally sustainable socioeconomic growth and development. Our next session is going to be on this topical issue of strengthening institutions. Let me conclude here with our heartfelt thanks and gratitude to our honorable chief guest for gracing this book launch event with her presence. I want to thank in particular Dr. Toufic Ahmad Choudhury, DG, BIBM and his team for publishing their volume. Many thanks to Principle, BBTA, my young from Bangladesh Bank and also Dr Ashikur of PRI and his team for making this event successful. Thank you so much to all of you. Page 3

Title: Speech at Go Live Ceremony of RTGS
text: Go Live Ceremony of RTGS Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : 29 October, 2015 Time : 10.15 am Venue : Jahangir Alam Conference Hall, Bangladesh Bank Mr. Chairperson, Deputy Governors, Executive Directors, General Managers and other fellow colleagues of Bangladesh Bank, high officials from banking industry, representatives of CMA Small Systems Ltd, Sweden, SWIFT, TCS, Spectrum and other organizations and members of printing and electronic media wishing all of you Good Morning. Today is a very exciting day for all of us indeed. The voyage which started with automation of cheque clearing system, today completing its first ever milestone by introducing countrys first real time, high value (upto one lac Taka), and gross settlement based clearing system: Bangladesh Real Time Gross Settlement (BD RTGS) system. In between, we took care of countrys first instruction based settlement system and interoperable card based system. Now, we proudly compare our payment and settlement system to any other payment system around the globe. From the bottom of my heart I congratulate the whole banking community, CMA Small Systems AB, Spectrum Engineering Consortium Ltd, SWIFT and all others concerned as well as the officials of Bangladesh Bank and participating banks who travelled with us to make it possible. I am very pleased to welcome you all in this auspicious occasion of the inauguration of BD RTGS. This is indeed another milestone achievement in our digital payment system. With the financial assistance of Asian Development Bank under the project Institutional Support for Migrant Workers Remittances, BD RTGS is implemented under Component A: Remittance and Payment Infrastructure Development. Timely completion of the project portrays the relationship that both of these esteem organizations share and I hope we will also work together in future to transform many of our dreams into reality. The job of transforming the countrys payment system to a most modern and fully digital one from scratch, for a developing country like Bangladesh, was not at all an easy task. Dedicated team within Bangladesh Bank rendered their best efforts for implementing this. To cope with the changes of time our banking sector has embraced new technologies very promptly. RTGS is a great achievement for the banking sector of Bangladesh which should also be treated as a landmark in the achievement of dream of Digital Bangladesh of the current government. 1 The system will have a substantial impact on current operations in the banks, particularly in the area of treasury, payment division, corporate banking and cash management. Banks will need to implement new strategies, processes, systems and organization. Trading in intra-day liquidity and efficient fund transfer will provide a boost to the secondary bond market which in turn offers opportunity to earn revenue. We will be more confident about critical systemically important payment transfers. Last but not the least, establishment of state of art payment infrastructures will convey a clear signal about our concerted effort of digitization in Bangladesh to NRB and foreign investors to remit, transfer and invest fund in Bangladesh. But we need to be aware that this technological advancement not only ensures the best of our payment activities but will also introduce a few risks. The introduction and implementation of new payment initiatives is merely the start of the process, only successful use of it by the end users will finally accomplish the goal. I hope, all the dignitaries who are present here will do their best to popularize all these initiatives among the end users. Again I would like to express my heartiest gratitude to all who were involved in successful implementation of RTGS. Thank you all. 2

Title: Speech at an international conference organized by Bangladesh Development Initiative
text: Stability outcomes of Bangladesh Banks developmental central banking initiatives Dr. Atiur Rahman Governor, Bangladesh Bank BDI Conference 2015 University of California, Berkeley 7 November 2015 Why developmental role for a central bank? Rounds of post GFC large scale QEs in advanced economies have achieved little in shoring up flagging global growth, instead debilitating monetary policy and creating deflation risks by driving down interest rates in major currencies to near zero levels. The hope that faster growing emerging economy groups like the BRICS will take over global growth stewardship has also dimmed. Global trade growth slipping below the sluggish global output growth has further deepened the gloom. Bangladesh, like other inclusive growth focused developing economies, has therefore gone about upholding growth with measured moderate monetary growth proportionate with real output growth expectations, alongside guidance for lenders in channeling the financing inclusively into output initiatives in all economic sectors. This attention to directional guidance has helped farm, non-farm MSMEs flourish in rural and urban communities, augmenting domestic output on the supply side and incremental employment and income on the demand side. Bangladesh Banks developmental initiatives Besides maintaining macroeconomic and financial stability, Bangladesh Bank has also been supporting rapid broad based inclusive economic growth through its multipronged financial inclusion initiatives. Bangladesh Banks engagement to inclusivity and sustainability is direct and explicitly pronounced in its monetary policy statements. The motivational thrust of ingraining a socially responsible financing ethos has sensitized the financial sector in reaching out to the underserved and excluded population segments with the financial services they need. The thrusts are on output initiatives in agriculture supporting food security and price stability; SME financing promoting output, employment and income generation; green financing supporting environmental sustainability; and digital inclusion facilitating the Digital Bangladesh vision of the government. In recent years, Bangladesh Bank has brought about deeper engagement of the financial sector in the development role with a social responsibility driven financial inclusion drive. Accordingly, Bangladesh Bank has taken up comprehensive reform and up-gradation of the countys financial market infrastructure, including: Setting up of fully automated nationwide online clearing and settlement system; Bangladesh Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS); Hastening automation in banks; Customer interest protection for new customer segments; Launching of mobile financial services (more than 28 million accounts); No frill accounts for the disadvantaged and students (more than 16 million accounts); Mandatory credit for agriculture, SMEs, renewable energy, and so forth Recent financial inclusion initiatives are supported by advanced technology, which has drastically reduced costs, increased the reach, and allowed new players to leapfrog constraints. Stability outcomes Output growth focused directional guidance in inclusive financing has helped Bangladesh maintain steady, stable spell of six-plus percent real GDP growth for well over a decade, which is around twice the rate of global output growth. Over the last decade, Bangladesh economy had the least volatile GDP growth and inflation in South Asia. Further, the growth performance is quite inclusive and balanced, reflected by steady growth in all economic sectors (agriculture, industry and service). Stable downward edging CPI inflation (now about six percent); low, single digit fiscal deficit, and strong gains in external sector viability with appreciation pressure on Taka, positive export growth amid demand weakness in external markets, buoyant foreign exchange reserves (USD 27 billion with 7 months of import cover), and remittance inflows (more than USD 15 billion in FY15) are the defining features of the Bangladesh economy. Socioeconomic performances are quite exemplary; Bangladesh has achieved most of the MDGs well ahead of time, with rapid fall in poverty from 48.9 percent in 2000 to 24.5 percent in 2015. The way forward The performance of Bangladesh economy is grounded on very inclusive and broad-based nature of growth, which already earned much global recognition. Now, our goal is to deepen, widen, and further improve the quality of inclusive financing programs to ensure environmentally sustainable economic development. All the government organs with the lead role of the private sector need to work hard to pace up our inclusive socioeconomic growth and development momentum towards attaining higher middle income country status by 2030 and advanced economy status by the decade of forties. We also need to put more attention towards long term mobilization of savings, and quick completion of the infrastructure projects. A USD 1 billion Taka Offshore Bond will be launched soon by the Bangladesh government with support from IFC, to invest in private infrastructure projects and PPPs. Bangladesh Bank has recently launched a USD 300 million investment fund to boost medium-and long-term investment, and another USD 200 million BB fund will be launched soon to facilitate green financing in the productive sectors, including textile and leather. The key requisites for upholding domestic demand driven growth will be the social empowerment of, and inclusive financing support for output initiatives of all population segments. Adaptation to looming global warming driven sea level rise threats, and broader countrywide transition to energy efficient low emission output practices are the other major new priority areas for attention.

Title: Speech at Bangladesh Conference at the University of California-Berkeley
text: Monetary Policy in a Developmental Central Banking Paradigm Dr. Atiur Rahman Governor, Bangladesh Bank Bangladesh Conference at the University of California-Berkeley November 7, 2015 While monetary policy is supposed to maximize employment by maintaining price stability, the real task in a developing economy like Bangladesh is not that simple. Unlike the developed nations, Bangladesh has enormous developmental deficiencies which only the government and the fiscal authority in particular cannot remove at a desirable speed. Herein comes the question of developmental central banking that strategies financial inclusion to make economic growth balanced and sustainable. We often face the question why a central bank should step in developmental initiatives. The answer is simple: the need for developmental initiatives is so huge and widespread that an all concerted and all pervasive measure is warranted particularly for an emerging economy like Bangladesh. In standard welfare economics, the answer banks on the notion of Pareto Optimality, which endorses any step that improves the state of welfare without causing disutility to any economic agent is optimal. That is what our central bank is doing now. We know that our government has a string of programs to expand social safety net that covers the vulnerable of the society. Is that enough? Not necessarily. Every government has resource constraints and Bangladeshs budget constraints are pretty evident. Here Bangladesh Bank can come forward with a hand of support for the governmental goals of poverty reduction and the improvement of standards of living. The roles of the government and the central bank are not mutually exclusive. Rather, they are complementary. The roles are friendly and inspirational for each other. If the government finds that the central bank has come forward to help the poor, to protect the vulnerable, and to empower the women of the society, the regime enjoys the synergy effect for addressing unemployment and inflation  the two vices of the economy. It is viewed as a two-prong attack on the deficiencies of the economy. The German and French central banks undertook developmental roles in the postwar reconstruction and rehabilitation of the respective nations. When the necessities were over, their central banks concentrated to the core function of price control and employment maximization. Bangladesh Bank has to wait a couple of decades to come to that stage. What we are doing is the call of the time. We are helping the farmers by extending agricultural loans so we maintain crop sufficiency for the nation once starved for food. We are giving credit to female entrepreneurs to embolden women empowerment so Bangladesh becomes a balanced county in female labor force participation. Women must get a bigger strength in decision making of their lives and livelihood. We extend loans to green projects and solar plants to vindicate our responsibility for the environment. Any injustice to the environment will make the imperative of sustainable growth simply impossible. We support exporters to build a trade resilient economy. And all the programs we undertake certainly do not overwhelm our main task as a central banker. We first make sure that our core objectives of ensuring sustainable growth and moderate inflation are achieved so macro stability is maintained. As data show over the last two decades (1995-2014), Bangladeshs average growth (5.73%) is the second highest after India (6.77%), but the standard deviation of growth is the lowest in the region, which is 0.57 percentage points. The success in the inflation front is unparalleled. The average inflation in Bangladesh over the last two decades is the lowest at 6.45% and its standard deviation is the lowest too at 2.44 percentage points in the region. As you have noticed, international evaluators have awarded the central bank for promoting inclusive growth on top of maintaining wonderful macro stability. Dear audience, I find your support to the central bank as unique and inspirational. With your guidance and suggestions, we believe we will be able to finish our journey of making a successful Bangladesh free of poverty and social disparity. We dream of a prosperous Bangladesh that will stand as a role model of development and Bangladesh Bank will keep on endeavoring to guide all commercial and developmental banks to reach and to empower the common people of the nation.

Title: Speech on Inclusive and innovative financing practices in Bangladesh
text: Inclusive and innovative financing practices in Bangladesh Dr. Atiur Rahman Governor, Bangladesh Bank UN Secretariat UNDESA, New York 05 November 2015 It is a great pleasure and honor for me to be invited at UN secretariat to talk about 'inclusive and innovative financing practices in Bangladesh'. I would like to thank UNDESA, in particular, Dr. Hamid Rashid for creating this opportunity for me. Distinguished participants and officials from UNDESA, a very Good Afternoon to you all. Incorporating Inclusive Financing in Financial Sector Bangladesh Bank (BB), the monetary and financial sector regulator in Bangladesh, strongly believes that conventional monetary and financial policy approaches focused on - business as usual - short term stabilization over business cycles are not enough to address the longer term needs of inclusivity and sustainability. The reality is that there is a huge investment gap for the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) despite hundreds of trillions worth of assets held in other traditional sectors. Directionless pumping of liquidity by the name of quantitative easing (QE) is yielding little in sustained growth optimism while heightening instability risks as very little of these reaching growth generating startups and SME businesses in the real economy. The bulk of QE funds is going into supporting environmentally hurtful traditional output and consumption patterns and into speculative outlays in asset and commodity markets. Very recent WEO update about downward growth and looming deflationary projection particularly for Russia, the euro area, and Japan strongly substantiate this argument. Besides, anthropogenic climate change threats are adding further to the potential destabilization risks. Mandated by its charter to support output and employment growth besides controlling inflation, BB stepped into impart a deliberate directional bias channeling financial flows towards inclusive financing of environmentally sustainable domestic demand driven output initiatives. To this end BB is pursuing a host of concerted initiatives drawn up consultatively with financial intermediaries and target client bases (i.e., NGOs, private and public stakeholders) in the relevant market segments. An ongoing campaign of ingraining socially responsible corporate ethos is helping instill the right motivations in support of the policy initiatives. This motivational consultative approach has drawn all banks and financial institutions in Bangladesh into enthusiastic engagement in the various sustainability initiatives; with their innovations of cost efficient new modes of reaching out to their new client bases with financial services. Setting Priorities and Targets for Socially Responsible Financing Environmentally sustainable approaches for rapid poverty eradication by narrowing down inequalities in advancement of opportunities, food and energy securities are our policy priorities in promoting socially responsible, inclusive and sustainable financing on four broad fronts, viz., underserved segments of agriculture, SMEs, modernization of payment system, and adoption of environmentally benign green output practices including renewable energy generation, waste treatment, adoption of low carbon output options. Priority of rural agriculture and women entrepreneurs in financing access also figured importantly in our initiatives. The consultatively set targets are incremental, aimed at raising and stabilizing sustainable financing to adequate levels. Agriculture yielding less than a fifth of annual GDP gets less than 5 percent share of total bank credit, mostly from the state owned banks. Private sector banks have therefore been tasked to enhance their agricultural financing to at least 2.5 percent of their total lending. SMEs contributing around 29 percent of GDP get about 26 percent of total credit; the targets here are intended mainly to maintain stable growth in financing. Like agricultural financing, total green financing in Bangladesh is still insignificant, with low single digit percentage share in total credit. The disbursement targets set for green financing are therefore higher, at 5% of total credit disbursements for older banks, at 3% for newly licensed banks, and at 4% for non bank financial institutions. Going forward, the target levels for green financing will heighten steadily as financing promotion in agriculture and SMEs focus increasingly on the newer green alternatives to the traditional high carbon options. By the end of 2016 every financial institution has to make sure to allocate at least 5% of its loan portfolio to green finance. Another element of BBs initiative of mainstreaming socially responsible inclusive financing is the promotion of the financial sectors CSR engagements in the communities they operate in. As per BB guideline all banks and non-bank financial institutions have to allocate at least 2.5 percent of their net profit for CSR activities towards fostering inclusive, equitable and sustainable socioeconomic growth and development. These include inter alia grant supports to socially and environmentally beneficial projects, importantly enhancing viability of these in the take-off stage. Ingraining Developmental Policy Support by Bangladesh Bank Refinance scheme for agriculture and SME sector: Refinance windows at BB provide low cost financing lines for banks and financial institutions against their sustainable financing in the above mentioned sectors. Development partners like the ADB and JICA are co-financing alongside BB the refinance lines for SMEs and green projects. Lately, idle cash surpluses of Shariah based banks and financial institutions have also been inducted into new refinance lines to support Shariah based SME and green financing. The refinance lines are intended to be transient support at take-off stage, to be phased off as the supported initiatives gain more viability through lenders spontaneous financing in them. For agriculture typically loaded with high output risk and price risk, mitigating mechanisms in the form of functional crop insurance schemes will however be also necessary. Inclusive financing support for underserved population: Sharecropper farmers had long been excluded from formal financial system because of lack of collateral. In FY10, BB launched a refinance scheme worth Taka 5.0 billion for landless sharecroppers in partnership with BRAC, the largest non-bank MFI in Bangladesh. This is a first ever initiative for this productive group of farmers. The scheme is promoting social collateral where peer pressure ensures loan repayments and mitigates default risks. Under this scheme, BRAC has provided loans to almost 906 thousand sharecroppers in 250 upazilas in 48 districts and refinanced Taka 14.34 billion till September 2014. Apart from this, state-owned banks also extend loans to sharecroppers, a sizable number of whom are women farmers. Some privately owned banks too are also coming forward to provide such loans to the sharecroppers recently, prompted by their CSR obligations. Mobile financial services, no-frill account and school banking: In order to provide banking services to the rural areas, Bangladesh Bank started the mobile banking services for the first time in 2010. Twenty six (26) banks have been licensed so far to run the mobile financial services with their agents. The number of mobile phone based accounts rose to about 28.6 million by the end of FY15, and the number of no frills Taka 10 deposit (equivalent to about 12 cents) bank accounts for the farmers, hapless freedom fighters, garments workers, stressed street orphans and the poverty-stricken people now exceed fifteen million. BBs policy measures and support initiatives have thus created a vast inclusivity momentum for inclusive and sustainable growth. Another inclusion program called 'School Banking' registered 905 thousand account holders whose total amount of deposits stood at Taka 8.25 billion (105.8 million) in FY15. Environmental risk grading: Macro-prudential support measures like lower equity margin requirements are being employed to favor the socially and environmentally beneficial initiatives and options. For example, financing for mass transit vehicles requires lower equity margin than for personal and family cars. BB is also among the few central banks that are pioneering environmental risk grading of financing proposals by the lenders; towards eventual adoption of differential loan pricing and differential equity margin according to environmental risk grading; lowering financing costs for lower environmental risk projects and encouraging risk mitigating modifications in the higher risk rated proposals. Besides the above outlined support and enablement measures, good performers in sustainable financing earn better BB supervisory (CAMELS) rating, with attendant preferential edge in permissions for business expansion. Automation in financial sector: BB is providing the financial sector with necessary enabling infrastructure and detailed guidance for adoption of low carbon, energy efficient internal processes and practices, including carbon footprint measurement and use of paperless e-processes. Countrywide BB led massive modernization of the financial sector IT infrastructure including fully automated online clearing and settlement of fund transfers has spawned exponential growth of off branch mobile phone based financial services, vastly benefitting the underserved and rural poor. Recent initiation of Bangladesh Real Time Gross Settlement (BD RTGS) system - the first ever milestone to real time, high value, and gross settlement based clearing system promote our payment infrastructure to a new height. Now, we proudly compare our payment and settlement system to any other payment system around the globe. Sustainability enhancing outcome Outcomes of BBs initiatives promoting socially responsible inclusive, green financing are thus far quite heartening, upholding macroeconomic stability in terms of price and financial stability supported by stable pace of inclusive output growth. Amid prolonged global growth slowdown the Bangladesh economy is on a six plus percent average annual real GDP growth for well over a decade now, with single digit inflation on a steady declining path. The socially responsible orientation of financing has kept agriculture, SMEs and green projects in Bangladesh free from credit crunch during and following the global financial crisis. Incremental output from inclusive financing of agriculture and SMEs has helped uphold output and price stability in the real economy; while also bolstering institutional stability in the financial sector by widening and diversifying their asset and liability in the new inclusion client bases. Directed lending to rural agriculture and new SME initiatives are creating new farm and offfarm employment in hundreds of thousands every year. Countrywide spread of green finance activities and mobile phone based financial service outlets are likewise creating new employment in manufacture, assembly, maintenance and other support services. Output growth and price stability in Bangladesh are strongest in the South Asia region, with the lowest volatility. Poverty is receding fast, quite a few of the key MDGs have been attained well ahead of timeline, and Bangladesh is now ahead of her higher income large neighbor on many counts of human and social development indicators. External sector position of Bangladesh economy has strengthened substantially; with debt-GDP ratio declining to around thirty five percent, rising foreign exchange reserves now sufficient to cover six months imports, and stable strong exchange rate of Taka. South Asias growth projections for up to 2019 indicate that Bangladeshs stable growth rate will be the highest in the region from 2017 onward, probably among the best global growth performances. Way forward in green financing promotion: Debt finance by non-financial corporates is still insignificant in Bangladeshs underdeveloped capital market. Green initiatives like other inclusive growth and development projects, therefore, remain overly dependent on financing from banks and financial institutions. Also, all the local inclusive and green initiatives are short-term in nature and generally too small in size. BB is therefore looking for ways of developing liaison between networks of local green project entrepreneurs and multilaterals like the WB, IFC that raise green bond funds on their own high credentials for investments in eligible green project initiatives. xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx

Title: Speech on BB commits to mitigate risks at early stage
text: BB commits to mitigate risks at early stage S.K. Sur Chowdhury All central banks work to ensure that banks and financial institutions (FIs) operate in a safe and sound manner and comply with applicable laws and regulations. Promoting a healthy risk culture is something that we have been speaking a good deal about here in Bangladesh for more than a decade now. Bangladesh Bank (BB), the countrys central bank, is also working to improve its ability to identify, monitor, and respond to emerging risks facing the countrys banks and financial institutions and touch upon some of the risks that building up in financial services industry. To strengthen the risk management practices of banks, Bangladesh Bank (BB) issued industry best practices as early as in 2003 for managing core risks in banking in six broad areas; namely- Asset Liability Management Risk, Credit Risk, Foreign Exchange Risk, Information & Communication Technology Security Risk, Internal Control and Compliance Risk, and Money Laundering Risk. Since the onset of the Financial Crisis in 2008, the global economy has continued to face rough weather. Different jurisdictions continue to be tormented by financial fragilities and macroeconomic imbalances.
