Although Bangladesh Bank has fortunately been spared some of the worst upheavals that have occurred in other countries, realizing the need to be constantly vigilant, the BB issued sets of guidelines starting from 2010 for capital adequacy in accordance with new Basel Accords and Stress Testing. To ensure that the banks are prudently managing their risks, especially those can cause systemic threats and jeopardize the stability of the entire financial system, the BB imposed prudential requirements to assess banks' risk management capacity and has instructed the banks to establish an independent Risk Management Unit (RMU). The RMU not only conducts stress testing for examining the bank's capacity of handling future shocks, but also deals with all potential risks that might occur in future. Considering the deteriorating environment and climactic scenario as well as challenging social issues in the country; the central bank of Bangladesh has been taking concerted efforts to guide banks and FIs in protecting their financing from environment and social risks. In January 2011, the BB issued 'Environmental Risk Management Guidelines for Banks and FIs' in Bangladesh. The Environmental Risk Management Guidelines are now being updated as 'Environmental and Social Risk Management Guidelines', focusing more on the concept of environmental and social risk management rather than only environment risk management and exemplify the sources of both environmental risks and social risks. The BB has issued the 'Risk Management Guidelines for Banks' in 2012 as a supplement to the core risk management guidelines issued earlier. This document promotes an integrated, bankwide approach to risk management covering the other most common risks in banking companies in Bangladesh; namely- Strategic Risk, Interest Rate Risk, Price Risk, Operational Risk, Compliance Risk and Reputation Risk. Very recently, in September this year, banks were asked to set up a separate Risk Management Division with an organogram prescribed by the central bank of Bangladesh for stronger and timely/updated risk management activities. The banking industry has changed the way of providing services to their customers and processing of information in recent years. Information and Communication Technology (ICT) has brought this momentous transformation. Electronic banking is becoming more popular and enhancing the adoption of financial inclusion. Security of Information for financial institutions has therefore gained much importance and it is vital for us to ensure that the risks are properly identified and managed. In this backdrop, the revised version of Guideline on ICT Security for Banks and FIs to be used as a minimum requirement and as appropriate to the level of technology adoption of their operations issued in May 2015. To keep pace with international initiatives and newly promulgated acts on prevention of money laundering and terrorism financing, there has been a tremendous need to review the Guidance Notes on Prevention of Money Laundering issued in 2003. In September 2015, Bangladesh Financial Intelligence Unit (BFIU) issued Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment Guidelines for banking sector and instructed banks to assess their own ML & TF risk considering their customers, products, delivery channels and geographical positions. They were also instructed to assess regulatory risk i.e. risk arises from non-compliance of AML & CFT measures. Rests of the Core Risk Management Guidelines i.e. Asset Liability Management, Credit Risk, Foreign Exchange, and Internal Control and Compliance are also currently being revisited for necessary updating to cope with changing scenarios. The BB commits a tremendous amount of time and resources to identifying, assessing, and communicating emerging risks of all kinds, allowing bank managers to develop and implement strategies to mitigate the risks at an early stage. In addition to Annual Financial Stability Report (FSR), publication of which commenced in 2011, Bangladesh Bank is preparing and publishing Financial Stability Assessment Reports from late 2014 with an aim to convey its assessment about key trends in the major segments of the financial system on a quarterly basis. The Report contains trends in macroeconomic indicators, banking and FIs sectors performances including their liquidity and capital adequacy, major risks to which they are exposed to and their resilience to plausible adverse events, in addition to the capital market developments. The ongoing earnings pressure due to sluggish business in the country may cause some banks to reach for yield and take on additional strategic risk that could contribute to future vulnerability. The BB also noticed competition for the limited lending opportunities that exist in the current market environment is intensifying and resulting in weaker collateralization standards, particularly in commercial and industrial loans. The shift towards digital banking strikes at the heart of the banking distribution model that has served the industry in the past. Consumers are increasingly using online and mobile to meet their banking needs. Increased business flow through the digital channel will result in the attraction of new customer segments with a higher fraud risk profile and also a potential behavioral shift within the existing customer base. Rapidly evolving cyber threats and information technology vulnerabilities requires heightened awareness and appropriate controls to identify and mitigate the associated risks. The same is true for confidentiality breach and money laundering risks that remain prevalent across the industry as money-laundering methods evolve and electronic bank fraud grows in sophistication and volume. As a consequence of the financial crisis and its contagion affects throughout the globe, banking regulations are getting increasingly globalized. The recent regulatory reforms are a response to the severity of the crisis, and the changes are intended to make the financial system more resilient. But, in the current sluggish economic context, the issue of whether banks are able to absorb all these regulations while at the same time generate sufficient resources to continue their activities is a big question. As a result, many banks elsewhere are re-evaluating their business models and risk appetites and are seeking new ways to generate returns. As members of the international financial community, the BB also is committed to implement these regulations in our jurisdictions. However, it is crucial to ensure that banks and financial establish and follow appropriate risk management processes as they explore new products, partnerships, and opportunities. This article is adapted from the speech of SK Sur Chowdhury, Deputy Governor of Bangladesh Bank, gave as the guest of honor at Asian Banking Summit 2015 held at Le Meridien in Dhaka on November 03, 2015. End

Title: Speech at Inaugural of ABB International seminar on 'Banking in Bangladesh: The Leap Forward
text: Inaugural of ABB International seminar on Banking in Bangladesh: The Leap Forward Speech of the Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : 14 November, 2015 Time : 9.00 am Venue : Raddisson Hotel, Dhaka Distinguished Special Guest the BAB chairperson, distinguished ABB Chair and Vice Chair, other ABB office bearers and members, all other attending guests and participants, my warm greetings and a very good morning to you all. I am happy to be invited to this boldly labeled ABB seminar focusing on the preparedness of ABB member bankers for a leap forward of our banking sector. The seminar program schedule focuses quite appropriately on asset and liability management, on technology use, and on business continuity management in events of breakdowns in the technology infrastructures. These subjects are of crucial importance in smooth conduct of financing operations of all sizes and scales, from mass scale inclusive small financing for farm/ non-farm MSMEs to large scale short and long term financing of larger businesses including infrastructure and other big project undertakings. Besides welcoming and supporting such spontaneous banking sector initiatives, BB has over the past few years been proactively driving necessary enablement initiatives for the banking sector like leading a countrywide massive modernization of the payments system and the financial sector IT infrastructure, including BACH, BEFTN, NPS, NID based e KYC, and most recently the RTGS. In view of scarcity of longer term domestic savings for financing longer term investments, 1 BB is working with the government towards putting in place pension savings schemes for general citizenry including NRBs, besides the existing pension and provident fund schemes for formal sector employees. As interim measure, we have already lined up a WB funded USD 300 million longer term local lending line in USD; another USD 200 million longer term lending line in USD from BBs own resources is being lined up to support green transition of our export oriented textiles/apparels and leather sectors. Further, the government and BB has given IFC the go ahead for their issuance of Taka denominated bonds up to USD 1.0 billion, proceeds of which will be used in longer term lending to projects in Bangladesh. Taken together, these initiatives will mean a massive transformation in access to funds for our financial sector over the near and medium term. The ball is thus on your court of now to rise up to the challenges of absorbing and investing the oncoming massive new volumes of financing resources inclusively in all productive initiatives, large and small, of all population segments of our society. I believe that with BBs promotion initiatives for socially responsible financing you are also keyed up to the urgency of financing transition from traditional polluting output practices in our manufacturing sector to the energy efficient green or environmentally sustainable options. Concerted whole hearted engagement of our financial sector in environmentally sustainable green and inclusive financing will enable the real sector of our economy to uphold export competitiveness (with green credential for the products), and also to uphold broad based domestic demand driven output growth amid persisting sluggishness in the global economy. With such engagement, the financial sector will indeed be able to assume a guiding role in fostering sense of social and environmental responsibility in our real sector businesses. Let me conclude by congratulating ABB for organizing this seminar, wishing it the best success, and assuring you that BB will as ever encourage and support all such spontaneous positive initiatives in our banking and financial sector. Thank you all for your patient attention. 2

Title: SDG based journey towards higher middle income country status outlined in Bangladesh's 7th FYP
text: E:\Attachment\2015\November\15112015\picture\DSC_0351.JPG SDG based journey towards higher middle income country status outlined in Bangladeshs 7th FYP Remarks by Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : 15 November, 2015 Time : 11.00 am Venue : BICC, Dhaka I heartily thank and congratulate Dr. Shamsul Alam for his concise yet well rounded depiction of our economys sustained robust dynamism of equitable growth; and for his outlining of the pathways sketched in our 7th FYP towards higher middle income country status. I am indeed fully on board with his presentation reflecting both opportunities and challenges of Bangladesh's development journey. Sustained steady spell of six-plus percent annual average real GDP growth for well over a decade, a particular 6.2 percent over last half of the decade amid global slowdown, job creation during 6th FYP outnumbering new job market entrants, and the attendant rapid poverty decline provides us strong confidence that we can attain the 7th FYPs sustainable development objectives on all major fronts; with real GDP growth well above the trend of our peer group economies if not fully up to the ambitious plan target levels amid global growth slowdown. Let me mention a couple of aspects that we shall need to focus particularly on in upholding and further strengthening our growth momentum over the 7th FYP period. Firstly, after decades of globalization driven growth, global trade growth has now slowed, and is actually trailing global output growth. This indicates that the potential for export-led growth will be weaker and harder to realize for our export sector unless it takes advantage of upcoming new opportunities in markets for goods and services that are produced using environmentally sustainable green output processes and practices. Bangladesh Government and Bangladesh Bank have already gained global attention by being early movers in this direction; with enablement and facilitation steps for green transition of output processes and practices in our businesses. To name a few of the steps, relocation of our leather sector manufacturers to an area well serviced with ETP facilities is nearing completion, and BB is lining up a USD 200 million longer term financing line to support green transition of manufacturing practices in the export oriented textiles/apparels and leather sectors. These are only small initial steps, with lots more to do in our intended countrywide transition to environmentally sustainable output practices and lifestyles; and I look forward to our development partners in supporting our efforts for green growth in both export and domestic sectors. In addition, we need to remove the remaining 'anti-export' biases to exploit the advantages that we still have in the field of exports originating mostly from our manufacturing and agro-processing sectors. Secondly, the more subdued prospects of export led growth means that we shall need to foster more in domestic demand led growth. Here again, Bangladesh clearly is an early mover, with our Governments attention towards broad based equitable socio economic development, and with BBs sustained initiative of promoting socially responsible inclusive financing of environmentally sustainable output initiatives. Some of our development partners are already engaged in supporting and co-financing of our enablement and facilitation initiatives, and we look forward to their broader, deeper engagement over the 7th FYP period. Let me mention in this context that we are vigorously pursuing financial markets development to enhance our financial sectors capacity in meeting the financing needs for realization of the 7th FYP growth goals. To name just a few, to redress the scarcity of longer term savings to finance infrastructure and other long term projects, we are working with development partners to introduce pension savings schemes for the general citizenry including NRBs, besides reforms in public sector pension schemes. As interim measures, we have put in place a WB supported local longer term lending line in USD for manufacturing businesses, besides, as I have already mentioned the other one being lined up for green transition in the export oriented textiles and leather sectors. To mitigate risks in agriculture sector financing, the government is also working with development partners towards introducing insurance products for crops, livestock and fisheries. BB is steadily strengthening financial sector regulation and supervision towards full convergence with Basel based international best practice standards in capital, provisioning, liquidity, leverage, governance and risk management in the financial sector; and with use of online reporting and real time surveillance practices. I look forward to yet more deepening in engagements with our development partners during the 7th FYP period, towards getting our financial sector in readiness for fuller integration with the global financial markets. Our financial sector has already demonstrated strong resilience and stability outcomes of our prudent monetary and fiscal policies. Besides sustained growth and falling inflation, our external sector stability has indeed been stunning. The impact of these macro-economic policy stabilities has been reflected in terms of significant transformation of our inclusive economic growth and impressive social development. We hope to consolidate these gains and move ahead ever faster with deeper support of our time-tested development partners. Let me conclude here. Thank you all for your attention.

Title: Opening remarks at Roundtable on the future of Mobile Financial Services in Bangladesh
text: Roundtable on the future of Mobile Financial Services in Bangladesh Opening remarks of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : 16 November, 2015 Time : 5.00 pm Venue : Pan Pacific Sonargaon Hotel, Dhaka, UNSGs Special Advocate for Inclusive Finance Her Majesty Queen Maxima of the Netherlands, stakeholders in Mobile Financial Services (MFS) from our financial sector, mobile telecommunications sector,partnering technology platforms, financial and telecom sector regulatory authorities, other distinguished invitees including government officials; a very good evening and my warmest welcome to you all. It is indeed our great privilege to have UNSGs Special Advocate for Inclusive Finance Her Majesty the Queen Maxima of the Netherlands with us today in this roundtable discussion on the future of Mobile Financial Services (MFS), a cost efficient off branch financial service delivery mode that BangladeshBank has embraced early on, spearheading a bank-led model with spectacular success in reaching out to virtually all population segments including those in far flung remoter locations, in a short time span of 3-4 years. With the initial phase of making payments services available through the MFS model to the hitherto excluded population segments by now largely achieved, the next phase is to foster optimal utilization of MFS for cost efficient off branch delivery of a broader range of banking, insurance and other financial services; in a healthy competitive market that is neither overcrowded with too many small unviable market players nor with too few dominant entities wielding undueoligopolisticinfluence. Experience thus far gives us some clear indications for the way forward: Firstly, orderly well-regulated financial services delivery is better served in abank led model under full oversight of financial sector regulatory authorities. Secondly, Mobile Financial Services delivery works much better with bank-led separate subsidiary structure than with these being housed within the bank where it risks losing focused attention amid numerous other areas of activities of a bank. Thirdly, multibank equity participation is a much more viable option thanunibank equity holding for an MFS licensee, given the scale requirements in terms of investment and size of customer base needed for viability. Brac Bank owning bKash, its MFS subsidiary, and a number of other uni-bank MFS licensees have already officially indicated to BB their willingness to take other banks in their equity. Multibank equity participation will hasten consolidation of MFS licensees into larger, fewer, more viable entities. Existing unibank MFS licensees that are yet to get returns from their already substantial MFS investment outlays can recoup much of those investments outright by selling part of their equity to other banks willing to joining in, at the same time enlarging their existing MFS client bases with clients of new equity partners. Fourthly, the bank led MFS subsidiaries will be well advised to take in non-bank equity partners who can bring in useful technological and business model innovations for promotion of MFS. bKash, the Brac bank owned MFS subsidiary has already done this successfully.We dont however intend to make this obligatory, individual bank-led MFS subsidiaries will remain free to make their own decisions about the extent of minority non-bank participation in their equity; with BBs regulatory framework and oversight seeing to it that no non-bank equity holder exercises undue influence due to its communication channel, technology or other specialized knowhow being used by the MFS subsidiaries. A few months ago we uploaded in our website for public consultation a new draft MFS guidelines based on the considerations outlined above. These draft guidelines have attracted widespread local and external attention, stimulating lively debate. We already have a rich trove of feedback from a broad range of local and external respondents, including multilateral agencies and international philanthropies. Brainstorming in todays roundtable graced by presence of Her Majesty Queen Maxima of the Netherlands will be a very befitting conclusion of our public consultation rounds on the issue. In todays face to face discussions we are looking forward not only to new insights but more importantly also to a better, deeper mutual understanding ofthe concerns and viewpoints of participating stakeholders from diverse backgrounds. Let me now cordially invite anyone among the participants around the table to kick-off our discussion round.

Title: Introductory remarks at a Seminar on National Financial Inclusion Strategy
text: Seminar on National Financial Inclusion Strategy Introductory remarks of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : 17 November, 2015 Time : 2.45 pm Venue : Conference Room, Bangladesh Bank We are deeply honored to have Her Majesty Queen Maxima's presence this afternoon. This is a special honor for us as Her Majesty has been closely following financial inclusion in Bangladesh. Honourable Advisor to the PM Dr. Towfiq-E-Elahi Chowdhury, H.E. Ambassador Ms. Cuelenaere, UNDP Country Director Ms. Tamesis, distinguished guests, and colleagues from all relevant agencies. A very good afternoon. Your Majesty, in 1971, Bangladesh grew out a strong national aspiration for freedom and equity after a painful war of independence. The dream of Bangladesh and the essence of our national spirit always embedded inclusiveness in it. Your Majesty, as you know, Bangladesh's journey started in a war-torn setting beset with many challenges and amid the difficult global environment of the 1970s. Mother nature was not always kind. Out of these challenges, emerged the early inclusion efforts through microfinance, health, and other home-grown social innovations. As Bangladesh's steady march continued, our financing needs evolved. Our financial system have grown and matured over the years, which enabled financing of a wider economic base. In recent years, we have actively leveraged the financial system for innovating and deepening empowerment initiatives, for example, in agriculture, MSME, women entrepreneurship, green financing, improving the quality of our growth. These initiatives also boosted domestic demand, helping us navigate the external shocks, especially in the aftermath of the recent global financial crisis. The government has taken an active, participatory, and learning-by-doing approach toward financial inclusion. This approach has been bottom-up, with a focus on maximizing impact, including the excluded and empowering the vulnerable. The experience and lessons gathered thus far make it an opportune moment for us to review, discuss, and forge a national financial inclusion strategy. The strategy can help us better leverage the synergies across initiatives, agencies, and programs through consultation, collaboration and innovation. In Bangladesh, echoing our national aspirations, we have worked towards making our financial access universal. We also want it to be digital to further democratize the inclusion. Your Majesty, distinguished guests, please accept sincere appreciation for being with us today as we embark on formulating a national digital financial inclusion strategy.

Title: Keynote Message at Regional Dissemination Forum on Green Financing jointly organized by Bangladesh Bank and APRACA
text: Regional Dissemination Forum on Green Financing Jointly Organized by Bangladesh Bank and APRACA Keynote Message Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Venue: Sky Ballroom, Level 16, Le Meridien Dhaka, Khilkhet, Nikunja, Dhaka Date: November 29, 2015 Time: 9:30 a.m. Secretary General of Asia-Pacific Rural and Agricultural Credit Association, Mr. Chamnong Siriwongyotha; Deputy Governor of Bangladesh Bank and Chairman of APRACA, Mr. Shitangshu Kumar Sur Chowdhury; Chief Financial Officer of Brac and Brac International, Mr. Shib Narayan Kairy; distinguished participants from home and abroad, friends from print and electronic media, a very good morning. The central bank of Bangladesh strongly believes that conventional short term business cycle focused monetary and financial policies do not address the longer term needs of inclusivity and sustainability. Rather, the directionless pumping of liquidity by the name of quantitative easing (QE) contributes little in sustaining growth while only heightening the instability risks, as a very little of these reaches to the growth generating startups and SME businesses in the real economy. For some years now, Bangladesh Bank has therefore stepped up to impart a deliberate directional bias channeling financial flows towards inclusive financing of environmentally sustainable domestic demand driven output initiatives. We have decided to go for Selective Easing for productive sectors, not wholesale quantitative easing as in the west. We have put the money in the ground not in the air. As we touched the ground, it is now bearing fruits. We are now facing the pleasant challenges of surpluses instead of deficits. Environmentally sustainable approaches targeting rapid poverty alleviation by opening up advancement opportunities for the unserved and under-served are our policy priorities in promoting a socially responsible, inclusive, and sustainable financing agenda. Bangladesh Banks financing strategy rests on ensuring adequate credit facilities for four thrust areas of agriculture; micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs); green output options; and digital inclusion. Stimulating rural demand and empowering women also bear significant importance in our financing strategy. Another element of Bangladesh Banks initiative of mainstreaming socially responsible inclusive financing is the promotion of financial sectors CSR engagements in community development. Accordingly, Bangladesh Bank has directed all banks and non-bank financial institutions to allocate at least 10 percent of their CSR funds in the climate risk prone areas. Page 1 of 3 Refinance windows available at Bangladesh Bank provide low cost credit facilities for environmentally benign green output options. Idle cash surpluses of Shariah based banks and financial institutions have also been inducted into new refinance lines to support SME and green financing. A USD 200 million longer term fund from Bangladesh Banks own resources is being lined up to support green transition of our export oriented textile and leather sectors. Bangladesh Bank is also among the few central banks that are pioneering environmental risk rating of financing proposals by the lenders. For ingraining the green or sustainability into agriculture, Bangladesh Bank has taken diverse policy and funding initiatives to promote sustainable agriculture. Channeling refinance to solar irrigation pump, vermicompost, bio-fertilizer, bio-gas, organic farming, saline, draught and flood resistant seed varieties, roof-top gardening; granting fund from CSR to conservation of wild life, forestation of coastal region, natural crop-reservoir (cold-storage) have really brought the financial sector to line up agricultural financing with green practices. Partnership has been the keyword in channeling needed fund to agriculture. Nearly one third of total agricultural credit goes through Bank MFI partnership. BB itself has developed a partnership with BRAC for revolving 5 billion TK. refinance for tenant farmers. Over the past few years, Bangladesh Bank has been proactively undertaking necessary enablement initiatives for the banking sector including a countrywide massive modernization of the payments system and financial sector IT infrastructure, with launching of Bangladesh Automated Clearing House (BACH), Bangladesh Electronic Fund Transfer Network (BEFTN), National Payment Switch (NPS), NID-based e-KYC, and most recently, Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS). These are indeed green initiatives as they cut down the use of papers. Outcomes of these initiatives are quite heartening. Bangladesh is on a steady spell of 6% real GDP growth for well over a decade now, with downward edging single digit inflation, massive inflows of workers remittances, rapid poverty alleviation, and impressive trends of social indicators. Its financial inclusion campaign has not only been democratising the financial system but also enhancing financial and social stability. Looking forward, we need to take a number of important measures to ensure a sustainable financial system in Bangladesh. The guideline and practice of environmental and social risk management should be continuously reviewed and strengthened accordingly. We are also focusing on greening the SME Credit Policy, and ensuring adequate financing facilities for alternative power generation options. These initiatives would be complementary to the real economy measures such as environmental regulations and fossil fuel subsidy reform. I would like to conclude here with a quote from the recently launched report on Designing a Sustainable Financial System in Bangladesh by the United Nations- where I was one of the members of the advisory council, there are opportunities to go further and accelerate progress to generate a vibrant green finance sector in Bangladesh. These ideas could be developed into a roadmap with leadership and involvement. So, I believe with our concerted effort towards building an environmentally sustainable green economy, we will be well positioned to achieve the new Sustainable Development Goals Page 2 of 3 (SDGs) of the United Nations well ahead of time as we did in case of the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs). I am quite confident that we can do this given the heightened level of motivations and commitment amongst our leaders of the financial community. Thanks for your patient hearing. Page 3 of 3

Title: Speech at the Opening Ceremony 17th SAARC Payment Council Meeting
text: Opening Ceremony 17th SAARC Payment Council Meeting Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date Time Venue : December 03, 2015 : 9.00 a.m. : Royal Tulip Sea Pearl Beach Resort, Cox's Bazar Chairman of the SAARC Payment Council; Deputy Governors; Executives and other delegates of the member countries; fellow colleagues from Bangladesh Bank; representatives from print and electronic media; a very good morning and warm welcome to you all in this 17th edition of SAARC Payment Council. The cooperation among the SAARC central banks regarding Payment and Settlement Systems, will lead us to the very much spirit of the 18th SAARC Summit 2014 - Deeper Integration for Peace and Prosperity. I believe adoption of a realistic, pragmatic, and step-by-step approach towards solution of issues will open up new avenues of cooperation among the SAARC nations. Effective communication and exchange of information in the region through SPC has helped most of the countries travel the first mile of payment systems with the establishment of Automated Clearing House, Electronic Fund Transfer Network, Interoperable ATM & POS, and the recently launched Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS). Along with the conventional payment system infrastructure, the SAARC countries have also experienced several innovations for including the excluded, empowering the vulnerable, stimulating rural demand through Mobile Financial Services & Agent Banking, and so on. I hope this unique platform will provide us an excellent opportunity to evaluate the past, and find solutions to combat the risks through exchange of fresh insights and ideas on: Implementation process of an effective oversight and supervision framework; Experience of resolving country specific problems; Managing operational and systemic risks in market infrastructure; Introduction of Tiered KYC for Mobile Financial Services and e-KYC for the entire banking sector; Leveraging technology to drive sustainable and stable growth; Impact of disruptive technologies and disruptive business models; Innovation in instruments, business models and adjacent technologies; And most importantly designing a process to appropriately contextualize the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) at the regional level in the payment systems arena. I believe discussion on these issues following presentations will spawn useful ideas on collectively sponsoring impact evaluation and analytical studies for establishing a sustainable and stable payment system in the region. Another area of focus would be on deepening familiarity and interest of the regions millennials in the evolving technology driven financial service options. We need to sort out the right instrument/payment platform for more effective communication with the tech savvy netizen generation. Dear audience, we also need to be vigilant in adoption of disruptive technologies like crypto-currencies with high systemic stability risks, and in combating the techno-fraudsters who always seem one step ahead of us. Regular and timely seminar on Cyber Security in Payment Systems would help us in this regard. I would like to inform you that, Bangladesh Bank is in process of establishing a third data center to ensure 99.99 percent of mission critical applications, and developing a cyber security strategy to identify and plug gaps with international best practices. Bangladesh Bank has also been continually updating and revising its ICT Security Guidelines for market participants, and improving Business Continuity/Data Recovery capabilities. Let me convey my sincere appreciation to the SPC Secretary General, his capable team, and the concerned officials of Bangladesh Bank for their excellent support towards making this Summit a success. On this note of optimism, let me now take the privilege of declaring the 17th SAARC Payment Council Meeting open. Thank you all.

Title: Speech at NRB Center Investment Conference on NRB Investment: Capital Market and Real Estate
text: NRB Center Investment Conference on NRB Investment: Capital Market and Real Estate Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date: December 05, 2015 Venue: The Pan Pacific Sonargaon, Dhaka Conference President, distinguished guests, organizers, and friends from print and electronic media; a very good morning to you all. Let me begin with saluting our NRBs whose relentless labors in abroad are keeping us well at home. Millions of our hard working NRBs are working abroad in almost 157 countries of the world. Because of their contribution, Bangladesh is now one of the global leaders in remittance earnings. As per the government statistics, nearly two and a half million workers migrated in last 5 years. In FY2015, the inflow of remittance was USD 15.3 billion which was almost 9 times the current account balance accounting for more than 60% of foreign reserves. This demonstrates the inherent strength of our external sector. We must give credit to the NRBs for attaining this strength and external stability. The remittance contribution from the NRB female workers are growing pretty fast adding a new dimension in the Non-Resident Bangladeshi portfolio. I hope our latest remittance enhancing initiatives will further encourage our NRBs to remit more using formal remittance delivery routes. The modernization & digitization of payment system and subsequent enhancements of mobile financial services in inward remittances are reducing the necessity of sending money through informal channels. Recent introduction of RTGS added a new dimension to the promptness of international money transfer. The NRBs can channel remittance now very swiftly from any corner of the world to anywhere of the country. Banks are now using the branch networks of the MFIs and Post Offices as the sub agents for remittance distribution. The Agent Banking outlets are also providing faster remittance delivery. The Financial Integrity and Customer Interest Protection Department of Bangladesh Bank is dedicated to promptly handle any complaints and suggestions of the customers or any stakeholders at home and abroad to ensure smooth and hassle free services. Any customers including the NRBs can address their grievances any time to Bangladesh Bank using the hotline 16236. Now, let me highlight the liberalization of regulations that we have rolled out keeping in mind higher flows of foreign direct/portfolio investments from the non-residents including the NRBs. You know there is an incentive for the NRBs in investing capital market of Bangladesh; 10% of the IPOs are reserved for them while they are free to invest even more as they deem. Both wholly foreign ownership and joint venture options with the private and public sector are open for non-resident investors including the NRBs. Up to 100 percent foreign ownership is freely permissible for FDIs in the industrial sector; FPI inflows are freely permitted in the local equity and bond markets. Post-tax profit or dividends earned by NRBs on that FDIs and FPIs are freely repatriable abroad including royalty/technical fee; disinvestment proceeds (at market value for listed companies and sale proceeds of foreign equity in unlisted companies at fair value based assets, income and earnings trend instead solely at net asset value) along with capital gains are like-wise also freely repatriable. Capital gains are free of income tax depending on investment patterns. Import tariff waivers/ concessions on capital goods and serviced industrial zones are available for foreign and local investors. Recent new facilitation include enhancement of family remittance ceiling for expatriates to 75% of their salaries. Taka term loan from the domestic market and 1 working capital financing in foreign currency from parent company are also now permissible for foreign owned/controlled companies engaged in manufacturing or services output activities in Bangladesh. Several incentives for the NRBs are under consideration if they invest in the special economic zones like hi-tech park, industrial park etc. Different savings instruments such as non-resident foreign currency deposit, US Dollar premium bond, wage earners development bond, etc., are available for investment by NRBs. BB has taken additional measures to attract NRBs to participate in these trading platforms which are now mostly digitized. Moreover, the government is also encouraging public-private partnership (PPP), tax holiday and other exemptions on investment to boost investment by the NRBs. Virtually all industrial sectors in Bangladesh are open for investment by the NRBs. They can engage in profitable investment by setting up cost effective labor intensive export manufacturing bases in Bangladesh producing for markets in host countries and elsewhere. In fact, some of them already invested in the areas of aviation, hotels & restaurants, fish and agro-processing industries. There is a growing real estate industry in Bangladesh, rapidly attracting the customers. Like other sectors, the NRBs are encouraged to invest in this sector also. The facilities available for other industrial enterprises are also available in this sector. Our NRB entrepreneurs are the path finders for other foreign investors who are eager to shift from other countries. I believe through this conference, the thought provoking discussions on ample investment potentials in Bangladesh, particularly for the NRBs, will bring in fruitful outcomes while the networking among the NRBs and others will unlock a new horizon of opportunities. I wish the NRBs will act in a more collective and united way better utilizing their talents and resources for our nations development. Thank you all for your patient hearing. 2

Title: Speech at a seminar on 'CSR and Early Childhood Development in Bangladesh'
text: CSR and Early Childhood Development in Bangladesh Atiur Rahman, PhD Governor Bangladesh Bank Date : December 22, 2015 Time : 10:30 am Venue : Hotel Six Seasons The CEO of the CSR centre Ms. Shahamin S. Zaman; special guest AKM Nesar Uddin Bhuya, Additional Secretary, Ministry of Women & Childrens Affairs; Mr. Brian Allemekinders, Counselor & Deputy Director Operations of the Canadian High Commission; Ms. Seliman Kassam; Ms. Dilshan Dossani, National Committee Member of Aga Khan Foundation Bangladesh; distinguished participants; ladies and gentleman; a very good morning to you all. It is quite heartening to see the CSR awareness and activism steadily deepening in our business and entrepreneurial community. I would like to thank and congratulate the CSR centre for its important role in promoting and coordinating the diverse initiatives, leading CSR activities progressing in our country. The CSR obligations towards promoting sustainability is not just a developed economy issue, rather is a global survival urgency in the face of looming risks from social inequality and insecurity, environmental degradation, and climate change threats arising mostly from the global conventional economic output practices. There is indeed no escape from the imperative of major global shift from polluting output practices towards equitable and environmentally sustainable options. Understanding this reality, Bangladesh Bank (BB) has been proactively pursuing ingraining of a socially responsible financing ethos in the corporate goals and objectives of banks and financial institutions. Progress thus far has been quite heartening; CSR activities in the financial sector of Bangladesh have expanded several fold over the past few years (8 times in the last 5 years), in direct support for socioeconomic empowerment of the less well off population segments with extensive schemes in areas of health, education and emergency disaster relief. We have also been promoting inclusive financing of productive Page 1 of 3 farm and off farm MSME initiatives of all population segments and transition from polluting, energy inefficient output practices to green, environmentally beneficial options. Bangladesh Bank issued CSR guidance circular in 2008 aiming at positioning banks and financial institutions as pioneers in ingraining and internalizing CSR in corporate goals and objectives. In 2014, Bangladesh Bank issued structured guidelines for CSR fund allocations and utilizations, including implication oversight to facilitate orderly planning and implementation of the CSR initiatives. Further, in the same year, Bangladesh Bank allocated its own fund for CSR engagements. The widening CSR activities in our financial sector have been significantly contributing towards ensuring inclusive, equitable economic and social development. Bangladesh Banks supervisory CAMELS ratings reward banks for their CSR performance, with recognition and competitive edge attendant with better CAMELS ratings. The government also provides some tax breaks as incentives supporting CSR initiatives in several sectors. For some years now, Bangladesh Bank has been issuing annual reports on financial sectors CSR initiatives, helping banks and financial institutions learn from others initiatives. The readymade garments industry acts as a catalyst for the economic development Bangladesh, fetching billions of dollars as export earnings, and creating jobs for millions of people. The Made in Bangladesh tag has also brought glory for us, making Bangladesh a prestigious brand across the globe. Bangladesh, once termed by cynics a bottomless basket, has now become a basket full of wonders. The country, with its limited resources but immense human capital potential, has been maintaining 6 percent plus annual average GDP growth rate for well over a decade, with better social and human development outcomes than her neighbors. According to our constitution, Bangladesh is a land of equal opportunity. However, many women need to stay home to take care of the children, and therefore become depended on their male counterpart. Every organization therefore should have a Daycare Centre so that mothers can work with full concentration. This is also important for the early childhood development. We need to understand that without proper development of the children it is not possible to sustain development in long run. Given that 85 percent of the workforce in the readymade garments industry is women, I would request the owners of garment factories to create and use their own CSR funds for improvements of their workers productivity. This would also motivate their female workers to deliver the highest effort. My special thanks to the CSR centre for bringing this excellent fact in their research. Research Findings are 55% responds thought ECD would be helpful for them as they will remain connected with the centre, better in established within/nearby community. The banking sector of Bangladesh absorbs a significant portion of the female workforce. In 2013, Bangladesh Bank directed all banks to establish a Daycare Centre, solely or in joint venture in suitable locations. Bangladesh Bank has established its own Page 2 of 3 daycare centre in 2007 which has expanded rapidly over time, from 32 seats in 2007 to 70 seats at present. Recently, 5 state owned commercial banks have jointly established a daycare centre in Motijheel with 65 seats. They can also provide this support to ECD and SFD of Bangladesh Bank A small motivation for the working mothers can ensure full concentration and dedication from their side. I strongly believe that with equal contribution of women in the economic development, our goal of becoming become upper middle income country by 2030 and higher income country by the 2040s can be achieved in stipulated time, where the RMG industry will play a crucial role in realizing the dream. I would like to conclude here thanking you all. Page 3 of 3

Title: 15th Nurul Matin Memorial Lecture on Ethics in Banking by Dr. Mohiuddin Alamgir: comments of Governor Dr. Atiur Rahman
text: 15th Nurul Matin Memorial Lecture on Ethics in Banking by Dr. Mohiuddin Alamgir: Comments of BB Governor Dr. Atiur Rahman Date : December 27, 2015 Time : 07.30 pm Venue : BIBM, Mirpur, Dhaka It is quite amazing how deftly has Dr. Mohiuddin Alamgir managed to pack in such a rich trove in the space of twenty five pages, comprising a recap of the preceding Nurul Matin Memorial Lectures on ethics in banking; a pinpoint-precision diagnostics of ethical failings of our banking sector, based on trends of its key performance indices; and pithy, practical recommendations towards the sectors way forward on a socially and environmentally responsible path of abidingly sound ethical grounding. Stressing on openness, transparency and accountability as key requisites for trust on ethical conduct of banking; Alamgir Bhai finds our banking sector out of sync with the desired optimum and behind banking sectors in peer group comparators, as reflected in indicators of loan default levels, capital adequacy, intermediation spreads and so forth. With unfailing precision he zeroes in on external influence of powerful elite on public and private sector banks as the root cause behind usurpation of credit resources by unscrupulous large borrowers and the nontransparent practices attendant thereto; at the same time pointing out that there is no need to panic, given BBs ongoing resolute remedial efforts. His advocacy for inclusive environmentally sustainable financing in transparent, accountable processes and practices towards establishing justice and fairness in allocation and pricing of credit resources is impressively prescient. It is heartening and reassuring that the approaches recommended by Dr. Alamgir are well in tune with Bangladesh Banks resolute thrusts towards instilling a corporate governance and internal controls culture firmly grounded on transparency and accountability; and towards ingraining inclusive and environmentally sustainable financing ethos in the financial sector. Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) driven initiatives of our banking sector, proactively guided by Bangladesh Bank, are also growing robustly; these ethically oriented social initiatives compensating to an extent for sub-optimal performance on other ethical criteria. Progress in addressing the financial sector weaknesses leading to ethical failings has been significant, as discernible in improvement trends of its relevant performance indices. The progress could of course have been better with a more congenial environment in our broader overall public life, but commitment of each banking professional to ethical conduct in his or her individual capacity can surely make significant difference cumulatively in resisting aberrant unethical influences. Quite appropriately therefore Dr. Alamgir has highlighted need for attention to proper grooming of our banking professionals in fostering ethical behavior. In my view, Dr. Alamgirs emphasis on inclusivity and environmental sustainability as important dimensions of ethicality in banking is an important new contribution to the rich series of Nurul Matin Memorial lectures on ethics in banking. While being fully on board with Alamgir bhai on his diagnostics and broad recommendations, I feel it necessary to disagree slightly about his suggestion on the need for a banking commission to rediscover the reasons behind banking sector failings and weaknesses that we all know well from eloquent articulations by himself and many others. Why should we be wasting valuable time in reinventing the wheel, instead of resolutely embarking headlong with needed remedial measures? 1 Let me conclude with my thanks and gratitude to Dr. Alamgir for his valuable lecture today, we look forward to benefit lots more from his continuing engagement in furthering the advancement of our financial sector. My thanks to DG BIBM and his team for their abiding engagement in regular holding of this event. As Alamgir Bhai has pointed out, BIBMs onus extends beyond holding this event onto fostering of ethical mindset and values in banking sector professionals through BIBMs training, workshops, seminars and consultation sessions. As always, we assure BIBM of all BB led support and wherewithal for this purpose. Thank you all for your patient attention. 2

Title: Speech at a seminar on Indian Banking Challenges and Opportunities held at BIBM on 28th December 2015
text: Talk on Indian Banking  Challenges and Opportunities Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : December 28, 2015 Time : 10.30 am Venue : BIBM, Mirpur, Dhaka Distinguished Chair, and attending banks executives, faculty members of BIBM, a very good morning to you all. We are deeply honored to have with us Mr. Chandra Shekar Ghosh this morning. This is a happy moment for us as Mr. Ghosh is a dedicated man for achieving financial inclusion which is also the prime motto of Bangladesh Bank. I feel quite happy to talk about a visionary man whose commitment for the poor is unparalleled. Starting from a tiny micro finance institution, he made an incredible journey and is now owning a private commercial bank named Bandhan Bank. Bandhan is a Bengali word meaning bond or togetherness. Bandhan Bank began operations as a full-fledged bank in August 2015 with the twin objectives of women empowerment and poverty eradication. So far as my knowledge goes, Bandhan Bank is the first instance in India of a microfinance entity transforming into a universal bank. Its statistics are also most fascinating. It started operations with 1.43 crore accounts, around Rs.10,500 crore loan book and 19,500 employees. Today, it has got 501 branches, 2022 service centers and 50 ATMs across 24 states. What is praiseworthy is that , the bank commits to open over 71 per cent of the branches in rural India, including at least 35 per cent in unbanked rural pockets. Now let me share some positive achievements of the banking sector of Bangladesh. As Bangladesh already got the status of Lower Middle Income Country and steadily marches towards Middle Income Country, our financing needs have evolved. Our financial system have grown and matured over the years, which enabled financing of a wider economic base. In accordance with needs and maturity, we have actively leveraged the financial system for innovating and deepening empowerment initiatives, for example, in agriculture, MSME, women entrepreneurship, green financing, improving the quality of our growth. These initiatives empowered poor community of the country and boosted domestic demand. I am happy to share with you the achievement of our Mobile Financial Services (MFS), a cost efficient off branch financial service delivery mode. Bangladesh Bank has embraced MFS early on, spearheading a bank-led model with spectacular success in reaching out to virtually all population segments including those in far remote locations. With one more vehicle we want to 1 reach to the unbanked people, that is Agent Banking. This strategy served as a milestone in financial inclusion. At the end of September 2015, the number of total agents was 533,485, and the number of registered customers was almost 29.2 million, of which active accounts were almost 11.27 million under Mobile Financial Services (MFS). The number of total transactions was 10.64 crore in September 2015 while the amount of total transactions was BDT 15.07 thousand crore at the end of the same month. Ladies and gentlemen, our movement is to take the financial services to door step of all Bangladeshi people. Mr. Ghosh has also similar dream. We believe in mutual learning and cooperation. I am very much hopeful that the insightful speech of MR. Ghosh will inspire us in future I congratulate the BIBM for arranging this program Thank you all for your patient attention. 2

Title: Speech on "Protection of Consumer Rights in Banking and Financial Sector of Bangladesh" Organized by BIBM
text: Bangladesh Bank Governor's Talk on Protection of Consumer Rights in Banking and Financial Sector of Bangladesh Organized by BIBM on 29 December, 2015 Date : December 29, 2015 Time : 10.30 am Venue : BIBM, Mirpur, Dhaka Distinguished Chair, keynote speaker, designated discussants and attending banks executives, faculty members of BIBM, a very good morning to you all. A financial system can protect consumer rights if it can offer transparency, appropriate choices, redress mechanisms and privacy of consumer information. BB is relentlessly working on each front. It established a full pledged department named Financial Integrity & Customer Services Department (FICSD) to protect the interests of customers, improve banker-customer relationship and ensure the standard of customer services of the banks and financial institutions. Now any person/ customer can lodge complaints and ask any question to the FICSD through dialing 16236. Since the inception of Help Desk in 2011 to protect customers' interest, followed by subsequent transformations into Customers' Interest Protection Center (CIPC) and the latest formation of the FICSD, Bangladesh Bank (BB) has been receiving complaints from the masses regarding general banking, loans and advances, cards, mobile banking, local bills, foreign bills, bank guarantee, remittances, and so forth in both written form and over phone. The FICSD has recently published its annual report for 2014-2015 highlighting the praiseworthy job it did in the last year. It is an excellent document for knowing how BB quickly responds to the complaints of clients and solves these complaints to their satisfaction. In FY 2013, the department resolved 68.5% complaints, with adept settlements of 95.9% complaints in the following FY 2014. BB's strict adherence to the assurance of resolving customers' any grievances and complaints are sheer evident with its latest statistics of 100% complaints resolved in FY2015. BB has also strengthened requirements for disclosing standardized, comparable pricing information on financial products. As a result, consumers have the scope to know simplified, adequate, and comparable information about the prices, terms and conditions, and inherent risks of financial products and services. Financial statements of all banks are now prepared in accordance with Bangladesh Accounting Standards (BAS) and Bangladesh Reporting Standards (BFRS). All the time, we are very closely monitoring the true and fair view of annual reports of banks for ensuring availability of proper information for stakeholders. Privacy, confidentiality, data integrity, and data protection of client information is also well regulated and enforced in the banking sector, including the rapidly growing branchless banking sector. However, other segments  microfinance, insurance, and securities markets  may not have yet acceptable levels of confidentiality. I will urge them to take care of this issue. Consumer consciousness is however of utmost importance to protect their rights. In this perspective, I would like to emphasize on two issues. One is financial literacy and the other is demand driven research. Bangladesh Bank firmly believes that financial knowledge is a key to protect consumers rights. As a result, a diverse financial education initiative has been undertaken in a rigorous manner by BB across the country. Creation of a dynamic and interactive web portal linked to BB website containing story books, games, videos, a calculator and informative writes up on different financial services; preparation of televisions commercials and radio broadcasting commercials; and awareness creating press layouts are included in this initiative. The recently concluded Banking Fair was one of the most successful Financial Literacy events of the banking sector. Thousands of consumers of financial services flocked in to the fair to know about their rights and various aspects of financial products. The interactive session between customers and CEOs of banks was the most fruitful engagement for customer interest protection. Additionally, BB has identified strengthening financial education initiatives as an important core objective in its recently announced strategic plan for 2015-2019. A very specific action plan as well as timeline for reaching this purpose has also been outlined in this document. I also stress the need for some demand-driven research on what information would be most beneficial to Bangladeshi consumers and what would be the most effective way of communicating this information. I am very much thankful indeed to Mr. Khondkar Ibrahim Khaled for contributing a very insightful paper on oevsKi mev co vqK Pwiio. The paper mainly highlights on issues like customers satisfaction, service charges, rate of profit and security of deposits. No doubt customers satisfaction has increased manifolds in the banking sector of Bangladesh because of growing positive mind set of banks young and talented executives as well as IT based virtual banking. Among others, consumers do usually complain more on service charge. BB is always watchful on this issue and has directed all banks to bring service charge to a reasonable level and to inform central bank regarding the charge list. Consumers also do complain on banks profit/interest rate. In an open market economy, interest rate is being determined by banks. BB has no scope to intervene here directly. But initiatives like several refinancing schemes, loan from the foreign sources, and rebate for the good borrowers have already started to give results in this area. Ladies and gentlemen, our movement towards customers satisfaction is bringing more unbanked people under the umbrella of bank services. It helps us in achieving financial deepening, inclusion and stability in the financial system. I congratulate the BIBM and CAB for this excellent initiative to discuss on Consumer Rights in Banking and Financial Sector in Bangladesh. I am confident that todays seminar would help generate new ideas we all can take back to our respective desk to help Bangladesh to move forward. Thank you all for your patient attention.

Title: Speech at Seminar on SME: "Small 'N' Smart is the Beautiful Future"
text: Small N Smart is the Beautiful Future E:\Attachment\2016\January\12012016\DSC_0130.JPG The Future of Manufacturing, New Age Business Challenges and Opportunities: How 2016 can be the year of collective growth for SMEs of India and Bangladesh Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date Time Venue : : : January 11, 2016 3.00 pm A K N Ahmed Auditorium, BBTA, Mirpur, Dhaka Principal BBTA; special guests; eminent speakers Mr. Rajiv Chawla and Dr. NK Pandey; guests from India, distinguished panelists, SME and women entrepreneurs and stakeholders; members of IamSMEofBangladesh; representatives of print and electronic media; ladies and gentlemen a warm welcome to you all. I am glad to see the dedicated SME force of Bangladesh coming together with the SME force of India today. I congratulate and convey my special thanks to the Indian team under the leadership of Mr. Chawla. It is a great pleasure to witness the joint-campaign to develop SMEs in this region, which started soon after the opening of new SME & Special Programs Department in Bangladesh Bank. Our entrepreneurs under close supervision of central bank have joined together on the platform of IamSMEofBangladesh to bring meaningful and positive changes in the country. The pro-active role of IamSMEofIndia has inspired us in many ways to establish IamSMEofBangladesh, and to advance SME activities. The quality of IamSMEofIndia has been acknowledged for its high standard and I am confident that through continuous communication and cooperation, IamSMEofBangladesh will also attain the standard and quality, essential for sustainable SME development in Bangladesh. It is heartening to see that within few months, IamSMEofBangladesh has been able to arrange a good number of programs and initiatives. Today's program is a step forward towards enhancing the knowledge and skill of the MSME entrepreneurs. The speakers have made excellent deliberations followed by a stimulating open floor and panel discussions. Dr. Pandey's deliberation shows how medical services can be rendered to the public in the most affordable and economic ways. I am sure the participants will explore this opportunity to enrich their knowledge with the external experiences to provide the much needed medical services in affordable ways. The key points made by Mr. Chawla, suggests how to make the new age businesses beneficial to the new generation. He has given a great idea of SME2SME business between the two countries. He also underscores diversified ways of bringing collective growth in SMEs in India and Bangladesh. I hope that our young entrepreneurs will learn from the experience of the business leaders and leading entrepreneurs present here today, and will work together to keep our SME sector moving. I thank Mr. Rajiv Chawla for his contribution and would like to request him to be in close touch with our IamSMEofBangladesh team. I hope Bangladesh Bank, BIBM, BBTA, banks, NBFIs; and other organizations will strengthen their cooperation and coordination in coming days. Special thanks to Mr. Sabur Khan, Mr. Sukamal Sinha Choudhury, Mr. Ali Sabet, and other distinguished panelists and participants for their support and contribution to make this program a success. Thank you all.

Title: Speech at Seminar on Green Finance for Sustainable Development Organized by Bangladesh Solar and Renewable Energy Association
text: Green Finance for Sustainable Development E:\Attachment\2016\January\12012016\DSC_0360.JPG Organized by Bangladesh Solar and Renewable Energy Association Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date Time Venue : : : January 12, 2016 9:30 am Ballroom , Pan pacific Sonargaon Eminent Chair, Her Excellency Ambassador of France in Bangladesh, special guests, Dr, Mizan R. Khan, distinguished discussants and resource persons, CEOs of banks and financial institutions, friends from print and electronic media, colleagues from Bangladesh Bank, ladies and gentlemen, a very good morning to you all. I would like to congratulate Bangladesh Solar and Renewable Energy Association for organizing this important conference on Green Finance for Sustainable Development, a quite pressing issue in the context of looming global climate change threats. In the evolution of sustainable development, three mutually reinforced pillars have been the key- people, planet and profit. In the light of 2030 SDGs, 3Ps have been upgraded to 5Ps- People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace, and Partnership. All countries and stakeholders are to implement the Sustainable Development Goals by 2030, with firm determination of taking necessary steps towards ensuring a steady, resilient, and sustainable development path. As we embark on this journey, we pledge to leave no one behind. Hence inclusive development, for which we need sustainable inclusive finance. Bangladesh falls into the group of most climate change vulnerable countries despite her insignificant share of global greenhouse gas (GHG) emission compared to other developing and developed countries. For developing economies like Bangladesh, roadmap for green investment will need charting of both the buildup phase by awareness creation, motivation and support measures, and its scaling up by putting in place policy reforms creating enabling conditions and incentives fostering larger investment partnerships for transition to energy efficient green infrastructure. The recent Paris pact on climate change also manifests our firm accord to stop global warming, where 195 countries commit to fight climate change by adopting a global climate treaty for the first time. It offers the hope that humanity can avert catastrophic climate change and ushers an energy revolution, which will reduce carbon emission and make this Earth better livable. Environmental sustainability and climate change resilience are the two key elements of Bangladeshs inclusive socioeconomic development strategy. Keeping this broad approach in mind, Bangladesh Banks resolute thrusts towards instilling a corporate governance and internal controls culture are firmly grounded on transparency and accountability; and towards ingraining inclusive and environmentally sustainable financing ethos in the financial sector. Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiatives of the banking sector, guided by Bangladesh Bank, are also growing significantly. These ethically oriented social initiatives are compensating to an extent for sub-optimal performance on other ethical criteria. Environmentally sustainable approaches for rapid poverty eradication by narrowing down inequalities in the advancement of opportunities are our policy priorities in promoting socially responsible, inclusive and sustainable financing. We have therefore identified four broad areas: agriculture, SMEs, modernization of payment system, and adoption of environmentally benign green output practices. Priority of rural agriculture and women entrepreneurs in access to finance also figures importantly in our initiatives. The consultatively set targets for these priority areas are incremental, aimed at raising and stabilizing sustainable financing to adequate levels. After decades of globalization driven growth, global trade growth has now slowed, and is actually trailing global output growth. This indicates that the potential for export-led growth will be harder to realize unless it takes advantage of upcoming new opportunities in markets for goods and services produced using environmentally sustainable green output processes and practices. Bangladesh Government and Bangladesh Bank have already gained global attention by being early movers in this direction; with enablement and facilitation steps for green transition. To name a few, relocation of our leather sector manufacturers to an area well serviced with ETP facilities is nearing completion. In addition to supporting ready 50 green products with Green Refinancing in Taka. Bangladesh Bank has also lined up a USD 200 million longer term fund called Green Transformation Fund in Fx to support green transition of manufacturing practices in the export oriented textiles and leather sectors. These are only small initial steps, with lots more to do in our intended countrywide transition to environmentally sustainable output practices and lifestyles. Social and Environmental Risk Management Guideline, we are also encouraging CSR support for innovative green products like natural cold storage, climate awards, desalinization of water in the coastal belt etc. I believe our concerted effort towards building an environmentally sustainable green economy will position us well to achieve the SDGs well ahead of time as we did in case of the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs). I am quite confident that we can do this given the high level of motivation and commitment in our financial community. For some years now, BSREA has been playing a major role in scaling up solar and renewable energy in Bangladesh through encouraging and facilitating green loans for projects like solar home and irrigation system, and assisting policymakers in offering incentives for renewable energy projects. I hope they will continue their effort in transforming Bangladesh into a fully fledged green nation. Last but not the least; I would like to express my sincere appreciation to BSREA for organizing this timely and fruitful event. I wish this conference a grand success, and hope that it will create enough incentives to the stakeholders to facilitate green investment in the coming days. Thank you all.

Title: Speech of Deputy Governor Mr. Shitangshu Kumar Sur Chowdhury on Green Finance for Sustainable Development
text: Green Finance for Sustainable Development Organized by Bangladesh Solar and Renewable Energy Association Address by Special Guest Shitangshu Kumar Sur Chowdhury, Deputy Governor, Bangladesh Bank Venue: Pan pacific Sonargaon Ballroom Date: January 12, 2016 Program Starts: 9:30 a.m. Speech Starts: 10.30 a.m. Honorable Chief Guest and Governor, Dr. Atiur Rahman; Special Guest Md. Anwarul Islam Sikder ndc and Mr. Mahmood Malik; Keynote presenter of the event Dr. Mizan R Khan; Chair of the conference Dr. Dipal C. Barua; participants from financial sector, corporate and 'green' business sector; friends from media and my colleagues of Bangladesh Bank; the organizers-Bangladesh Solar and Renewable Energy Association; GOOD MORNING. Achieving a happy, prosperous and enlightened Bangladesh which is free from hunger, poverty, inequality, illiteracy, and corruption and belongs completely to its citizens and maintains a healthy environment. - the key statement of National Sustainable Development Strategy of Bangladesh spells out our vision and motto for initiatives we have taken and are still taking in Bangladesh Bank. In the era of growing discontent with the dominant view of finance, we have ingrained green finance into heart of banking and financial sector. Green finance, environmental risk management and green banking are no more glamour content for financial sector. The historic Paris Summit in September 2015 has changed the direction of advancement of human civilization. Now, environment is not a consideration, its responsibility. We have to move hand in hand, we have to believe in partnership. The endorsement of SDGs by the member countries of UN has made the pathway for better partnership towards collaborative prosperity. So, achieving a global green transition is one of the most important challenges of our time. A challenge that calls for global leadership, collective action and innovative solutions. This has to be pursued in our country. Cross-sectoral engagements of green entrepreneurs and financial sector will boost up the environmental sustainability, economic viability and social equity. It will drive the sustainable finance, help to build up a sustainable financial system, expedite the sustainable development process. Bangladesh is one of the most climate vulnerable countries of the world. It has challenges in the future and also success at the present as well as past in combating this problem with its own resilience, policy and resources. United Nations Environment Program has awarded our Honorable Prime Minister as one of the "Champions of the Earth" in 2015 for the outstanding leadership in the frontline of climate change. One of the major reasons for this award is that she has set the example for other leaders, providing that investing in the environment can achieve sustainable development. In Bangladesh the central bank has played a leadership role in pursuing sustainability priorities within its mandate of maintaining monetary and currency stability in order to foster growth and development in the national interest. As a part of ongoing financial sector reform there is a concerted effort not just to deepen the financial system and make it more efficient and inclusive, but also to make it greener. Bangladesh Bank has sought to align regulation and policy to national goals, while avoiding negative unintended impacts. Identification of product line by Bangladesh Bank for green refinance has already touched half-century mark. Innovation in green finance is going on even in foreign currency credit. Despite all these achievements, the prospect of achieving sustainable development is not free of challenges. The biggest challenge is one of mind-set and attitude. We all have to be green in mind and soul for a start the mind-set amongst bankers-its in your own interest too for long run growth of your profits. So in financial sector we now need to make that cultural shift among ourselves. I believe, with our strenuous effort towards building an environmentally sustainable green economy we will be well positioned to achieve the SDGs as we did in case of MDGs. I am quite confident that we can do this given the heightened level of motivations and commitment amongst our leaders of the financial community. To conclude, I would like to thank the organizers for initiating this conference on such an timedemanding issue. I hope you all will have very productive deliberations and find this seminar very useful. Thanks for your patient hearing.

Title: Speech at Seminar on "Plastic Waste Management and Way Forward"
text: Seminar on Plastic Waste Management and Way Forward Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date Time Venue : : : January 21, 2016 2.30 pm Media Centre, BICC Agargaon, Dhaka Mr. Callum Chen, Mr. Jasim Uddin, other organizers of the seminar, Bangladesh Plastic Goods Manufactures & Exporters Association (BPGMEA); domestic and foreign representatives from Asia Plastic Forum (APF), distinguished speakers; guests, friends from print and electronic media; ladies and gentlemen; a very good afternoon. I am happy to present here at the seminar on Plastic Waste Management and Way Forward, a quite pressing issue for Bangladesh on her way towards implementing the sustainable development goals (SDGs). I am delighted to see the representatives from the APF member countries gathering here not only to promote their products but also to find effective solutions to managing plastic waste. I believe this 11th International Plastic Fair 2016 has been an excellent opportunity for all the stakeholders to improve the quality of plastic businesses while also taking into account its negative impact on environmental sustainability, and therefore exploring the best possible ways to manage its disposal. It is true that plastic has become an indispensible part of our economy, widely used in the production of household and business goods, construction, telecommunication, packaging, and so on. Around 5,000 plastic industries generate employment for more than a million people. Besides, many export-oriented factories meet the growing external demand for film plastic, garment accessories, and household plastic items. Each year Bangladesh imports more than 150 thousand metric tons of plastic raw materials. However, the non-biodegradable nature of plastic gives rise to great environmental concern. According to a United Nations Enquiry Programme (UNEP) report, production of plastic materials has grown at the rate of 5 percent per annum over the past 20 years. In developing countries, the use of plastics is even higher due to economic growth, and changes in consumption and production pattern. Lack of efficient waste management system therefore poses serious threats to environment and human health when plastic wastes are not disposed of properly. The negative impacts of plastic waste can be addressed by recognizing the fact that it has a great potential for resource conservation when converted into valuable resources. We therefore need to ensure 100 percent recycling of plastic wastes in the most innovative and cost effective ways. This will not only help protect environment but also will create massive employment in the recycling industry. Plastic waste disposal is an emerging problem in Bangladesh, particularly in the urban areas. According to a survey, around 5 percent of the total waste generated in Dhaka City is plastic. A majority of population does not have access to proper waste disposal services, leading to a significant proportion of wastes dumped in open lands. Plastic waste also leads to blockage in the drainage system leading to flooding in the streets during rainy seasons. We therefore need to adopt an integrated approach to improve the plastic waste management system with combination of different methods presently available in Bangladesh: formal system (municipalities/city corporations), community initiatives (CBOs and NGOs), and informal system (informal labor force involved in plastic waste recycling trade chain).We need to build up a strong partnership between these existing three systems to ensure an effective plastic waste management system. Over the past few years since I took the responsibility of the central bank governor, Bangladesh Bank has been promoting financing of environment friendly green output options and practices through ensuring adequate financing for green products as well as providing timely guidelines for green banking. We have created Taka 2 billion refinance scheme for 50 green products of which 4 relate to solid waste management. Any plastic waste management initiative falling into these categories is therefore eligible to access this refinance line. I would highly encourage you to exploit this opportunity. We have created another Green Transformation Fund of UDD 200 million for export sector. Last but not the least rapid economic growth is of high urgency and priority but not at the cost of environmental instability. Rather, our development plans should seriously consider environmental sustainability, social equity, and economic stability. As an advocate for sustainable growth, I would therefore request all of you present here today to contribute to the next decade of inclusive and sustainable growth in Bangladesh through ensuring a proper waste management system. I would like to congratulate the organizers again, and wish the 11th International Plastic Fair- 2016 a grand success. Thank you all.

Title: Speech at Inauguration of Representative Office of Punjab National Bank in Bangladesh
