text: Inauguration of Representative Office of Punjab National Bank in Bangladesh Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date Time Venue : : : January 24, 2016 7.00 pm Le Meridien, Nikunja, Dhaka Ms. Usha Ananthasubramanian, MD & CEO of Punjab National Bank (PNB), India; Executives from Indian Bangladesh Chamber of Commerce & Industry, Financial Institutions & Banking Fraternity, Non-resident Indians, distinguished guests from the financial and business sectors, a very good evening to you all. I congratulate the Punjab National Bank, one of the 'Big Four' banks of India, for its opening of a representative office at Dhaka, hopefully as a prelude to deeper engagement in our financial sector with eventual opening of branch or subsidiary in Bangladesh, to benefit from win-win engagements in the ongoing vibrant growth processes in Bangladesh. While trade integration has proceeded with fair momentum in South Asia, financial and investment integration has remained somewhat lagging, and I see this opening of representative office in Bangladesh a welcome step in the right direction. We are pleased to know that the PNB has a banking subsidiary in the UK, as well as branches in Hong Kong, Kowloon, Dubai and Kabul. It has representative offices in Almaty (Kazakhstan), Dubai, Shanghai, Oslo and Sydney. With its extensive network across the globe, the PNB will be well placed for promoting smoother trade transactions between Bangladesh and her trade partners in India and elsewhere. In fact, the growing resilience of the Bangladesh economy has not gone unnoticed by the Indian businessmen and entrepreneurs; many of them have come with direct and joint investments in selected service and manufacturing sectors to take advantage of the increasing Indo-Bangla trade, which has grown by 25 percent between 2011 and 2015. I am sure that the very presence of the Punjab National Bank in Bangladesh will help improve the environment of trade finance businesses between the two friendly countries. I look forward to PNB's active participation in direct and portfolio investments in Bangladesh by its large corporate clients including capital goods manufacturers and institutional investors including pension funds, green investment funds, social investment funds and so forth. I am also expecting its engagement in our incipient initiatives of promoting and supporting transition of output practices and processes in the real sector of our economy to the environmentally sustainable green options. Even in absence of a branch, the representative office of PNB can aid this transition process both in Bangladesh and India, by helping build up of liaison and mutual learning networks between financial institutions, technical experts and civil society organizations active in this area. Inclusive financing of farm and non-farm MSME output initiatives is another area where the PNB can engage gainfully in fostering cooperation and liaison between financial institutions in South Asia. IamSMEofIndia and IamSMEofBangladesh are now working hand in hand to promote MSME investments. PNB too can facilitate this cooperation. I am aware that growth recipes like this may look rather unconventional for a commercial bank and its representative office, but Bangladeshs financial sector has taken up socially responsible inclusive green financing as institutional ethos, and even the orthodox global multilaterals like the IMF and WB have now taken on board inclusivity and environmental sustainability as among their core concerns. I wish PNB's representative office in Bangladesh the happiest beginning in a promising, exciting journey towards much more in terms of rewarding, enriching engagements. Thank you all.

Title: Investment & Policy Summit 2016: Session on the Policies and Opportunities for Alternative Investment
text: Bangladesh Investment & Policy Summit 2016 Dr. Atiur Rahman Governor, Bangladesh Bank Session Chair Date : 25 January 2016 Time : 2:00 PM Venue : Hotel Radisson, Dhaka Session: Policies and Opportunities for Alternative Investment (Chairpersons summary of session deliberations may be followed by concluding remarks along lines drafted below): The keynote paper by Dr. Arif Khan has dwelt at length on the regulatory frameworks issued by BSEC enabling operation of Alternative Investment (AI) funds in Bangladesh. Intermediaries operating in the capital market and non-bank financial institutions can now engage in taking up roles in sponsoring and managing AI funds, besides investing in them. To widen further the pool of resources available for investment in AI funds, BB has issued DOS Circular no 02 dated 24th November 2015 permitting bank investments in AI funds up to Taka 2.0 billion (USD 25 million) for each bank, treated as outside their capital market exposure. The market thus already has more than the critical mass of fund availability needed to launch and start operating AI funds in right earnest. Let me share with you just two figures: size of the financial system is USD 150 billion and national savings is USD 60 billion. So there is no constraint in the aggregate savings. Perhaps there is tenor mismatch; the main problem is implementation. Bangladesh Investment Development Authority (BIDA) is working towards upgrading institutional reform, improving investments and easing doing business. Sponsors of AI funds need not worry about lack of demand for their services, the pent up demand is huge. According to the Boston Consultancy Group, the tech-savy middle income group in Bangladesh is increasing. As per a recent BBS survey, economic units doubled during the last decade. Over the last five years, as many as 2.95 million SME entrepreneurs have drawn SME loans from banks; 21.7% of these in manufacturing, 4.6% in services, and 73.7% in trade. Around 10% of these SME entrepreneurs are women. All these entrepreneurs now need additional investments to scale up, but with their borrowing capacity already used up, banks do not find them creditworthy for additional loans. AI funds can come in handily by buying into equity of the SMEs aspiring to scale up, the widened equity base will in turn make these SMEs eligible for such further bank borrowing as may be necessary. I would urge all potential AI fund sponsors in the Bangladesh market to capitalize proactively on the vast field of local opportunities, picking rich rewards eventually from helping our SME entrepreneurs in realizing their growth aspirations. All the new PPP projects, mostly infrastructure, e.g. elevated expressway, power plants, hotels, resorts, hospitals need sufficient fund. We can accumulate those fund by issuing bond.

Title: Speech at Financial Inclusion Literacy for Strengthening Entrepreneurial Capacity
text: Financial Inclusion Literacy for Strengthening Entrepreneurial Capacity \\hodma03gsec13\Attachment\2016\February\03022016\DSC_0187.JPG \\hodma03gsec13\Attachment\2016\February\03022016\DSC_0215.JPG Speech of the Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date : Time : Venue : February 03, 2016 9.30 am The Westin, Dhaka Event organizer MasterCard Bangladesh, distinguished invitees, senior management from banks & financial organizations, ladies and gentlemen, a very good morning to you all. At the very beginning, I would like to convey my heartfelt thanks to Mr. Porush Singh, Division President, South Asia & Country Corporate Officer, Mr. Vikas Varma, Executive Director, South Asia, MasterCard, Mr. Syed Mohammad Kamal, Country Manager, MasterCard Bangladesh, Mr. Zakir Hossain, Executive Director, BURO Bangladesh & the team from MasterCard & Buro Bangladesh for continuing their effort for the Financial Literacy program for the underprivileged people of Bangladesh. Financial literacy is a prerequisite for optimum exploitation of any new payment initiatives. Todays inauguration of phase 3 financial literacy program of MasterCard is a timely effort to disseminate various aspects and concepts of payments system, in conjunction with other already launched platform like Bangladesh Automated Clearing House (BACH), National Payment Switch Bangladesh (NPSB), etc,. Recognizing the positive linkage between technology and sustainable growth, we at Bangladesh Bank, developed and implemented broad based Networking, Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP), Banking Application, Enterprise Data Warehouse (EDW), Open Data Initiatives, a highly interactive Website and Intranet, E-tendering, E-recruitment and many other in-house software. BB is also very keenly engaged for improving the interoperability and resiliency of banking, payment and securities infrastructures. Recently Bangladesh Bank implemented Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) allowing us immediate payments settlements on an individual order basis without netting to fulfill the requirement of a high value payment system in the country. With a focus to the future, this system is open to both VPN and SWIFT connectivity as well. It is worthwhile to mention that the launch of financial literacy program for women entrepreneurs in 2013 was among MasterCards first steps as part of its philanthropic efforts in Bangladesh. I am happy to hear that, financial literacy training has been provided to 100,000 Women Entrepreneurs through Buro Bangladesh. In the second Phase, MasterCard along with Buro Bangladesh & NRB Global Bank ensured Business and Financial Literacy to Ten Taka Account Holders. I was present personally at both the launch events. By now Buro Bangladesh has given training to 10,000 participants of Taka 10 account holders at Gazipur, Comilla, Tangail, Narayangonj, Bogra & Rangpur districts & disbursed BDT 16.40 million to beneficiaries under refinancing project of Bangladesh Bank. Bangladesh Bank is working for the development of SME sector in Bangladesh. SME sector has experienced a tremendous development in last 5 (five) years. That has created a skill gap in the sector. To meet this skill gaps as well as to create new entrepreneurs SMESPD has undertook a project titled "Skills for Employment Investment Program (SEIP)", assisted by Asian Development Bank (ADB) and Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC). Under this program, Bangladesh Bank is working on training of about 10,200 people in three years for soft skills (Entrepreneurship Development), up-skill and employment generation skill training from 5 (five) fields like IT, Garments, Light Engineering, Industrial Electrical Maintenance etc. through 8 (eight) outsourcing of skill training providers. The outsourced firms will be responsible for at least 70% or more job placement after the training. About 40% of 10,200 trainees will be selected from women, people with disabilities, ethnic minority and indigenous people. I am happy to know that MasterCard with the help of Buro Bangladesh will be conducting Financial Inclusion Literacy for Strengthening Entrepreneurial capacity aiming to give financial literacy to 25,000 entrepreneurs. This would be 3rd phase of financial literacy project of MasterCard. I strongly believe such training will help effectively enhance the entrepreneurial capacity of the country. Thanks to Mastercard for continuing their endeavor for giving back to the community. I feel very happy to be a part of this launch ceremony as well. Now, I formally announce the launch of the third Phase of Financial Inclusion Literacy for Strengthening Entrepreneurial capacity. Let me conclude here by thanking you all for your patient hearing.

Title: Speech at Prize Giving Ceremony-2nd International Nature Summit 2016
text: Prize Giving Ceremony-2nd International Nature Summit 2016 Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date Time Venue : : : 13 February 2016 3:00-4:30 pm Notre Dame College Dhaka Honorable Principal of Notre Dame College, Dr. Fr. Hemanto Pius Rozario, CSC; Dr. Charles C. Villanueva, Pro-Vice Chancellor, AIUB; Mr. Muqeed Majumder Babu, Chairman of Prokriti O Jibon; Professor Sirajul Islam, NSU; Fr. Sushantu Anthony Gomes, CSC; participating students and guests, representatives from national and international environmental organizations, media partners, other participating members; ladies and gentlemen; a very good afternoon to you all. It's my immense pleasure to be an attendant at todays prize giving ceremony of the event, Green Inspiration 2016 organized by the Notre Dame College in collaboration with Ministry of Forest & Environment, IUCN, Prokriti O Jibon Foundation, JICA, UNDP, USAID and so on. I thank the organizers for bringing together a distinguished cluster of nature experts and environmental delegates to discuss on environmental issues. E:\Attachment\2016\February\14022016\DSC_0302.JPG In this increasingly swelling quick-gain-making anthropogenic deeds driven climatic-threats-prone endangered world, green inspiration for sustainable development is crucial that ensures development of the current generation without impeding the development opportunities for the future generation. Let me call it 'green development' for 'sustainable development'. Green Energy synonymous to Sustainable Energy, and Renewable Energy is the main engine of green development to preserve our nature. Green energy is replenished from inexhaustible sources like solar, wind, water, biomass, and other geothermal sources while the fossil fuels such as oil, gas, and coal run out eventually. In addition to being renewable, the use of green energy is critical in limiting green-house gas emission. To promote sustainable energy in Bangladesh, the government has prepared a Renewable Energy Policy and has undertaken various action plans with the targets of generating 5 percent and 10 percent of total power production by 2015 and 2020 respectively. Besides, the government has initiated setting up of a Sustainable and Renewable Energy Development Authority (SREDA) and has also finalized Sustainable Energy Development Act, 2011. Economic, social, and environmental sustainability receive high priority in the policies of Bangladesh Bank, the central bank of the country. Bangladesh Bank has undertaken and implemented a good number of initiatives to help implement energy and environment related programs of the government. The Bangladesh Bank circular on Policy Guidelines for Green Banking is a notable step towards developing green banking practices in the country. Renewable energy has also received special attention of the central bank since 2010. Bangladesh Bank has launched 50 green products under 11 categories to be eligible for refinancing facilities available at the central bank. In 2010, Bangladesh Bank has set up a 20 kilowatt solar panel in its Head Office, and has also advised banks and financial institutions to extend finance for solar energy, bio-gas plant, Effluent Treatment Plant (ETP) and Hybrid Hoffman Kiln (HHK) related projects. Bangladesh Bank introduced a Taka 2.0 billion revolving fund in 2010 to finance in these areas. Some of the development partners also came forward to pertain with this timely initiative of Bangladesh Bank. In 2012, the ADB supported a refinance scheme of Taka 50 million for improving the efficiency of brick kilns. Bangladesh Bank has also recently introduced a green fund of USD 200 million for low-cost, long-term foreign currency projects to be disbursed to green apparel and leather entrepreneurs. As endorsed by international bodies like UNEP and IISD, let me share our approach in banking sector that uses mainly five levers, such as: (i) Enhancing market practices through environmental risk management and reporting guidelines followed by developing a protocol for financing key technologies and areas such as clean energy; (ii) Leveraging private capital with public finance; a critical step to review and continue to develop green refinance scheme. Leveraging public backing for green insurance to de-risk low carbon solutions and achieve more green, bankable projects; (iii) Directing finance through policy, another important aspect to consider is setting a specific targets for key areas of green investment; (iv) Encouraging cultural transformation, a key step to raise awareness and motivation in the banking sector towards understanding of environmental risks and opportunities; (v) Upgrading governance, Bangladesh Bank is leading the green finance practices in the country, steps are also taken to integrate green finance more fully into the governance of Bangladesh's financial system. A further step would be to explore how best to align monetary targets with sustainability objectives and to introduce a specific green finance chapter to the governments long-run planning documents. By properly addressing the above issues we can mainstream the green finance practices in future replacing the present 'business as usual' conventional financing practices. I thank all the foreign and local experts for sharing their experience and opinion, making the summit a huge success. I believe the discussion of this summit will significantly contribute to save our planet and help achieve sustainability goals. I congratulate all the participants for their efforts to save the nature. To conclude, I would like to express my gratitude again to the organizers, especially the Notre Dame College for hosting this summit. I appreciate the endeavors of the organizers and wish them very success. Thank you all.

Title: Speech at Launching ceremony of 'Green Banking for Energy Sustainable Economy'

Besides, the government has initiated setting up of a Sustainable and Renewable Energy Development Authority (SREDA) and has also finalized Sustainable Energy Development Act, 2011. In 2010, Bangladesh Bank set up a 20 kilowatt solar panel in its Head Office, and has also advised banks and financial institutions to extend finance for solar energy, bio-gas plant, Effluent Treatment Plant (ETP) and Hybrid Hoffman Kiln (HHK) related projects. I came to know that this particular project will do extensive and pragmatic research, arrange Focused Group Discussions (FGDs), Key Informant Meetings (KIMs), workshops and trainings involving multi-stakeholders to streamline access to finance for renewable energy. Title: Speech at the National Dialogue on Developing NFIS
text: National Dialogue on Developing NFIS Speech of Dr. Atiur Rahman, Governor, Bangladesh Bank Date Time Venue : : : 13 February 2016 10.00 am Grand Ball Room The Westin Dhaka Honorable Principal Secretary, BFID Secretary, BTRC Chairman, fellow practitioners, and friends from the media. Good afternoon. It is wonderful to spend the whole day together to brainstorm on developing national financial strategy. Many thanks to DFID Bangladesh for being a close development partner, and supporting our financial sector work. Today, we have gathered here to think together, across, and ahead. It has been a very productive day. I feel we have achieved that goal. We learned where we came from, where we want to go, and what we can learn from each other and from other countries. Before I discuss financial inclusion, let me digress a bit, but for a reason you will soon understand why. Winter - especially the winter month of Maagh - has a special place in my heart. Now is a special time: February and March are our sacred months; these are months when we protected our language and proclaimed our independence. For All. What month can be a better time to reflect on where we came from, what kind of society we want to build, where we want to go and how best finance can play its part? If we go back to February 1952 or March 1971 or the time preceding those years, it becomes self-evident that the language and the subsequent independence movements were inclusive. They drew their strengths from their deep roots into the society, from all classes and professions: middle class and poor, urban and rural, labourers and farmers, big and small. The mighty river of national aspiration grew out of collective dews of individual aspiration. For those of you here who are too young to remember or live through those times, I urge you to carry these thoughts back with you and think how finance can foster that aspiration. I also urge you to read the Articles 8-21, Fundamental Principles of State Policy of our constitution of 1972, to fully appreciate how our dreams and aspirations were inclusive from the very beginning. If you then read the recent MDGs or SDGs, you will feel proud how our constitution envisioned social inclusion, empowerment, and justice well ahead of its time. It is in that constitutional spirit, we embark on institutionalizing this journey of social inclusion and empowerment through finance. Finance is and should be for the society, not the other way around, as we were so painfully reminded during the recent global financial crisis. Going back, Bangladesh started out in a war-torn setting beset with many challenges and amid the difficult global environment of the 1970s. Mother nature was not always kind. Out of these challenges, emerged the early inclusion efforts through microfinance, health, and other home-grown social innovations. As Bangladesh's steady march continued, our financing needs evolved. Our financial system have grown and matured over the years, which enabled financing of a wider economic base. In recent years, we have actively leveraged the financial system for innovating and deepening empowerment initiatives, for example, in agriculture, MSME, mobile financial services, women entrepreneurship, green financing, improving the quality of our growth. These initiatives also boosted domestic demand, helping us navigate the external shocks, especially in the aftermath of the recent global financial crisis. But there is more to do to deepen and to widen the access; to add products such as insurance; to develop institutions and industries, such pension. The government has taken an active, participatory, and learning-by-doing approach toward financial inclusion. Bangladesh Bank provided all support to move this agenda forward. Our approach has been bottom-up, with a focus on maximizing impact, including the excluded and empowering the vulnerable. The experience and lessons gathered thus far make it an opportune moment for us to review, discuss, and forge a national financial inclusion strategy. The strategy can help us better leverage the synergies across initiatives, agencies, and programs through consultation, collaboration and innovation. The strategy of formulating inclusion has to be inclusive itself. Our target is clear: it is financial inclusion for all. In Bangladesh, echoing our national aspirations, we have to work together to make finance work for all, to make our financial access universal. Let's work hard and together. Thank you.

Title: Speech at an International Conference on Development of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in Bangladesh: Sharing Asian Experiences
text: International Conference on Development of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in Bangladesh: Sharing Asian Experiences Dr. Atiur Rahman Governor, Bangladesh Bank Southeast University 5 March, 2016; 10.35 am -10.45 am Honorable Chair and Vice Chancellor of Southeast University, Prof. Dr. Anwar Hossain; special guests Dr. Cecep Effendi, DG-CIRDAP, Dr. Toufic Ahmad Choudhury, DG-BIBM, Prof. Dr. Mustafa K. Mujeri, ED-Institute of Inclusive Finance and Development; Guest of Honour Mr. Md. Rezaul Karim, Chairman, Board of Trustees, Southeast University Trust; Conference Director Prof. M. A. Hakim, and Co-Director Mr. Sukamal Sinha Choudhury; my fellow colleagues from Bangladesh Bank; university teachers; foreign guests and experts; CEOs of Banks and NBFIs; representatives from business chambers; SME Foundation; media representatives; distinguished guests; ladies and gentlemen; a very good morning to you all. At the very outset my profound homage to the memory of millions of martyrs who shed their blood for independence under the leadership of father of the nation. I would like to congratulate Southeast University for organizing this international conference on Development of MSMEs in Bangladesh. Unlike previous such conferences organized, todays is the first one arranged by a university, a sign of growing academic commitment to sustainable development of MSMEs. This conference offers an excellent opportunity for cross-country knowledge sharing from Asian Region. As you all appreciate, the MSME sector is the key driver of sustainable development. In Bangladesh, MSME accounts for 24 percent of total credit portfolio, 25 percent of total labor force, 32 percent of GDP, 40 percent of employment, and 80 percent of industrial jobs. We have a young population who needs more and better jobs. We have actively leveraged our financial system for empowerment initiatives in agriculture, MSME, women entrepreneurship, and green financing. These initiatives have created jobs and underpinned our domestic demand. The ever growing Domestic Demand is emerging as a second engine of our vibrant inclusive growth process. The first being export sector. Page 1 of 2 Bangladesh Bank has tried its best to provide regulatory and financial support to MSMEs. We worked on both demand and supply side constraints. Let me share a few of our initiatives: Bangladesh Bank has launched a dedicated department for SMEs in 2009. A target-based and marketfriendly lending approach was instituted in 2010. Alliance for Financial Inclusion recognized it as a global best practice for SME financing. Between 2010 and 2015, total SME lending more than tripled, reaching over 725 thousand recipients. You will also be happy to know that since 2010, credit disbursement always exceeded the target. Banks and financial institutions were required to ensure that small entrepreneurs receive at least 40 percent of their total SME portfolio. Bangladesh Bank has created its own refinancing facility to MSME women entrepreneurs, dedicating at least 15 percent of total lending. They can receive collateral-free loans up to Taka 2.5 million. We also have a policy of group-based lending of Taka 50,000 or above, targeting micro women entrepreneurs. Bangladesh Bank led the way by opening a Women Entrepreneurs Development Unit in its head office and branch offices. All banks and NBFIs have been encouraged to follow the lead. Recently, the MSME entrepreneurs of Bangladesh have created an Association called IamSMEofBangladesh. All this contributed significantly in achieving a robust, broad-based inclusive growth process in Bangladesh over the recent years. Last year 6.5 plus growth achieved. This year GDP growth could touch 7 plus. To conclude, we value MSME as one of the critical drivers in our upper middle income transition. The global financial crisis acutely reminded us we need two growth engines: export and domestic demand. Fortunately, we have been working on both of these engines by empowering MSME. I am confident your brainstorming will provide critical inputs to future policy design and implementation. I look forward to your active participation in this conference and receiving your guidance. I can assure you Bangladesh Bank will be a good listener. And I wish the conference a grand success. Thank you all. Page 2 of 2
